Preface to the Pioneers Georg Bühler and Johann Kirste, *pia memoria*

The *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī* is, alongside the approximately contemporary but much shorter *Dhātupradīpa* by the Buddhist Maitreyarakṣita, the oldest extant commentary on Pāṇini’s *Dhātupāṭha*. Aufrecht’s *Catalogus catalogorum* records two manuscripts of this work: (Bühler’s) *Report* (of a tour in Kaśmīr etc. XIX, and L(ala Mitra, *Notices of Skr. mss.*) 2588.
Both manuscripts were available to me for the edition; the first is now in the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (Deccan College MSS No. ...).

No. 287 of 1875–76), kindly mediated by the India Office Library in its original form; the second is a fine copy that Theodor Aufrecht had prepared from the Calcutta manuscript and which is now located in the IOL (Aufrecht Collection no. 80, cf. JRAS 1908, p. 1054–55).
The Kashmiri manuscript, hereafter designated as K, consists of 224 folios (measuring 17 × 13 cm) made of local paper, each containing between 11 and 16 lines per page, written in Śāradā script.

According to Mitra, the original of the Calcutta manuscript (C) was written on Kashmiri paper and thus likely originated from Kashmir as well. Despite numerous minor variations, both manuscripts ultimately go back to the same archetype, as evidenced, among other things, by the fact that they share a large lacuna extending from X, 140 to 189.
In addition to the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*, Bühler’s report lists under number 288 a *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇīsaṃketa* (S) in 57 folios, which was sent to me from Pune at my request.

This is an excerpt from the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*, in which, for each class of the *Dhātupāṭha* divided according to phonetic form and function into smaller groups (*praghaṭṭaka* or *paryaṭṭaka*), the first and last root of each group is always presented in the text.
VIII.

The commentary cited is usually complete, though occasionally abbreviated; for those roots treated in this manner, the Kṣ.S. thus serves as an additional manuscript source. The manuscript is inconsistent in quality, generally correct but in places highly corrupt.
It gives the impression that the scribe had before him a text that was partially destroyed in places and was unable to supplement the corrupted passages from another source.

When I had completed the printing of the text as far as it could be established by these aids, I happened upon a passage in the notes to Oka’s edition of the *Amarakośa*, in which he cites a quotation from the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī* that does not appear in this form in either of the two manuscripts available to me.

I turned to Poona for clarification and, through the kindness of the ever-helpful Professor Belvalkar, learned that Oka had passed away; that, indeed, a manuscript of the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī* had been found among his estate; and that it had been acquired by the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute and was available for loan under standard conditions.

Thus, through the kind mediation of the IOL, I also obtained this manuscript (no. 42 of 1919–24), a paper manuscript on 118 folios (29 × 13 cm) with 10 to 12 lines per page. It turned out that this manuscript (P) does not belong to the narrower family of the other two and also contains the roots X, 140–189.

The citations that Kṣīrasvāmin favors due to his great erudition (cf. his commentary on the *Amara-kośa*) are occasionally abbreviated in P. Otherwise, the text is for the most part consistent, such that one cannot speak of an independent recension. For Dramiḍa, P regularly writes Dramila. As for the manuscript in general...

It is very faulty, especially the grammatical citations, which are usually distorted beyond recognition. Nevertheless, it was of great value to me, both for supplementing the aforementioned lacuna and for verifying manuscripts K and C—which ultimately represent only a single source;
only through it was I able to provide a text that I considered satisfactory and reliable.
Where K and C differ, P almost always agrees with K, so that this manuscript appears to offer the more faithful tradition.
Breslau, June 1930. IX

[The chariot] beautiful with its waves, possessing a network of tinkling bells like honey-bees.
Victorious is the Lord Vighnajit, who raises his hand with its trembling, lotus-red fingertips,
lifting the surface of the world as if it were the banner of victory resulting from the destruction of insurmountable evils. (1)

Because it pacifies the imbalance of the [three] humors, this commentary on the *Sūtras* produced by Kṣīrasvāmī, titled the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*, nourishes the speech of the virtuous; it contains the collection of grammatical operations belonging to the various groups (*gaṇas*).

The properties of being *seṭ* or *aniṭ*, the voice (*upagraha*), and the result of the suffix *it*— those specific applications of verbal roots shown in each case within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* are [to be understood] from those specific instances. (3)
We have proceeded by that very path which was seen here by the Pārāyaṇikas, those who explain [the text], while closing our eyes like elephants;
for we did not examine the practical applications, since the Pārāyaṇikas were intent upon that alone.

Even though there are six types of verbal roots (*prakṛti*) that are not illustrated even when a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows—those where the followers of the *Pārāyaṇa*, Candra, and others have been bewildered—we have nonetheless resolved to explain those roots; oh, how profound they are! (5–6)

O brothers! You who were born from the Creator of the Universe, who were gradually refined by the sages, and who are words—though you have fallen into corruption through association with the unrefined, today the Goddess of Speech has, by my decree, made me her sole refuge. Therefore, [I shall restore] us by means of myself.
Six modes of livelihood have been ordained for you to follow the righteous path.

Now, for the purpose of understanding the accentuation, derivation, time [of application], and so forth of the eternal words well-known in both worldly and Vedic usage—such as *bhavati* and others—their exposition is undertaken by means of the conceptual division into base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus, the bases are set forth in aphorisms.

The root *bhū* is accented acute (*udātta*) in the sense of "being" (*sattā*). This citation as *bhū* without a case-ending is for the purpose of dispelling confusion, or else it follows the Vedic rule *suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), since "the Sūtras are like the Veda. Thus, *sattā* here is the state of being (*sato bhāvaḥ*), existence, the general meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha-sāmānya*). As they say: "It is eternal; it is the Great Self; the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth, denote it. When its sequence [of manifestations] is reached in particular instances, that very [Being] is designated as action (*kriyā*). They declare it to be both the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu-artha*)."

(Vākyapadīya I.3.34–35). This means that it is the *jāti* (universal). As the Vaiśeṣikas maintain: "The universal is of two kinds, the higher and the lower; the higher is *sattā* (Being), because its scope is the greatest. Furthermore:

"The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), when isolated and pure, is designated as *bhāva* (action/state). Likewise, "where another verb is not heard, there the verb *as* (to be) or *bhū* (to become) should be employed. For this very reason, and because of its auspicious nature, its employment is made first;
thus, one meaning has been demonstrated here in order to declare its status as denoting action.

It should be inferred from its usage, for roots have multiple meanings (cf. X, 392). Thus, the root *bhū* occurs in some instances in the sense of "existence": *asya bahūni dhanāni bhavanti* means "he has many riches," i.e., they exist; in other cases, it refers to the manifestation of what was previously non-existent: *kṣīrabhojinyāḥ putraḥ śrutandharo bhavati* means "a son of one who eats milk becomes a retainer of sacred learning," i.e., he is born; and in some cases, it refers to the sense of "becoming" (*saṃpad*), consisting in the transformation of something into that which it was not: *pataḥ aśuklaḥ śuklo bhavati* means "the cloth, being not white, becomes white," i.e., it comes into being as such.

Moreover, by the power of various prefixes (upasarga), such and such a meaning is manifested from a verbal root (dhātu): for instance, *prabhavati* has the sense of "lordship" (*svāmya*) and "first perception"; *parābhavati*, *paribhavati*, and *abhibhavati* signify "initial disparagement"; *saṃbhavati* signifies "birth"; *anubhavati* signifies "experience" (*saṃvedana*); *vibhavati* signifies "pervasion" (*vyāpti*); *ābhavati* signifies "attainment of a portion" (*bhāgāgati*); *udbhavati* signifies "emergence" (*udbheda*); and *pratibhavati* signifies "being a match" (*lagnakatva*).

Because *udātta* lacks the quality of being *anudātta*, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini] VII.2.10 (*ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt*) does not apply; thus, there is the presence of *seṭ*. By virtue of the rule *valādeḥ* (Pāṇini VI.1.40), when the suffix is *seṭ* or *aniṭ*, the root is designated as such by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*). Furthermore, because it lacks the markers for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) or the dual voice (*ubhayapada*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) applies according to *śeṣāt kartari* (I.3.78). And since there is no exception (*apavāda*), the default (*autsargika*) verbal suffix *śap* is applied: *bhavati*, *bhavan*, *bhavitā*.

Because the vowel *u* lacks the *anunāsika* (nasal) quality, it does not receive the technical designation *it*; for this very reason, [the rule] says "udātta" and not "udāttet. As the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) states: "The *it*-designation is traditionally taught for the roots *daridrā*, *jāgṛ*, *dīdhīṅ*, and for monosyllabic roots ending in *r* such as *ciri* and *jiri*, as well as for those ending in long *ā* such as *ṛṇauti*, *vevīṅ*, and *laḍi*; but it is not so taught for others. However, for roots like *edh* and the rest, because the initial *e* lacks the *anunāsika* quality, it does not receive the *it*-designation; furthermore, even if the *e* were elided in forms beginning with *a*, the *it*-designation would still not apply simply because they remain monosyllabic.

The *ātmanepada* ending is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) when there is a reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), and in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). For example: *vyatibhavate*. The meaning is that one performs the act of becoming which was intended to be performed by another. Indeed, in the case of reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), where there is an exchange of mutual actions, the singular number would not be appropriate.

In the case of a state (*bhāva*), however, there is only the singular number for the verb, because, since it refers to that which is not a substance (*asattvavṛtti*), it lacks number and so forth. If that is so, how can there even be a singular number? It is because of the unity of non-difference (*abhedaikatva*), even though the singularity that is the opposite of duality and so forth is absent. For the *Bhāṣya* states: "The singular number shall be made the general rule" (I.1.42). Thus: *caitreṇa bhūyate* ("Being is manifested by Caitra"). For this very reason, the second and first persons also do not exist: *bhūyate tvayā* ("Being is manifested by you"), *bhūyate mayā* ("Being is manifested by me").

"Experience" means that pleasure is felt. Because it functions here with a different meaning [than its primary sense], even an intransitive verb may become transitive, and even a transitive verb may become intransitive. As they say:
"Because a verbal root functions with a different meaning, and because [the action] is subsumed within the meaning of the root itself..."

"Due to conventional usage and because the object is not intended to be expressed, an action [denoted by] a root becomes intransitive despite having an object (*Vākyapadīya* III.7.87, p. 234 of the Benares edition). Because the root functions with a different meaning or a different effect, even though the verbal root is transitive, its meaning is rendered intransitive. For example: *bhāraṃ vahati* means "he carries" or "he lifts up"; *nadī vahati* means "the river flows. Intransitivity arises from the object being included within the meaning of the root, as in *jīv* in the sense of "sustaining life" (I.594)."

The root *jīv* (to live) is transitive; the root *nṛt* (to dance), which means "the shaking of limbs" (IV.9), is used as *nṛtyati*. In these cases, the actions known as "breathing" (*prāṇa*) and "shaking of limbs" (*gātra*) are already included within the meaning of the verbal root itself. Because the object is well-known [and not explicitly intended], the roots are treated as intransitive (*akarmaka*), as in: "The god rains" (*devo varṣati*). But it is not so here: "Pārtha rains arrows" (*Pārthaḥ śarān varṣati*). This is because the agent does not intend to express those two [actions]. Thus... [end of commentary]. 1 P tayorj. 2 P ṛkārādau 3 Cabhedatvāt 4 P addit: because it is taught first in the remainder [of the rules]. 5 KP vartamānād 14.
From a transitive verb as well, there is a verbal suffix (ākhyāta) in the sense of the abstract state (bhāva), as in: "it is not cooked here," "it is not eaten here."

And as for its being intransitive (*akarmakatva*): [one might ask] "What does it do? because expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) and the like cannot be further questioned; yet there certainly is the expression "What is it? [to which one replies] "It exists" (*bhavati*). True, but this [usage] is based on the action itself as its object (*kriyākhyakarman*), and does not depend on an external object, since the meaning understood is "it performs the act of becoming" (*bhavanaṃ karoti*). For action is the internal object (*antaraṅga-karman*) of all verbal roots; and for this very reason, grammarians record that adverbs [qualifying] actions function as objects: "The jar becomes beautiful. (*śobhanaṃ ghaṭo bhavati*)

Time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), distance (*adhvan*), and location (*deśa*) are unavoidable as objects (*karman*) for all verbal roots, because they pervade every action: e.g., *māsam āste* (he sits for a month), *godoham svapiti* (he sleeps during the milking of the cows), *krośam krīḍati* (he plays for the distance of a *krośa*), *Kurūñ śete* (he lies in the land of the Kurus). If it is asked, "How is the distinction between transitive and intransitive [verbs] maintained? we reply: it is based on the object that is a substance (*dravyakarman*). As stated in the *Karmayogamṛtataraṅgiṇī*:
"The suffix occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) after an intransitive root; it occurs in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) after a transitive root."

"The distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs is based on the object as a substance. Regarding this very point, Bhaṭṭa Śaśāṅkadhara offered the following "teacher's secret" (gurumuṣṭi): "The meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is twofold: *bhāva* and *kriyā*. For this very reason, it has been explained by the learned that 'the verbal root is the state of being (*bhāva*) and action (*kriyā*') (Kātantra III.1.9). Among these, *bhāva* is that which is to be accomplished by means of instruments (*sādhana*) that do not involve physical movement, whereas *kriyā* is that which is to be accomplished by means of instruments that do involve physical movement."

Therefore, a verbal root whose meaning is a state (*bhāva*) is intransitive (*akarmaka*), while a verbal root whose meaning is an action (*kriyā*) is transitive (*sakarmaka*); and "state" and "action" are synonymous, being not far removed from one another. Regarding whether the meaning of a verbal root is thus applicable or not, the wise are the authority here. This has been explained; let us now follow the subject at hand. There may be the pure form (*śuddhā prakṛtiḥ*), the causative (*ṇyantā*), the desiderative (*sanantā*), the causative followed by the desiderative (*ṇici sanparā*), the intensive (*yaṅantā*), and the intensive without the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅlugantā*); there is no other [form] besides these that serves a purpose. The pure form has already been illustrated. Regarding the causative suffix (*ṇic*, Pāṇini III.1.26): it causes someone who is becoming (*bhavantam*) to act; it means "he brings about" (*bhāvayati*), i.e., "he makes. As they say:

That which is eternal does not undergo becoming (*bhavana*), nor does that which is eternally existent; for these two possess no state of being produced (*kriyamāṇatva*), like a sky-flower or space. Therefore, those who know *bhāvanā* call "becoming" (*bhāvanā*) the instigating action (*prayojaka-kriyā*) of a thing that has attained the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to its manifestations (*bhūti*).
In the sense that "one should bring about the inner light," because [the root] has multiple meanings, the meaning is "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*).

1. *P* explains that the verb (*ākhyāta*) is the application (*prayoga*), such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) and so forth; *j* notes that in *K* and *C*, it reads "by which he acts. 2. *P* reads *āntaram*; *j* reads *spandamāna* for *spandana*. 3. *P* says "we say"; that which was stated by me myself in the *Amṛtataraṅgiṇī*. 4. *KC* says "right here. 5. *P* reads "of two-fold form" (*dvidhārūpa*). 6. *P* reads *abhavanam*; *j* reads *tenaiva bhūtikartṛtvam*. 7. *P* reads *bhāvānām*. 8. *I* [notes the variant]. 1. The verb is the application, such as "he cooks" and so forth; in *K* and *C*, it is "by which he acts. 2. *P*: internal; *j*: vibrating. 3. *P*: indeed, non-becoming; *j*: vibrating. 4. *P*: for non-becoming; *j*: by that very [means], the state of being the agent of manifestation. 5. *P*: of entities. 6. *KC*: right here. 7. *P*: of a dual nature. 8. *P*: vibration; *j*: vibrating. 9. *P*: indeed, non-existence; *j*: by that very [means], the agency of manifestation. 10. *P*: of things. 11. *I*: [variant].

In the *cur-ādi* group, *bhū* in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*) is *ātmanepada* when followed by *ṇic*: *bhāvayate padam*, meaning "he attains the state. According to *ā dhṛṣād vā* (Pāṇini III.1.264), in the alternative where *ṇic* is not applied: *utsāhād bhavate lakṣmīm*, "fortune arises from exertion. With the sense of "mixing" (*avakalkana*), *bhū* takes *ṇic*: *sarpiṣā saktūn bhāvayati*, meaning "he mixes the barley meal with ghee. From roots ending in *ṇi*, as well as *ās* and *śranth*, the suffix *yuc* is applied (Pāṇini III.3.107): *bhāvanā*. The suffix *san* is applied [to express desire] (Pāṇini III.1.7): *bubhūṣati*. By the rules *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini VII.2.11) and *sani grahaguhoś ca* (Pāṇini VII.2.12), the augment *iṭ* is not inserted. The suffix *u* is applied after roots ending in *san*, *āśaṃs*, and *bhikṣ* (Pāṇini III.2.168): *bubhūṣuḥ*.
From a root ending in *ṇic*, the desiderative suffix *san* is added: *bibhāvayiṣati*. By the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* (Pāṇini VI.4.80), the vowel *i* is substituted for the reduplication vowel;
this applies also to the intensive (*yaṅ*) suffix: *bobhūyate*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṅit*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used (Pāṇini I.3.12).

When there is elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*), one obtains *bobhavīti* or *bobhoti*. According to the rule *carkarītaṃ parasmaipadam* (Pāṇini III.1.6), these forms take the *parasmaipada* endings.

The specific details are as follows: *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini I.4.31) [defines] the *apādāna* [kāraka]: "The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat. By the rule *gāti-sthā-ghu-pā-ā-pā-bhū-bhā-jña-dṛś-aṃ kyaṣ* (I.3.20), the *sij* affix is elided; by *abhūt* [is illustrated]. By *bhuvo vug luṅ-liṭoḥ* (VI.4.88), there is an absence of *guṇa*: *abhūvan*. Precisely because of this restriction regarding the elision of *sij*, the *jus* substitution for *jhi* does not occur by the rule *sij-abhyasta-vidibhyaś ca* (III.4.109). [Examples: *babhūva*, *babhūvuḥ*.

By the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini I.2.6), there is the designation *kit*; by *bhavateraḥ* (VII.4.73), the substitution of *a* occurs for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of the root *bhū*. Some say that the substitution of *a* does not occur in the reflexive (*bhāva*) or passive (*karman*) voices: "It was desired to exist by you" (*bubhūve tvayā*), "He intensely desired happiness" (*anububhūve sukham*). By the rule *abhṛśādibhyo bhuvy acveḥ* (III.1.12), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied: one who is not intense becomes intense, *bhṛśāyate*. Regarding the rule *āmaḥ kṛñ anuprayujyate*, because *kṛñ* is used as a representative term (*pratyāhāra*) for the group of roots beginning with *kṛ*, there is the subsequent application of *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*: "He caused [it] to be done" (*kārayām-babhūva*).

The suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *bhū* when expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*): *brahmaṇo bhavanam* = *brahmabhūyam*. By the rule *bhavyageya* (Pāṇini III.4.68), it occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*): *bhavyaḥ pumān* ("a man who is to be"). By the rule *bhāvakarmaṇor aco yat* (Pāṇini III.1.97), the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of the abstract state or the object: *bhavyaṃ tvayā* ("it is to be done by you") and *anubhavyaṃ sukham* ("pleasure to be experienced"). By the rule *or āvaśyake* (Pāṇini III.1.125), the suffix *ṇyat* occurs in the sense of necessity: *bhāvyam* and *avaśyabhāvyam*. According to the Kāśikā on Pāṇini VI.1.144, the word *avaśyam* is elided before a *kṛtya* suffix. By the rule *grahādau* (Pāṇini III.1.134), we have *paribhāvī*; in the sense of the past, *abhibhāvī*.

Regarding the root *bhū*, the suffix *ṇa* should be stated as optional (Pāṇini III.1.143, Kāśikā): from *bhavati* comes *bhāvaḥ* (becoming) and *bhavaḥ* (being). By the rule *āśite bhuvaḥ karaṇabhāvayoḥ* (III.2.45), the suffix *khac* is applied: *āśito bhavaty anena* ("that by which one becomes satiated") results in *āśitaṃbhava odanaḥ* (rice that causes satiety); likewise, *āśitasya bhavanam* (the becoming of one who is satiated) results in *āśitaṃbhavo vartate*. By the rule *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau* (III.2.57), the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are applied when the agent (*kartṛ*) refers to those beginning with *āḍhya* (wealthy) in the sense of the *cvy-artha* (the process of becoming), provided the state of being [already] so does not exist: *anāḍhya āḍhyo bhavati* ("one who was not wealthy becomes wealthy") results in *āḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ* and *āḍhyaṃbhāvukaḥ*.
The suffix *iṣṇuc* is also applied by the rule *bhuvaś ca* (III.2.138); however, its Vedic character (*chāndasatvam*) is not desired here.
1. The subsequent application of *pratyāhāra* (Pāṇini 1.1.71). 2. *kavīnām* added by Patañjali (Kātyāyana). 6.
The first person plural (*I*).

(Vgl. Candra-S. I, 2, 93): *bhaviṣṇuḥ*. [From *glājisthaś ca* III, 2, 139]: *bhūṣṇuḥ*; because of the rule *kkṅiti ca* I, 1, 5, there is no *guṇa* substitution here, since the letter *g* has become a *cartva* substitute. [From *laṣapatapada* III, 2, 154] with the suffix *ukañ*: *bhāvukaḥ*. [From *jidṛkṣi* III, 2, 157] with the suffix *ini*: *paribhavī*. [From *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayoḥ* III, 2, 179] with the suffix *kvip*: *Svayaṃbhuḥ*, *pratibhūḥ*.

By the rule *viprasambhyo ḍvasaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini III.2.180): *vibhuḥ*, *prabhuḥ*, *saṃbhuḥ*. By the inclusion in the *mitadru* group (Kāśikā on III.2.180), [we have] *śaṃbhuḥ*. By the rule *ṝdor ap* (III.3.57): *prabhavaḥ*, *vibhavaḥ*, *anubhavaḥ*. By the rule *śriṇībhuvo ’nupasarge* (III.3.24), the suffix *ghañ* [is applied]: *bhāvaḥ*. From *nadyaprabhāvāt*, we have *prabhāvaḥ*. By the rule *parau bhuvo ’vajñāne* (III.3.55), the suffix *ghañ* is optionally [applied]: *paribhāvaḥ*, *paribhavaḥ*.

And after the agent or the object of the roots *bhū* and *kṛ*, when used in the sense of *cvī*, the suffix *khal* is applied [provided there is no difficulty]: "He becomes wealthy without difficulty by means of one who is not wealthy," or "It becomes easy for you to become wealthy. When a suffix beginning with *t* follows a word denoting a limb of the body, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied after the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*: "from the side..."

*bhūyāste*, having become by the side, [expresses] the state of being by the side (*pārśvatobhāva*). According to Pāṇini III.4.62, *nādhārthapratyaye cvyarthe*: *nānābhūyāste*, having become separate, [expresses] the state of being separate (*nānābhāva*); *dvidhābhūyāste*, having become twofold, [expresses] the state of being twofold (*dvidhābhāva*). According to Pāṇini III.4.63, *tuṣṇīmi bhuvaḥ*: *tūṣṇīṃbhūyāste*, having become silent, [expresses] the state of being silent (*tūṣṇīṃbhāva*). According to Pāṇini III.4.64, *anvacy ānulomye*: *anvagbhūyāste*, having become compliant, [expresses] the state of being compliant (*anvagbhāva*).

Examples of established meanings (*nirūḍha*): *bhūḥ*, *bhaṅktiḥ*, *bhasma*, *bhūtā grahāḥ*—derived from the sense "everything exists in this"; *bhavanam gṛham*—derived from the sense "it exists in this. Also, in the *Kṛt-pariśiṣṭa*: "In the future tense, [the suffixes] *gamya* and others [are used]" (III.3.3): *bhāvī*. From the root *bhū* with the suffix *kmin* (cf. *Uṇādi* IV.45): *bhūmiḥ*. From the roots *adi*, *śadi*, *bhū*, and *śubhi* with the suffix *krin* (*Uṇ.* IV.65): *bhūri*. From the roots *adi* and *bhū* with the suffix *ḍutac* (*Uṇ.* V.1): *adbhutam*. From the root *bhū* with the suffix *kyun* (cf. *Uṇ.* II.80): *bhuvanam* (1).

The root *edh* means "to grow. From here, thirty-five roots ending in *kattha* are both udātta-accented and anudāttet. Consequently, because the vowel *e* is udātta, this root is *seṭ* (Pāṇini VI.1.2.35); and because the vowel *a* is anudātta, it takes the ātmanepada by the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* (I.3.12): thus *edhate*, *edhamānaḥ*, *edhitā*. Furthermore, by the rule *etyedhatyūṭhsu* (VI.1.89), there is no substitution of the single substitute for the preceding form (*pararūpa*) when the prefix ends in *eṅ*: hence *praidhate*.

"Do not cause [the root] to reduplicate," [it is said]; because the subsequent rule applies, once the short vowel has been substituted, reduplication occurs by the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*). With the suffix *asun* (Uṇ. IV, 188), we have *edhas* meaning "fuel" (*indhanam*), as in the example: "The fire is well-kindled with *edhāṃsi*" (RV 1.145.4). Furthermore, according to the rule *avodaidhaudmapraśrathahimaśrathāḥ* (Pāṇini VI, 4, 29), there is also a form *edha-* ending in *-a* due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of the root *indh* with the suffix *ghañ*. Also, by the rule *guroś ca halaḥ* (Pāṇini III, 3, 103), the suffix *ap* is applied:
*edhā*. 1. *ksnuḥ* (K); 2. *yathaidhaḥ susamiddho 'gniḥ* (S). 7. [End of section].

*Spardha* means rivalry (*saṃgharṣa*). Rivalry is the desire to overcome another. "He rivals his brother" (*spardhate bhrātuḥ*) means he engages in rivalry with his brother. Regarding *spardhamānaḥ*, *spardhitā*, and "rivaling Kṛṣṇa" (*spardhamānaḥ sa kṛṣṇam*), the phrase "having reached Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ prāpya*) must be supplied as an ellipsis. By the rule *aṇau akartari ca* (Pāṇini I.3.88), the *parasmaipada* ending is used for the causative suffix (*ṇi*).

In *spardhayati*, when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), in the case where the *iṭ* augment is applied (*laṅ* with *iṭ*), we have *apāspardhīt*; in the case where *iṭ* is not applied, we have *apāspart*. By the rule *rāt sasya* (Pāṇini VIII.2.24), there is no elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). However, in the case of the *sip* ending, after the elision of *sip* by *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (VI.1.68), *jaś*-ness applies by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle; thus, for the *sip* ending, the substitution of *ru* for the root-final *dh* optionally applies by *daś ca* (VIII.2.74).

75) Thus, in the view that *r* is substituted [for *s*], by the elision of *r* (*rori*, VIII. 3. 14) and the lengthening (*dīrgha*, VI. 3. 111), the form is *apāspā*. In the view that *r* is not substituted, however, it is like a word ending in *ti*. From the rule *anudāttetaś ca halādeḥ* (III. 2. 149), the suffix *yuc* is applied: *spardhanaḥ*. By the rule *guroś ca halaḥ* (III. 3. 103), the suffix *ap* is applied: *spardhā*. Due to the irregularity (*bāhulaka*) of the rule, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied (III. 2. 138): "As if by another Himālaya mountain, which was eager to rival Mount Meru, the sky was supported" (3).

The root *gādh* is used in the senses of "establishing a foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*), "desire to obtain" (*lipsā*), and "binding" (*grantha*). "Foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) refers to a support; "desire to obtain" (*lipsā*) is the wish to acquire; "binding" (*grantha*) is the act of tying together. Its separate recitation [in the Dhātupāṭha] is for the sake of its rare usage. From *gādhate*, the past passive participle is *gādhitā*. Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ṛ* (ṛdit), the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāhrasvo nāglopiśāsvṛditām* (Pāṇini 7.4.2) does not apply, and thus there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel in the causative *caṅ* form: *ajagādhat*. *Agādha* means "bottomless," that is, "not touching the bottom" (*atalasparśa*). (4)

The root *bādh* means "to strike" (*roṭana*). Striking is resistance (*pratighāta*). [From the root: *bādhate*, *bādhitā*, *ababādhat*. [The agent noun] *bādhanaḥ* is formed with the suffix *ana*. By the rule *guroś ca hala* (Pāṇini III.3.103), the suffix *a* is applied to form *bādhā*. By the rule *bādhas tv aci* (Pāṇini III.1.134), and by the rule *arjidṛśikamyamipaṃsibādhām* (Uṇādi I.28), the suffix *ku* is applied; furthermore, there is the substitution of *ha* for *dha*: thus, *bāhuḥ* (the arm). (5)

The roots *nādh* and *nāth* are used in the senses of begging (*yācñā*), affliction (*upatāpa*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and benediction (*āśis*). Here, "affliction" means injury (*upaghāta*). Since the meanings of "begging" and "affliction" are actions (*kriyā*), while "sovereignty" and "benediction" denote the mere properties (*dharmamātra*) manifested [by the action], [the following examples illustrate this]: "the bell rings" (*ghaṇṭā dhvanati*), "the palace shines white" (*śvetate prāsādaḥ*), "it joins" (*saṃyujyate*), "it inheres" (*samavaiti*), "it exists" (*asti*), and "it throbs" (*gaṇḍati*). In these cases, qualities (*guṇa*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), existence (*sattā*), and substances (*dravya*)—though already established—are perceived through the verb as being in a state of being accomplished (*sādhyatvena*). As stated in the *Nirukta*: "One expresses a process consisting of prior and posterior stages by means of a verb. (*pūrvāparībhūtaṃ bhāvam ākhyātenācaṣṭe*)

"I" (I, 1). He does not protect (*nādhate*), he has not protected (*ananādhat*), and likewise he protects (*nāthate*). The *ātmanepada* ending occurs because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "the root *nāth* is used in the sense of wishing" (I, 3, 21, 7), and the genitive case follows from the rule (II, 3, 55): *sarpiṣo nāthate*, meaning "he wishes for ghee; may ghee be mine. In other cases, *nṛpaṃ nāthati* means "he begs of the king"; *ripuṃ nāthati* means "he torments the enemy"; *svāmī nāthati* means "the master rules. [The word] *nātha-* [is formed] by III, 1, 134. Because of the restriction that the root *nāth* (I, 3, 21, 7) takes the *ātmanepada* only when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the *ātmanepada* does not occur here: [with a prefix, it is *parasmaipada*].
Alas! This [tree] is seen to possess a pale luster with a dark center, like a *tinduka* fruit that has ripened slowly; indeed, it is fit for the touch of the beautiful hands of a Pulinda woman.
1. Also at VI, 1, 36 (Kāśikā). 2. *grathanaṃ* (P). 3. *pratīghātaḥ* (G). 4. *vartate* (K), with a marginal gloss: *lakṣyate pā°* (I⁸).

O daughter of the village chief, this herd of elephants, distressed by its plea for the gift of life, entreats you: do not cover your pair of breasts with the leaf-garments. These two [words] are not examples of the rule; for as they say: "All roots beginning with *ṇ* are taught with *ṇ* (ṇopadeśa), with the exception of *nṛt*, *nand*, *nard*, *nakk*, *naṭ*, *nādhṛ*, *nāthṛ*, and *nṝ*" (cf. Pāṇini VI.1.65 Bh.). Thus, according to the rule "of a root taught with *ṇ* following a prefix, even in a non-compound" (VIII.4.14), the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur here; therefore, one says *pranāthate*. [The aorist form is] *ananāthat* (6.7).

The root *dhā* means "to hold. [In the present tense: *dadhate*, *dadhete*, *dadhante*; in the absence of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*), [the forms are] *dādadhīti* and *dādaddhi*. According to the rule *dadhas tathoś ca* (Pāṇini VIII.2.38), the substitution of *bhaṣ* does not occur here, for that rule specifically refers to the root *dhā* (to suck). However, Kauśika has transposed the readings *dada* in the sense of "holding" (cf. 17) and *dadha* in the sense of "giving," citing: *dadate maṇim* (Nirukta I.2) and *dadhate dhanam arthibhyaḥ*. As to what is correct or incorrect in this matter, the learned scholars are the authority.

For we have achieved our purpose merely by demonstrating the differences of opinion; how could we possibly entertain doubt regarding the words of the foremost sages? For even we, when we stumble, would surely not be censured by others! (8) *Skud* means "in a downward slope. *Āpravaṇa* means "leaping over" or "bounding," or alternatively "an assault," according to Śrī Bhoja; however, [others] say it means "lifting up. According to Pāṇini VII.1.58 (*idito num dhātoḥ*), the augment *num* is added to the root: *skundate*. When the final *d* is dropped, it becomes *kunda* (cf. Uṇādi-sūtra IV.98). (9)

**śvidiśvaitye**: in the sense of the action of whiteness (*śvetaguṇakriyā*). *ṣvindate prāsādaḥ* ("the palace becomes white"). Although the quality of whiteness is already established (*siddha*), it is expressed by the verb as if it were something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), having a single form [with the action]. However, by the very nature of the power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*), even the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—though established—is expressed as something to be accomplished by the primary suffix (*kṛt*), just like "cooking" (*pāka*) and so forth. (10)

The root *vad* is used in the senses of salutation and praise. One salutes or greets one's teachers (*gurūn vandate*: *abhivādayate*); one salutes or praises the gods (*devān vandate*: *stauti*). [Derivatives: *vanditā* (one who has saluted). By Pāṇini III.2.173, *āru* is added to the roots *śri* and *vandi*: *vandāruḥ* (one who salutes). *Vandī* refers to a wandering bard (*maṅkhaḥ*), formed with the suffix *ṇini*. However, when formed with the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini III.1.134), *vandī* means a woman abducted by force. By the supplementary rule to Pāṇini III.3.107, the suffix *yuc* is added after the roots *ghaṭṭi*, *vandi*, and *vidi*: *vandanā* (salutation). In the *uṇādi* list, *vandākaḥ* denotes a wish-fulfilling tree.

*Bhadi* means "in what is auspicious (*kalyāṇa*) and in happiness (*sukha*). *Kalyāṇa* refers to excellence, welfare, auspiciousness, and so forth; *sukha* is the arising of one's own virtuous qualities. [The root] *bhand* is used in the sense of praising; [the forms] *bhandate*, *bhanditā*. By *Uṇ.* III, 130, *bhadantaḥ* denotes a mendicant (*śramaṇa*). In the *cur*-class (X, 74a), [one uses] *bhandayati*. (12) *Madi* is used in the senses of praise, joy (*moda*), intoxication (*mada*), and sleep (*svapna*). *Moda* is delight; *mada* is pride; by the mention of sleep, indolence (*ālasya*) is also indicated. Candragomin, however, stated only *madi* in the sense of dullness (*jāḍya*) (*Ca. Dh.* I, 315). [The forms] *mandate*, *manditā*. [The word] *mandaḥ* [is formed from this root]. By *Uṇ.* I, 39, *mandi-vāśi-mathi-* etc., the suffix *urac* is applied: *mandurā* is a stable for horses. *Iṣi-*... [text fragment]
1. Cf. *Kāryaprakāśa*, ed. BoSS 1917, p. 269. 2. P reads *āplavanam*. 3. P reads *sādhyaikyam*. 4. This is found in C and K; C includes the gloss *Māgadhaḥ*. 5. Cf. Hemacandra, *Uṇādisūtra* 34. 9I.

From the root *mad* ("to rejoice"), by the rule *timṛprathṛ...* (Uṇ. I, 52), the suffix *kirac* is applied to form *mandiram* ("palace"); by the rule *sphāyitañcivañci...* (Uṇ. II, 13), the suffix *rak* is applied to form *mandraḥ* ("deep sound"); from the root *mad*, [the suffix] *ru* is applied to form *madraḥ*, and likewise *madirā* ("wine"); by the rule *aṅghradimandibhya āran* (Uṇ. III, 134), *mandāraḥ* ("celestial tree") is formed; by the rule *kṛdarādayaś ca* (Uṇ. V, 41), *Mandaraḥ* ("Mount Mandara") is formed; by the rule *khajer ākaḥ* (Uṇ. IV, 13), the suffix *āka* is applied by way of extension (*bāhulakāt*) to form *mandākaḥ*; and when the possessive suffix *ini* (V, 2, 115) is added, *Mandākinī* is formed.

(13) The root *spadi* means "to move slightly. [Derivatives include: *spandate* ("he throbs"), *spanditā* ("one who throbs"); [gerund] *spanditum*; [agent noun] *spandanaḥ*; [action noun] *spandaḥ*. (14)

*klid* is used in the sense of lamenting (*paridevana*). Lamenting means grieving. From the root *klid*, [the form] *klindate* occurs because it is recited among the roots with the *udātta* accent (Pāṇini 1.3.72); however, *klindati* is not mentioned among those with the *svarita* accent. The use of the *parasmaipada* ending, even when the action benefits the agent, is for the sake of the specific rule (Pāṇini 1.3.72). (15)

The root *mud* means "joy. It forms *modate* [present], *muditaḥ* [past participle]. Because of the optionality of *kittva* by the rule *ralo vyupadhād dhalādeḥ saṃś ca* (Pāṇini I.2.26), one has both *muditvā* and *moditvā*. From the desiderative, *mumudiṣate* and *mumodiṣate*. By the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (III.1.135), *modanaḥ* [agentive noun]. From the same root with the suffix *ka*, *kumudam* [lotus]. With the causative suffix *ṇic*, *modayati*. With the suffix *ka*, *modakaḥ* [sweetmeat]. By the rule *iṣitimimadimudi-* (Uṇādi I.52), the suffix *kirac* gives *mudiraḥ* [cloud]. By the rule *mudigror gaggau* (Uṇādi I.127), *mudgaḥ* [mung bean]. By the rule *sphāyitañci-* (Uṇādi II.13), the suffix *rak* gives *mudrā* [seal]. In the *curādigaṇa*, *muda* in the sense of "contact" (*saṃsarga*) [X.200] forms *modayati*. (16)

The root *dada* means "to give. [In the present tense: *dadate*, *dadete*, *dadante*; [in the periphrastic future: *daditā*, *daditārau*, *daditāraḥ*. By the rule "na śasadadavādiguṇinām" (Pāṇini VI.4.126), the substitution of *e* for *a* (*etva*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) do not occur in the perfect tense (*liṭ*): *dadade* (17).

*ṣvada* and *svarda* mean "to taste. Tasting is licking with the tongue. One tastes for Caitra (*caitrāya svadate*). Because it is taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*), the rule *iṇkoḥ* [Pāṇini VIII.3.57] and *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* [VIII.3.59] applies, resulting in the substitution of *ṣ*: *asiṣvadat*. However, due to the restriction *stautiṇyor eva ṣaṇi* [VIII.3.61], the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur in the desiderative: *sisvadiṣate*, *sisvādayiṣati*—for by the rule *saḥ svidisvadisahīnāṃ ca* [VIII.3.62], there is no substitution of *ṣ*. The word *svadanaḥ* is formed with the suffix *uṇ* according to the rule *kṛvāpājimisvadityādinā* [Uṇādi I.1].

*svāduḥ*; in the *cur*-class (X), *ṣvada* is listed as "to conceal" (263): *svādayati*. *Svard-* is not taught with an initial *ṣ* (*aṣopadeśa*), according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*): "The roots beginning with *sa*, followed by *a* or a dental, are taught with an initial *ṣ*, as are *smi*, *sviḍ*, *svad*, *svañj*, and *svap*, excluding *sṛp*, *sṛj*, *stṛ*, *stṛ*, *styai*, *sekṛ*, and *sṛ*" (cf. VI.1.64 Bh.): *svardate*, *asisvardat* (18. 19). *Urda* means "measuring" and "playing. Its primary meaning is "measurement" (*māna*). According to Durga, because of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the root list], it also means "tasting. *Ūrdate*; [the lengthening of the penultimate vowel] occurs by the rules "lengthening of the penultimate *u* or *r*" and "also before a consonant" (VIII.2.76, 77). (20)

1. All manuscripts read *modayate*. 2. *so* (*guṇinām*) all manuscripts. 3. P reads *bhavataḥ*. 4. P reads *asaśvadat*. 5. An error of Kṣ.; the lengthening of *u* follows Aṣṭādhyāyī VIII.2.78: *upadhāyāṃ ca*. 10. I.

The roots *kurd*, *gur*, and *d* are used exclusively in the sense of playing (*krīḍā*). Here, the restriction regarding their meaning serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that verbal roots possess multiple meanings. From *kūrdate*; because of the teaching of the long vowel in *sphūrj* (I.254), they say that the lengthening of the penultimate vowel before *r* and *v* is not obligatory: hence *kurdate*; *kurdanaḥ*. *Gurdanaḥ*. In place of *gurd*, the followers of Durga read *khurd*. In place of *gud*, some read *gudh*; however, the Teacher explained that there are two roots for the act of playing with the anus, namely *gud* and *krīḍ* specifically for the movement of the anus. Regarding this, the learned authorities say: "That is not so."
*gudate*, *jugudiṣate*, *jugodiṣate*; [the root] *gud* [is mentioned] in [Dhātupāṭha] III.1.135.

*ṣūda* means "to flow" (*kṣaraṇe*). Flowing is emission (*nirasana*). [Present: *sūdate*; [past participle: *nisūditaḥ*. In the *cur*-class (X), *ṣūda* means "to cause to flow out" (*niḥsrāvaṇe*): *nisūdayati*. In the *nandya*-class (III.1.134), *sūdanaḥ*; in the *pacādi*-class (III.1.134), *sūdaṭ*: *sūdaḥ*; [agentive suffix] *sūdī*; and because of the rule *sūdadīpadīkṣāṃ ca* (III.2.153), the suffix *yuc* does not apply: *sūditā* (25).

*Hrād* is used in the sense of an indistinct sound. "Indistinct" means having letters that are not very clear. A drum *hrādate*. In the term *nūpurahrādaḥ*, the vowel is shortened by virtue of its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group (Pāṇini VI.3.109): thus *hradaḥ*. (26) *Hlādī* is used in the sense of pleasure (*sukha*) and, because of the word *ca* ("and"), also in the sense of an indistinct sound. [The root] *hlādate*. With the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it becomes *āhlāditaḥ*; there is no *iṭ* augment in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) due to the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām* (VII.2.14). In the past participle, the vowel of *hlād* is shortened by *hrasvaḥ* (VI.4.95): *prahlannaḥ*. It is also desired in the feminine abstract noun (*ktin*): *prahlattiḥ*. (27) *Śvāda* is used in the sense of tasting (*āsvādana*). [The root] *svādate*. *Svādanaḥ*. (28)

The root *pard* occurs in the sense of a contemptible sound; it refers here to the sound of the anus. Others, considering the downward wind to be soundless, say it means "without sound. [From the root] *pard*, [we have] *pardanaḥ*. According to Uṇādi-sūtra III.80, *pṛdākuḥ*—meaning a snake—is derived from *pard*, with the prefix *ni*, vocalization (*prasāraṇa*), and the elision of the vowel *a*. (29)

The root *yat* is used in the sense of "exertion" (*prayatna*). One exerts oneself (*yatate*). Having exerted oneself (*yatitvā*); because it is marked with the *īt* indicatory letter, there is no insertion of *iṭ* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām* (Pāṇini VII.2.14): *yattaḥ*. By the rule *yajayācayataviccha* (III.3.90), the suffix *naṅ* is applied: *yatnaḥ*. By the rule *yater vṛddhiś ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra II.98), the suffix *ṛn* is applied: *yātā*, meaning "the husband's brother's wife" (*devarabhāryā*); dual: *yātarau*. In the *curādi* group, *yata* is used in the senses of "humiliation" (*nikāra*) and "embellishment" (*upaskāra*): *yātayati* (30).

The roots *yutṛ* and *jutṛ* mean "to shine. One says *yotate*; [the aorist] *ayuyota*. However, Kauśika considers *juti* and *jyuti* to be for the sake of establishing the word *jyotis* (light); and *jyotis* is established by the rule *dyuteḥ asij ādeś ca jaḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra II.111). Durga states that *jutir* is used in the sense of *ajutat* and *ajotīt* (Pāṇini III.1.57). (31–32) The roots *vithṛ* and *vethṛ* mean "to entreat" (*yācane*). One says *vethate*; [the imperfect] *avivethat*. There is a distinction regarding the *kit* suffixes: *vithitaḥ* and *vethitaḥ*. However, Kauśika says that *yātana* is for the sake of establishing *vithura*, but that is not correct, because it is already established by the rule *vyatheḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ kic ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra I.40). (33–34)
1. K and P: *anekārthatva-liṅgam*; 2. P: *kurdasthāne*; 3. P: omits; 4. P: *nirāse*; 5. All manuscripts read *so*. 11. I.

The root *śrath* means "to loosen. Looseness (*śaithilya*) is a lack of firmness. According to the rule stating "and [the root] *śranth*" (VI, 4, 122, Kāśikā), the substitution of *e* for *a* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur; for in that rule, by the inclusion of the term *śranthi*, there is the selection of the root *śranth* in the sense of "binding" or "composing" (cf. IX, 39, 41): *śaśranthe*. Others also say this regarding this case. Due to the presence of the marker *it*, there is no elision of the nasal (cf. VI, 4, 24). As for the example *śrethe*, the author of the *Vṛtti* was mistaken.

By the rule *nopadhāt thaphāntād vā* (Pāṇini I.2.23), the suffix *ktvā* is optionally *kit*: *śranthitvā* or *śrathitvā*. [The words] *śithilaḥ* and *ślathaḥ* [are derived from the root] *grathi* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*). Crookedness means both deceitful movement and binding. [Thus one says: *granthati*, *grathyate*; *granthanā*; *grathitvā* or *granthitvā*; *grathitaḥ*. By the rule *khanikaṣyañjyasivasi* (Uṇādi IV.139), the word *granthiḥ* is formed. In the *kry-ādi* class, the roots *śrantha* and *grantha*—meaning "to string together" (*saṃdarbha*)—are both *udātta*-accented and transitive (cf. IX.39, 41).

The forms *śrathnāti* and *grathnāti*, as well as *śrathyate* and *grathyate*, undergo the elision of the nasal according to Pāṇini VI.4.24 (*aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*), resulting in *śrethuḥ* and *grethuḥ*. The two forms *śaśranthuḥ* and *jagranthur* belong to the *curādi* class; according to X.264 (*ā dhṛṣād vā*), they optionally take the causative suffix (*ṇic*), yielding *śranthayati* and *śranthati*, or *granthati* and *granthayati* (X.294).

In the case of the *karmakartṛ* (the agent as the object), when the suffix *ṇi* follows roots beginning with *kṛ*, the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur according to Pāṇini 3.1.90 (*śranthi-granthi-brūñ-ātmanepadākarmakāṇām*). Thus: *śranthate* "he unties himself," *śrathnīte*, *aśranthiṣṭa*; *granthate*, *grathnīte*, *agranthiṣṭa*.

(36) The root *kattha* is used in the sense of "boasting" (*ślāghā*). Boasting is the attribution of qualities one does not possess. [Examples: *katthate*; having boasted (*katthitvā*); "one who boasts" (*vikatthanaḥ*). By the rule Pāṇini 3.2.143 (*vau kaṣalasakattha*), the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied: "one who is boastful" (*vikatthī*). (37)

Those roots that have an acute accent (*udātta*) on their final vowel are *anudāttet*. This has already been explained. In the *Bhvādi* class, the first section was taught as a single unit because it begins with roots ending in the *tavarga* (dental stop) group. Thus, one should follow the respective [rules] accordingly. 36.

The root *ita* means "to go continuously. Going continuously is constant motion (*nityagati*). From this point on, there are thirty-five roots that are udātta, possess the *iṭ* augment, and have an udātta vowel, and they take the *parasmaipada* endings. *Atati*, *atan*, *atitā*. Because of the rule *na gatihiṃsārthebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini I.3.15), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings do not occur in the sense of reciprocal action (*vyatihāra*); thus, one does not say *vyatyatate*. From the rule *atyavicamītyasac* (Uṇādi III.117), the suffix *asac* is added: *atasī*. From the rule *ṛtanyañjivanyañjītyathin* (Uṇādi IV.2), the suffix *ithin* is added: *atithiḥ*. From the rule *ajyatibhyām iṇ* (Uṇādi IV.130), the suffix *iṇ* is added.

*Ātiḥ* means "bird"; and [from the root *pad*] with the suffix *i*: *padātiḥ* ("pedestrian"), where *pādasya* becomes *pad* before *ājyati* (cf. Pāṇini VI.3.52). From the roots *sā* and *tan*, with the suffixes *manin* and *maniṇ* (cf. Uṇādi IV.152), [we have]: *ātmā*. (38) 1. Mādhava quotes this passage and adds: "In this context, 'the author of the Vṛtti' refers to the author of the Dhātuvṛtti. 2. Cf. Kāśikā on Pāṇini III.1.89 and Candra-Sūtra I.4.100.112.

The root *cit* means "to perceive" (*saṃjñāna*). Perception is consciousness (*saṃvitti*); it perceives (*cetati*). According to Pāṇini VII.2.14, the augment *iṭ* is not applied before the suffix *niṣṭhā*: thus we have *cittam* and *cittiḥ*. Alternatively, by Pāṇini I.2.26 (*ralo vyupadhād dhalādeḥ saṃś ca*), there is optionally *kittva* [before the suffix *ktvā*]: hence *cititvā* or *cetitvā*; and *cicitiṣati* or *cicetiṣati*. With the suffix *kvip* (Pāṇini III.3.94, Kāśikā), we have *cit*; with the suffix *asun* (Uṇādi IV.188), *cetas*. By Pāṇini III.1.138 (*anupasargāl limpavinda-*), the suffix *śa* is added: *cetayaḥ*. In the *curādi* class, *cita* means "perception" (*saṃvedana*) (cf. ...).
X, 135) Thus, it is *ātmanepada*: *cetayate*, *cetanaḥ*, *cetanā* (39).

*Cyuti* means "pouring out" (*āsecanam*). Pouring out is a slight sprinkling. [From the root] *cyut*: *cyotati*, *cyotitā*. According to Pāṇini III, 1, 57, *irito vā*, there is optionally the suffix *aṅ* in the *luṅ* tense: *acyutat* or *acyotīt*. [The gerunds] *cyutitvā* or *cyotitvā*; [the desiderative] *cicyutiṣati* or *cicyotiṣati* (I, 2, 26) (40).

*Ścyuti* means "oozing. Oozing is flowing. Here, *ś* is palatal; for if it were dental-initial, in the case of *ṣaṭ ścyotanti*, because the substitution of *ś* for *s* would be considered unestablished (*asiddha*), the augment *dhuṭ* would apply by the rule *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ* (Pāṇini VIII.3.29). The Draviḍas also say that the root is *cuti*: *cotati*, *acutat*, *acotīt*. However, Kauśika considers the root *ścuti* to have the letter *y* as its penultimate: *ścotati*. (41)

The roots *kuth*, *puth*, and *luth* signify injury (*hiṃsā*) and affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Injury is the harming of living beings; affliction is distress. *kunthati*, *kunthyate*; because it has *n* as its penultimate letter and ends in *th* or *ph*, [the suffix] *kit* is applied by rule I.2.23: *kunthitvā*, *kuthitvā*. In the *kryādi* class, *kunth* means "to join" (cf. IX.42): *kuthnāti*. *punthati*, *lunthati*. *manthati*, *mathyate*; past passive participle *mathitam*; gerund *manthitvā*, *mathitvā*; from *manth* (Uṇ. IV.11), with the suffix *ini* and *kit*: *mathin*, *manthāḥ*.

By *aci* (Pāṇini III.1.134), *manthaḥ*; by the *uṇādi* suffixes, *manthānaḥ*; and [the suffix] *śānac*. In the *jvalādi* group, for the root *math-* in the sense of "churning" (1.90): *mathati*, *mathaḥ*, *māthaḥ*. In the *kryādi* group, for *manth-* in the sense of "churning" (IX.40): *mathnāti*, *mathyate*. According to the followers of Durga, there are also *mathi* and *māthi*: *manthati*, *manthyate*, *mānthati*, *mānthyate* (44–47).

The root *ṣidhu* means "to go. From it come *sedhati*, *siṣedha*, and *parisedhati gām*—the latter meaning "he causes [the cow] to go. Regarding the root *sedh* in the sense of "going," there is no substitution of *ṣ* according to Pāṇini VIII.3.113; however, in other senses, such as *niṣedhati pāpāt* ("he wards off evil"), there is the substitution of *ṣ* by Pāṇini VIII.3.65. Because of the specific mention of *sedha* [in the rule], the substitution does not apply to the root *sidh* (Pāṇini IV.83), as in *nisidhyati*. According to Pāṇini VII.2.56 (*udito vā*), the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ*.

*siddhvā*, *sidhitvā*, *sedhitvā*: there is optionally *kittva* by rule I.2.26 (*ralo vyupadhāt...*). By rule VII.2.15 (*yasya vibhāṣā*), there is no *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* [past participle]: *siddhaḥ*; however, in the reading where the suffix lacks the *anubandha*, it is *sidhitaḥ*. There is optionally *kittva* by rule I.2.26 (*ralo vyupadhāt...*): *sisidhiṣati*, *sisedhiṣati* (48). 1. P adds *ṇau*. 2. All manuscripts read this. 3. Cf. Mādhava on *mantha* in the sense of "churning" (I.85): *manthānaḥ*; [the suffix] *ānac* is added by Uṇādi-sūtra II.89 (*samy ānac stuvah*), and by virtue of the irregularity (*bāhulaka*), it is also applied here. 4. From the reading of P. 13.

The root *ṣidh* is used in the sense of "teaching" (*śāstra*) and "auspiciousness" (*māṅgalya*). "Teaching" refers to instruction concerning the scriptures, while "auspiciousness" refers to an action pertaining to auspiciousness. In this specific context, it is marked with the *ū*-diacritic (*ūdita*); however, in other meanings, it is not so marked. Because it is *ūdita*, the rule *svaratisūti* (Pāṇini VI.1.44) applies, allowing for the optional *iṭ* augment: *seddhā* (the meaning being "he has taught"), or *sedhitā*. In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), the *iṭ* augment is compulsory by the rule *krādiniyamāt* (Pāṇini VII.2.13): *siṣidhiva*. By the restrictive rule *vasvanekājādghasām* (Pāṇini VII.2.67), there is no *iṭ* augment after the suffix *kvasu*: *siṣidhvān*.

The root *ṣidhu* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhi*) is without *iṭ* in the *divādi* class (IV.83): *sidhyati*, *seddhā* (49). The root *khādṛ* in the sense of "eating" (*bhakṣaṇa*): *khādati*, *acakhādat* (VII.4.2). Because of the prohibition [of the *karmasaṃjñā*] for the roots *ad*, *khād*, *nī*, and *vah* (I.4.52, 5), there is no designation as the object (*karmasaṃjñā*); thus: *khādayati piṇḍīṃ caitreṇa* ("He causes Caitra to eat the ball"). By the rule *nindahiṃsakliśakhāda* (III.2.146), the suffix *vuñ* is applied: *khādakaḥ* (50). The root *khada* in the senses of "firmness" (*sthairya*) and "injury" (*hiṃsā*): *khadati*. By the rule *aci* (III.1.134), the feminine form is *khadā*. By the rule *ajiraśiśira* (Uṇ. I.54), *khadiraḥ* (51) is formed.

The root *bad* is used in the sense of steadiness (*sthairya*). It is conjugated as *badati* and *badyate*. *Badara* refers to a jujube fruit and the like; *badau* [is its dual]. *Badira* begins with a labial. However, the root *vad*, meaning "to speak articulately" (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*), begins with a dental and a labial: it is conjugated as *vadati* and *udyate*. Kaṇṭha says *padeti*; [he gives the example] *padati* (52).

The root *gad* is used in the sense of "distinct speech. From *gadati*, by Pāṇini VIII.4.17 (*nergada*), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the initial of the prefix: *praṇigadati*. By Pāṇini III.1.100 (*gadamadacara...*), the suffix *ya* is applied to form *gadya*. Alternatively, by Pāṇini III.3.64 (*nau gadanadapaṭha...*), the suffix *ap* is applied to form *nigadaḥ*. With the suffix *ghañ*, it becomes *nigādaḥ* (Pāṇini III.3.18). It appears as *gadā* in the *bhidādi* group (Pāṇini III.3.104), and as *gadaḥ* with the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini III.1.134).

The reduplication in *carcara*, *varvara*, *gadgada*, *ghurghura*, *gharghara*, *jarjara*, *jliarjharaka*, *karkara*, *bharbhara*, *sarsara*, *budbuda*, *murmura*, *narmara*, *dardara*, *purpura*, and so forth, occurs twice according to Pāṇini VI.3.109, because they belong to the class beginning with *pṛṣodara*. In the *curādi* group, the roots *stan* and *gad* (X.313–314) end in *-a*: thus, *gad-ayati* (53). The root *rad* means "to scrape" (*vilekhane*). Scraping is tearing out. Thus, *radati*. With the suffix *lyu* (III.1.134), we have *radanaḥ* (teeth); with the suffix *ac* (III.1.134), we have *radaḥ* (tooth) (54).

The root *ṇad* means "inarticulate sound. From *nadati*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by rule VIII.4.14 (*upasargād asamāse ’pi*), resulting in *praṇadati*. By rule III.3.64 (*nau gadanada*), the suffix *ap* is optionally added, yielding *ninadaḥ* or *ninādaḥ*. In the *pacādi* group (III.1.134), the suffix *naṭ* is applied, giving *nadaḥ* (a river) and *nadī* (a river). From Uṇādi III.52 (*anuṅ nadeś ca*), the suffix *anuṅ* is added to form *nadanuḥ*. In the *curādi* group (X.238), it has the sense of "causing to shine" (*bhāsārtha*), as in *nādayati*. (55)

The root *ard* means "to go" and "to beg. It is conjugated as *ardati*. Some authorities state that it also means "to torment": thus *arditaḥ*, meaning "tormented" or "afflicted. From this root, by the rule *nuḍ dvihalaḥ* (Pāṇini VII.4.71), the augment *nuṭ* is added in the perfect tense (*liṭ*): *ānardha*. By the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* (Pāṇini VI.1.3), the letter *r* is not reduplicated. [Note: 1. *vāsarādau*; cf. Uṇādisūtra III.131 comm. and 132. 2. All manuscripts read *°pūrvādi°* (or similar); however, it should be *°purpurādi°*; cf. Hemacandra’s Uṇādivṛtti 10 I.14.]

*ardidiṣati*. [The suffix] *lyuḥ* (Pāṇini III.1.134): *janārdanaḥ*. Regarding the rule *ardeḥ saṃnivibhyaḥ* (VII.2.24), there is no *iṭ* augment in the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes]: *samarṇṇaḥ*. Regarding *abheś cāvidūrye* (25): *abhyarṇe sene āsāte*. In the *curādi* [class], *arda* is listed as meaning "to injure" (X.285): *ardayati* (56). *narda* and *garda* mean "sound. [Examples: *nardati*, *praṇardati*. The status of having a nasal (*ṇ*) as the initial element of the root (*ṇopadeśatvam*) is not mandatory because it is merely enumerated [in the list of exceptions] (VI.1.65 Bh.). [Examples: *gardati*. From the roots *śṝ*, *kṛ*, *śal*, *kali*, and *gard*, the suffix *abhac* is added (Uṇādi III.122): *gardabhaḥ* (57, 58).
The root *tṛd* is used in the sense of piercing (*hiṃsā*). It forms *tardati*. *Vitardikā* refers to a raised platform or altar (*vedī*).

(59) The root *kard* is used in the sense of a contemptible sound. It forms *kardati*. According to the rule *kalikardyor amaḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra IV.84), the word *kardamaḥ* (mud) is derived. (60) The root *khurd* is used in the sense of a biting creature (*dandaśūka*). "A biting creature" refers to an action characterized by reprehensible biting; or, when the mere act of biting is to be expressed, the mention of the instrument (*sādhana*) is for the purpose of including it within the usage where the instrument is predominant. Even if the reading were *danta-śūka*, it would ultimately result in the same meaning: "one whose teeth are like needles. It forms *khardati*. (61)

*Ati* and *adi* mean "binding. From *antati*, we have *ānanta*; from *antati*, *antakaḥ*. From *andati*, *ānandaḥ*. Regarding *andū-dṛnbhū* (cf. Uṇādi-sūtra I, 95), *andūḥ* means "an anklet for the foot. The reading *adi* is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*); others read *ati* as "binding. *Intāṃcakāra* (62, 63).

*Idi* means "supreme sovereignty" (*paramaiśvarya*). Supreme sovereignty is the activity of supreme lordship. From *indati*, [we derive] *indraḥ* (64) by the rule *ṛjrendrāgravajra* (Uṇādi-sūtra II, 28), which prescribes the suffix *rak*.

*bid* means "to go to a certain place" (*ekadeśagata*). [In the sense of] the action of going to a specific location: *bindati*. *Binduḥ*: by the rule of diversity (*bāhulakāt*, Pāṇini III.3.1 or VIII.3.92), the suffix *u* is applied. *Vinduḥ* and *icchuḥ* (Pāṇini III.2.169) are irregular forms (*nipātanam*) derived from the root *vid* (II.55).

*ṇidi* means "in contempt" (*kutsāyām*). *Nindati*. *Nindā*. By the rule *niṃsanikṣānindām* (VIII.4.33), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*: *praṇinditā* / *praninditā*. By the rule *nindahiṃsa* (III.2.146), the suffix *vuñ* is applied: *nindakaḥ*. (66)

The root *ṭunadi* means "to prosper" (*samṛddhau*). It takes the form *nandati*. From the causative (*ṇyantāt*), the suffix *lyuḥ* (III. 1. 134) is applied: *nandanaḥ*. From the simple root with the suffix *ac* (III. 1. 134): *Nandaḥ*. In the group beginning with *prajñā-* (V. 4. 38), we have *nāndaḥ* and *nāndī*. With the suffix *ini* (Uṇ. IV. 6; V. 2. 115): *Nandī*. With the suffix *ṇvul* (III. 1. 133): *nandakaḥ*. With the suffix *athuc* (III. 3. 89): *nandathuḥ*. According to Uṇādi-sūtra II. 99, which states "after *nañ* and *nandi*, [the suffix] *ṛn*": *nanāndā* (a husband’s sister), and *nanāndarau*. [Also from] *ruhinandijīvi-* (Uṇ.).

(III, 127) Thus, from the root *nand* with the suffix *jhac*: *nandayantaḥ*. By [Pāṇini] VI, 4, 55, *ay* is substituted for the suffixes *āman*, *tṛ*, *ālu*, and *āyya*; by [Uṇādi] III, 29, *itnuc* is added to the causative (*ṇi*): *nandayitnuḥ*. *Nandā* is the sixth lunar day (*tithi*). 1. C reads *vedikā*. 2. P adds: from the roots *nṛt* and *śṛdh*, the suffix *kū* is applied (Uṇ. I, 93): *andūḥ* (cf. the commentary on Uṇ. I, 95). 3. P reads *pādakaṭakaḥ*. 4. C reads *so* (for *ran*); K and P omit this. 5. P reads *patyuḥsvasā*. 6. P omits this.

15. *cad* [is used] in the senses of gladdening (*hlādana*) and shining (*dīpti*). *candati*. By [the rule] *rak* (Uṇ. II, 13): *candraḥ*, *candrikā*. By [the rule] *iṣitimimadimudikhidibhidichidimandicandi* (cf. Uṇ. I, 52), [the suffix] *kirac*: *candiraḥ*. By [the rule] *bahulam anyatrāpi* (Uṇ. II, 78), [the suffix] *yuc*: *candanam*. By [the rule] *cander ādeś ca cho* (Uṇ. IV, 218), *suṃś ca*: *chandaḥ* [referring to] the *gāyatrī* and other meters. Due to the principle of "abundance" (*bāhulaka*), it is also [found] ending in *-a*: "one's own nature follows the inclination" (68). *trad* [is used] in the sense of movement (*ceṣṭā*). *trandati* (69).

The roots *kadi*, *kradi*, and *kladi* mean "to call" and "to weep. From *kandati*: *kandaḥ* ("root"), *kanduḥ* ("place of cooking"), *kandukaḥ* ("ball"), *kandarā* ("cave"). From *krandati*: *ākrandaḥ* ("shout"); with the suffix *lyu* (Pāṇini III.1.134): *saṃkrandanaḥ* ("Indra"). The three roots *kadi*, *kradi*, and *kladi* all belong to the *ghaṭādi* group (Dhātupāṭha 70–72), which are *ātmanepada* verbs meaning "to be distressed" (I.809–811).

*klid* is used in the sense of lamenting (*paridevana*). It means "he laments" (*klindati*), that is, "he grieves. The first [root] is *anudātta*: *klindate*; *klindyate*, *klinditaḥ*. In the *divādi* class, *klidū* is used in the sense of becoming moist (*ārdrabhāva*): *klidyati*, *klidyate*, *klinnaḥ*. *śundha* is used in the sense of purification (*śuddhi*). *śundhati*; *śudhitaḥ*. In the *divādi* class, *śudha* is used in the sense of cleansing (*śauca*): *śudhyati*, *śuddhaḥ*. In the *curādi* class, *śundha* is used in the sense of performing purification (*śaucakaraṇa*): *śundhayati*, *śundhitaḥ*. [These roots] end in an *udātta* vowel and have an *udātta* *it*-augment. (71)

*Śīkṛ* means "to sprinkle. From here until the end of *ślāghā* (DhP 118), forty-three [roots] are udātta, take the *iṭ* augment (*seṭ*), are anudātta, and are ātmanepada. Examples: *śīkate*, *śīkitā*, *aśiśīkat*. *Śīkanam*, *śīkā*. By *artikamibhrami* (Uṇ. III, 132), we have *śīkaraḥ*. In the cur-ādi class, *śīka* means "to endure" (X, 283): *śīkayati*, *aśīśikat*. *Lokṛ* means "to see. Examples: *lokate*, *alulokat*. *lokaḥ*, *ālokaḥ*. In the cur-ādi class, *lokṛ* has the meaning of "shining" (X, 236): *vilokayati*. *Ulūka* [is derived] from "looking upwards" (cf. Uṇ. IV, 41 and Hem. Uṇ. 61). (76)

The root *ślak* means "to collect," "to join together," or "that which is being joined. It takes the form *ślākate*. *Śloka* refers to a verse (*padya*) and fame (*yaśas*) (cf. *Amarakośa* III, 3, 2).
(77) The roots *drekṛ* and *dhrekṛ* mean "excitement of sound" or "arrogance of sound. Candra says they mean "increase" (*vṛddhi*) (Ca. Dh. I, 336). [Examples: *drekate*, *adidrekat*; *uddrekaḥ*.
(78–79) The root *rekṛ* means "doubt" (*śaṅkā*). Here, doubt means uncertainty (*saṃśaya*). [Example: *rekate*. They say *āreka* means "uncertainty" (*saṃśaya*). (80)

*śīkṛ*, *sekṛ*, *srekṛ*, *śraki*, and *ślaki* have the meaning of "motion. Because of a difference in meaning, *śikṛ* is recited again [in the list]; for this very reason, Candragomin did not study it. Others [add] "delighting" (*āhlādana*) as the meaning. [Note: Pāṇini adds "delighting" (*āhlādana*) and "gladdening" (*ānandana*).]

16. They recited *ṣekṛ* with an initial *ṣ* optionally for the sake of the grammatical operations pertaining to roots taught with an initial *ṣ*: *sekate*, *asisekat*, *asiṣekat*. Here, the last two [roots] begin with a palatal (*tālavya*) [sibilant] (81, 81, 82, 84, 85). *Śaki* in the sense of "doubt" (*śaṅkā*): doubt is fear of what lies ahead; *śaṅkate*. In the *uṇādi* list (I, 37), *śaṅkuḥ*; *śaṅkulā* is a weapon (86).

The root *aki* is used in the sense of "marking" (*lakṣaṇe*). A "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) is a sign (*cihna*). From the root *aṅk* [meaning] "to mark," with the suffix *ghañ* (Pāṇini III.3.19), we have *aṅka*; with the suffix *a* by the rule *guroś ca halaḥ* (III.3.103), we have *aṅkā*. By the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* (VI.1.3), the *n* is not doubled: *añcikiṣate*. In the *curādi* group (X.382), one says *aṅkayati*; with the suffix *yuc* by the rule *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc* (III.3.107), we have *aṅkanā*, which refers to the polishing of swords and the like. By the rule *mandivāśi* (Uṇādi I.39), the suffix *urac* is applied: *aṅkuraḥ* (87).

The root *vaṅk* is used in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilya*). One *vaṅkate*. [From this,] by *Uṇ.* IV.66, *vaṅkaḥ*; and *vaṅkriḥ* means a rib (*parśu*), as in *vaṅkry-ādi*. By *Uṇ.* I.13, from *vañc*, *vakraṃ* [is formed]; however, [the form] *vaṅke* is incorrect. (88) The root *maki* is used in the sense of adorning (*maṇḍana*). One *maṅkate*. [From this,] *maṅkanaḥ* and *maṅkanā* mean a garment. By *Uṇ.* I.41, *makuraḥ*. (89) The root *kak* is used in the sense of longing (*laulya*). Longing is both thirstiness (*satṛṣṇatva*) and fickleness (*cāpala*). One *kakate*. *Kākaḥ* is derived according to *Pāṇini* VI.3.109 (*pṛṣodarādi*). (90)

The root *kuk* means "to seize" (*ādāna*). From it, *kokate*. By [Pāṇini III.1.135], *ke* is added to *kuk*, yielding *kekaraḥ*. In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), *kokaḥ* means the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*). In the *uṇādi* section (I.55), *kokilaḥ* is formed. From the root *vṛk* ("to cover" or "to seek"), *varkate*. *Vṛkaḥ* is formed. In the causative (*ṇau*) with the *caṅ* aorist, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*, VII.4.1), or optionally *ur* for *ṛt* (VII.4.7): *avīvṛkat* or *avavarkat*. In the *uṇādi* section (III.131), *varkaraḥ* is formed. (91, 92)

**Cak in the sense of satiety.** *cakate* (he is satiated). *cakitaḥ* (frightened). From the roots *kaṭhi* and *caki*, the suffix *oraḥ* is applied (cf. Uṇādi-sūtra I, 65): *cakoraḥ* (a partridge). From *caki* and *rami*, the suffix *uc* is applied with the substitution of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) (Uṇādi-sūtra II, 14): *cukram* (sour gruel). Since *caka* in the sense of satiety and obstruction belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group and is marked as *mit* (causing the elision of the penultimate vowel), it forms *cakayati* (he causes to be satisfied). (93)

*kaṅk*, *śvaṅk*, *traki*, *ḍhaukṛ*, *traukṛ*, *ṣvakka*, *vaska*, *maska*, *ṭikṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, *raṅgh*, *lagh*: these have the sense of "going. *kaṅkate*; *kaṅkaḥ*. *Śvaṅki* begins with the palatal (*tālavya*) [sibilant]. *Ḍhaukate*; *aḍuḍhaukat*. Durga reads *ṭaukṛ*: *ṭaukate*. *Svakkate*; due to the prohibition regarding the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvakk* among the *sub-dhātu*s (cf. Pāṇini VI.1.64), there is an absence of the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*. *Ṭekate*. *Ṭīkate*; *aṭiṭīkat*. *Raṅghate*; by virtue of the rule for "excessive productivity" (*bāhulaka*, III.3.1), [we derive] *Raghuḥ*.

From the rule *laṅghate, laṅghibaṃhyor nalopaś ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra I, 30), the word *laghu* is derived. In the *cur*-class (*curādi*), it has the meanings of "shining" (X, 253–254): *raṅghayati*, *laṅghayati*. [The root] *laghi* also means "cessation from eating. Because of the particle *ca*, it also means "going": "a case of new fever is to be treated with fasting" (*navajvaro laṅghanīyaḥ*). 1? So K and C; P omits. 2 All manuscripts read *paśuḥ*. 3 P adds *maṅkaḥ*. 4 P reads *gaIwaś*. 5 P reads *adane*. 17 I.

The roots *aghi*, *vaghi*, and *maghi* mean "impelling motion. Impelling motion (*gatyākṣepaḥ*) refers to movement with speed or the commencement of going. From these, one forms *aghati*; according to the *uṇādi* suffixes, *agham* [is derived], while some say *aṅghriḥ* is formed according to *vaṅkryādi* (Uṇ. IV, 66). *Maghi* means "deceit" (*kaitavaṃ*) as well as "deceit" (*kaitavaṃ*); *maṅghate*. According to *śvanukṣan* (Uṇ. I, 158), [one forms] *Maghavan*, and *Maghavā* is Indra (sūtras 109–112).

The roots *rāghṛ*, *lāghṛ*, *drāghṛ*, and *dhrāghṛ* signify capability (*sāmarthya*). One says *rāghate* and *lāghate*. Regarding the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), when not preceded by a prefix, [the suffix *kta* is replaced] by *phulla*, *kṣība*, etc., according to Pāṇini VIII.2.55; thus one has *ullāghaḥ* meaning "recovered" (*nīruk*)—it should be *ullāghitaḥ* otherwise. Others did not recite *drāghṛ*; however, *drāghṛ* signifies exertion (*āyāsa*), which is torment (*kadarthana*). Kauśika, however, stated that it means extension (*āyāma*), that is, an action characterized by length.

For when the division into root (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is merely conceptual, forms such as *drāghimā* are established as roots themselves in certain grammatical systems; likewise, *nediṣṭha* and others [are derived] from *nedati* and so forth (I, 921). *Drāghate*, *adadrāghat* (113–117); *ślāghṛ* means "to boast. Boasting is the proclamation of one's excellence. By the rule *ślāghahnuṅsthā* (I, 4, 34), there is the dative case: *caitrāya ślāghate*, *aśaślāghat* (118). These are the roots with raised (*udātta*) vowels that have unraised (*anudātta*) indicatory vowels. 114.

*Phakk* means "to go downwards. Going downwards refers to slow movement or improper conduct. From here on, forty-five roots ending in *iṭ* are *parasmaipada*. *Phakkati*, *phakkitā*. *Phakkitaṃ* means swallowed; *phakkā*, *phakkikā* (119). *Taka* means "to laugh. Durga says [it means] "to endure. *Takati* (120). *Taki* means "to live in hardship. *Ātaṅkati*; *ātaṅkaḥ* (121). *Śuka* means "to go. *Śokati*. By *ke* (III, 1, 135), *śukaḥ* is formed; in the *uṇādi* list (II, 28) [it is derived thus].

*Śukla-śukrau* (123). *Bukk* in the sense of barking; some say "bhaṣaṇe" (in the sense of barking). A dog barks (*bukkati*); *bukka* is a fragrant substance ground into a paste. (122) *Kharkha* in the sense of laughing. One laughs (*kharkhati*); *kharkhā* is the vulva. Durga says: *khakkheti*; *khakkhaṭaḥ* means firm. (124) 5. *Okhṛ*, *rākhṛ*, *lākhṛ*, *drākhṛ*, *dhrākhṛ* in the senses of drying up and being sufficient.

*okhati*; by *eṅi pararūpam* (VI.1.94), *prokhati*; [the forms] *okhāñcakāra* and *uvokha* are erroneous; [the form] *mā bhavān ocikhat* [is used], for because it has an *ṛt* vowel, it does not have an *aut* vowel due to association (125–129). *śākhṛ* and *ślākhṛ* mean "to pervade. *śākhati*, *aśaśākhat*; *śākhā*; the *śākhoṭa* tree (130, 131). 1. Cf. Hemacandra’s Uṇādisūtra 110. 2. Pāṇini: *dhātoḥ*. 3. Pāṇini omits. 4. Kāśikā commentary omits. 5. 123 is before 122. 6. Pāṇini: *okhikhat*. 7. Kāśikā: *śākhoṭakaḥ*.

I.18: *ukha*, *ukhi*, *vakha*, *vakhi*, *makha*, *makhi*, *nakha*, *ṇakha*, *ṇakhi*, *rakha*, *rakhi*, *lakha*, *lakhi*, *ikha*, *īkhi*, *valgā*, *ragi*, *lagi*, *agi*, *vagi*, *magi*, *tagi*, *tvagi*, *śragi*, *ślaɡi*, *igi*, *rigi*, *ligi*—these have the sense of motion (*gaty-artha*). *Okhati*, *prokhati*; *ukhā* means a cooking pot (*sthālī*). The root *ukhi* ending in *i* is not Vedic (*anārṣa*), as it is cited for such meanings as "the *nyuṅkha*s are sixteen *oṃkāra*s. *Makhati*; *makha* means a sacrifice. *Maṅkhati*; *maṅkha* means a bard (*vandī*). The doubling of *nakha* is for the purpose of optional inclusion of the nasal (*ṇopadeśa-vikalpa*).

*praṇakhati*, *praṇakhati*; *ekhati*. Some say that because it follows *idam*, [the forms] *iṅkhati*, *preṅkhati*, and *preṅkhā* [are derived from this root]. *valgati*, *valgaḥ*, *valgā*. *raṅgati*, *raṅgaḥ*. *laṅgati*, *laṅgaḥ*; this [root] is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) for a specific kind of bird that limps. Regarding *laṅgi* and *kampya* in the sense of affliction and bodily distortion [Pāṇini VI.4.24.1], due to the elision of *n*, there is *vilagitaḥ paśuḥ*. *aṅgati*; *aṅgam*; by [Uṇādi-sūtra] IV.50, "from *aṅg* there is elision of *n*," we have *agniḥ*; by [Uṇādi-sūtra] III.134, "from *aṅgi*, *madi*, and *mandi* there is *āran*."

*Angāraḥ*; [from the rule] *ṛtanyañji* (Uṇ. IV.2), *aṅguliḥ* [is derived]; and by another etymology, [from the rule] *amer gur iraś ca lo vā*, it is made known that for conventional words (*nirūḍhāḥ*), the root and suffix may be postulated in any way whatsoever. The root *vaṅg-* is conventionally used in the sense of "impairment of movement": *vaṅgati*, *Vaṅgaḥ*. From *maṅg-* with the suffix *-alac* (cf. Uṇ. V.70): *maṅgalam*. The root *tag-* is conventionally used in the sense of "stumbling": *taṅgati*, *iṅgati*, *iṅgitam*. *Āliṅgati*, *liṅgam*; and in the *curādi* group, *ligi* in the sense of "making a mark" (X.199): [the form *lepayati*].

Liṅgayatī. According to the *Rikhi* of the Dramiḍas: *riṅkhati*, *riṅkhaṇaṃ* means stumbling. And Candra [states]: *traṅgī* (Ca. Dh. I, 38): *traṅgati*. *tvagi* also means trembling: *tvaṅgati* (132–146; 151–160; 162–166).

*yugi*, *jugi*, *vugi* mean to avoid: *yuṅgati*, *juṅgati*; *joṅganī* is a vessel for a goldsmith. *bhugi* means roasting, according to some; *daghi* means protecting, and by the inclusion of "and" (*ca*), also avoiding: *daṅghati* (167–169; 171).

*Ghaggh* means to laugh boisterously; *ghagghati*. *Ghaggharī* means a water-jar (*kalaśī*). Some say [the root is] *gādi*: *gagghati*. Kaṇṭha says both [roots apply]. (170) *Śighi* and *āghrā* mean to smell. Smelling is the taking up of fragrance. *Śiṅghati*. [The suffix] *-ana* is added after *lū*, *śiṅghi*, and *dhāñ* (cf. Uṇ III.83): *śiṅghāṇakaḥ* means catarrh (*pīnasaḥ*). (174) 4 These roots are udātta and have an udātta indicatory vowel (*udāttet*). 159

*Varc* in the sense of "to shine. The twenty roots ending in *ī* and *īj* (Pāṇini 1.2.1) are *seṭ* (taking the augment *iṭ*) and take the *ātmanepada* endings. [From *varc*: *varcate*, *varcitā*. *Suvarcikā* is a chisel; *suvarcalā* is a vegetable. [The suffix] *asun* (Uṇādi IV.188): *varcas* means impurity and luster (175). *Ṣac* in the sense of "to sprinkle. *sacate*, *asīṣacat*. By the rule *sitanigamisa-cimasi* (cf. Uṇādi I.70), the suffix *tun* is applied: *saktavaḥ* (barley meal). *Ṣac* in the sense of "to associate"; from this, *sacati*, *sacivaḥ* (minister). (176, 1046)

1 *plekhanam* 2 *so* [K *kalaśiḥ*, P *kalaśaḥ*] 3 K *kalaśiḥ*, P *kalaśaḥ* 4 171 see under 169 5 P *saktuḥ* 19 I *locṛ* in the sense of seeing (*darśane*). Present: *locate*; Perfect: *alulocat*. Past passive participle: *ālocitaḥ*; noun: *locanam*; agentive noun: *locakaḥ*; also denotes a woman’s head-cloth and a helmet (*śirastra*). In the *curādi* group, it has the meaning of shining (*bhāsārtha*) [X, 237]: *ālocayati*; abstract noun: *ālocanā* (177).

The root *śac* is used in the sense of manifest speech; it begins with the letter *tālavya* (the palatal *ś*). One says *śacate*; *śacī*. [Next,] *śvac* and *śvaci* are used in the sense of moving. One says *śvacate*, *śvañcate*. [Next,] *kac* is used in the sense of binding. One says *kacate*. *Kacaḥ*, *kācaḥ*, *kācaraḥ*. *Kac* in the sense of sound is accented on the first syllable (*udātta*); one says *kacati*. *Khaca* (Dhātupāṭha X, 392) exists as a worldly [root]; one says *khacati*. [Next,] *kaci* is used in the senses of shining and binding. One says *kañcate*, *kañcyate*. *Kāñcanam*, *kāñcikam*, *kāñcī*, *kañcukam*. Some say that the first *kaci* is marked with the *it*-sign (*idit*), while the latter is not marked with the *it*-sign (*anidit*).

*Mac* [is used] in the sense of deceiving (*kalkana*). *Kalkana* means hypocrisy (*dambha*) and boiling (*kvathana*). It is conjugated as *macate*. According to Candra (cf. Ca. Dh. I, 359), it is also *muc*: *mocate*, *muñcate*, *muñcyate*. In the *tudādi* class, *mucḷ* in the sense of releasing (*mokṣaṇa*) is conjugated as *muñcati*, *mucyate* (184, 185). *Maci* is used in the senses of holding, rising, and honoring. It is conjugated as *mañcate*. *Mañcaḥ* (a bed); in the *uṇādi* suffixes, *mañcukā* (a small bed) and *mañcikā* (a small bed)—so say the refined scholars (186).

The root *paci* is used in the sense of manifestation (*vyaktīkaraṇe*). It forms *pañcyate*, meaning "it is elaborated" (*prapañcyate*). By [Pāṇini] III.1.134, we have *pañcaḥ* (as in *Pañcikā Nyāsaḥ*) and *pañca* (as in *Pañcālāḥ*). By [Pāṇini] III.3.18–19, with the suffix *ghañ*, we have *paṅkaḥ* (mud). In the *cur*-class (*curādau*), *paci* is used in the sense of expansion (*vistāravacane*) [X.109]: *prapañcayati*. Because the rule *er aj* (III.3.56)—which prescribes the suffix *ac*—is stated to be generally applicable (*prāyikatvāt*) only to roots ending in *aṇ*, the form *prapañcaḥ* is derived with *ghañ*; however, for this root, there would be *kutva* (the change of *c* to *k*) by VII.3.52. Durga states that it ends in a short vowel (*adanta*). The root *ṣṭ̣uca* is used in the sense of satisfaction (*prasāde*). It forms *stuocate* and *tuṣṭ̣uce*. With the suffix *ghañ* (III.3.19), we have *stokaḥ*. (187) (188)

The root *ṛj* is used in the senses of going straight, standing, acquiring, and exertion. Exertion (*ūrjanam*) means breathing or strengthening. One says *arjate*, *upārjate*, and *ānṛje*. Others, however, consider this root—which begins with *ha*—to have the meaning of depletion or abundance. (189)

The roots *ṛji* and *bhr̥jī* mean "to roast. Roasting (*bharjana*) is a mode of cooking. [From *ṛji*: *ṛñjate*, *ānṛñje*; according to the *Uṇādisūtra* (IV.22), *ṛjīka* means "a vessel for baking flour. [From *bhr̥jī*: *bharjate*. With the suffix *ghañ*, the form is *bhr̥ṣṭaṃ* [by Pāṇini VI.4.27]; [in the imperfect: *abībhṛjat*, *ababharjat*. With the suffix *kyap*—by rule III.1.110, "after a root with *ṛ* in the penultimate syllable, except for *kḷp* and *cṛt"—we have *bhṛjyam* and *avaśyabharjyam*. In the suffix *ṇya*, by rule VII.3.65, "in the sense of necessity," there is no change to *k* (*kutva*). In the *Uṇādisūtra* (190, 191), *bharjū* means "a frying pan."
1 P adds: *śaci śvacīti* Kauśikaḥ; 2 cf. I, 199; 3 cf. Hem. Dh. I, 656; 4 cf. I, 242; 5 cf. Hem. Dh. I, 666; I 20.

The roots *ejṛ*, *bhrājṛ*, and *bhrājṛ* signify shining. From *ejate*: by rule VI.1.94 (*eṅi pararūpam*), we have *prejate*. Regarding the form *mā bhavān ejijat*, one should not argue that the designation *ṛdit* (having *ṛ* as an indicatory letter) is redundant because, after reduplication has occurred due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*) and because the rule is not universal (*anityatva*), there would be no occasion for shortening (*hrasva*). This is not so, because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in Pāṇini I.4.82. By rule III.1.138 (*anupasargāl limpavinda*), the suffix *śa* is applied: *udejayaḥ*. From the root *ejṛ* in the sense of trembling (I.253), we have *ejati*; likewise, by rule III.2.28 (*ejeh khaś*), we have *aṅgamejayaḥ*.

The root *bhrāj* shines. By the rule *bhrājabhāsabhāṣadīpa* (VII. 4. 3), there is optionally the substitution of *ā* for the radical vowel: *ababhrājat* or *abibhrajat*.
