*kraṃsate*. By the rule *udito vā* (VII, 2, 56), the augment *iṭ* is optional: *kramitvā*, *krāntvā*; in the case where *iṭ* is not applied, by *kramaś ca ktvi* (VI, 4, 18), there is optionally lengthening: *krantvā*. In the *uṇādi* group, *kramukaḥ*. By *nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau* (III, 1, 23), the intensive suffix *yaṅ* is applied: *caṅkramyate*. By *jucaṅkramya* (III, 2, 150), the suffix *yuc* is applied: *caṅkramaṇaḥ*. By *nodāttopadeśasya* (VII, 3, 34), there is no *vṛddhi* when the suffix *ghañ* is applied: *kramaḥ*, *upakramaḥ*.

By the rule *janasanakhan* (III, 2, 67), the suffix *viṭ* is applied; by *viḍvanor āt* (VI, 4, 41), the long *ā* is substituted [for the root vowel], resulting in *dūrākāḥ*. By *kramitamistambhām ata ic ca* (Uṇ. IV, 121), the suffix *ki* is applied: *krimiḥ*; and by virtue of the "abundance" (*bāhulakāt*, III, 3, 1), there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*): *kṛmiḥ*. By *śakadhṛṣajñāglā* (III, 4, 65), the suffix *tumun* is applied: *prakramate bhoktum* ("he proceeds to eat"). These [roots] ending in an udātta vowel are udāttet. (502) 469.

*aya*, *vaya*, *paya*, *maya*, *caya*, *taya*, and *naya*—these forty-nine roots, ending with *revṛ*, are *seṭ* and *ātmanepadin*. In *ayate*, by the rule *upasargasyāyatāv* (Pāṇini VIII.2.19), the substitution of *l* for *y* occurs: *palāyate*, *palyayate*. According to the Kāśikā commentary on *upasargasyāyatāv*, "that by which there is no intervention" is understood to mean intervention by a single phoneme; thus, it does not apply here in *pratyayate*. By the rule *dayāyāsaś ca* (Pāṇini III.1.37), the suffix *ām* is added in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*): *palāyāṃcakre*. *Vayate*; [the suffix] *asun* (Uṇādi).

IV, 188): *vaya-* means age, such as childhood, etc., and a bird (*pakṣin*); from the root *vi-* with the suffix *-asun* (ṇit) [Uṇ. III, 120], we have *vāyasaḥ* (crow). From *payate*, *payaḥ* (milk). From *mayate*; also from *meṅ* (DhP. I, 1010), one has *mayate*. From *cayate*, with the suffix *ghañ* (Pāṇ. III, 3, 18–19), *cāyaḥ*; from *cinoti* (DhP. V, 5), *cayaḥ*. From *nayate*, in the *liṭ* tense, *neye*; from *ṇīñ* in the sense of leading (*prāpaṇe*) (DhP. I, 950), *nayati*, *nayate*, *nināya*, *ninye*. From *taya* in the sense of protecting (*rakṣaṇe ca*): *tayate*; *Tāyī* is the Jina (Sūtras 503–509).

The root *day* is used in the senses of compassion, giving, protection, and non-injury. In the sense of "to have compassion for" (*dayate*), the genitive case is used according to Pāṇini II.3.52 (*adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi*): *mātuḥ dayate* ("he has compassion for his mother"). The forms *dayyate*, *dayitā*, and *dayā* are derived from the same root. According to Pāṇini III.1.37 (*dayāyāsaś ca*), the suffix *ām* is applied in the perfect tense (*liṭ*): *dayāṃcakre*. According to Pāṇini III.2.158 (*spṛhigṛhipatidayi*), the suffix *āluc* is applied to form *dayāluḥ* ("compassionate"). Because it belongs to the *bhidādi* group (Pāṇini III.3.104), the feminine form is *dayā*. The past passive participle is *dayitam*. The root *deṅ* (I.1011) means "to protect": *mātaraṃ dayate*, *dīyate*, *dātā*. The root *ray* (I.510) means "to go": *rayate*. From this come *rayaḥ* ("speed") and *nirayaḥ* ("hell," I.511).

*Ūyī* [means] "to weave" (*tantu-saṃtāne*). [Examples: *ūyate*, *ūyitā*, *ūyāṃcakre*. By the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām* (Pāṇini VII.2.14), there is no *iṭ*: *ūtaḥ* (512). *pūyī* [means] "to rot" (*viśaraṇe*) and "to have a foul odor" (*durgandhe*). [Examples: *pūyante yavāḥ* ("the barley grains rot"); *vraṇaḥ pūyate* ("the wound suppurates"); *pūyitā*. [Past participle: *pūtaḥ*; [gerundive: *pūtiḥ* (513). *knūyi* [means] "to sound" (*śabda*) and "to moisten" (*undane*). Moistening (*undana*) means becoming wet (*kledana*). [Examples: *knūyate*, *knūyitā*. [Past participle: *knūtaḥ*. Because of the rule *na ya* (Pāṇini III.2.152), the suffix *yuc* does not apply; therefore, for the agent (*kartṛ*) characterized by such a habit (*tacchīla*), etc., only *tṛn* (Pāṇini III.2.135) applies: *knūyana-śīlaḥ* ("one who has the habit of moistening"), *knūyitā*. [The root *arti-*...]

1. Cf. Hem. Uṇ. 53. 2. All manuscripts read thus. 3. P reads *ekonapañcāśat*. 4. Cf. Hem. Dh. I, 797. 5. P: *vipūyante*; I 42: by [the rule] *hrī-vlī* (VII, 3, 36), the suffix *puk* is added before *ṇi*: *knopayati*; by [the rule] *cele knopeḥ* (III, 4, 33), the suffix *ṇamul* is added: *vastraknopaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (514).

The root *kṣmāyī* is used in the sense of shaking (*vidhūnana*). It forms *kṣmāyate* and *kṣmāpayati*. The roots *sphāyī* and *opyāyī* signify growth (*vṛddhi*). From *sphāyate*, in the causative (*ṇau*), there is the substitution of *v* for *y* according to Pāṇini VII.3.41: *sphāvayati*. In the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), *sphāyaḥ sphī* (VI.1.22) applies: *sphītaḥ*. The fact that *sphāyī* has the marker *īt* is a sign that its replacement [by *sphī*] is not obligatory: *sphātaḥ*. In the *uṇādi* group, we have *phenaḥ* (Uṇ. III.3), *sphiro bahuḥ* (Uṇ. I.54), and from *sphāyi* with the suffix *rak* (Uṇ. II.13): *sphāram*. From *pyāyate*, the suffix *ciṇ* may optionally apply in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to Pāṇini III.1.61: *dīpajanabudha...*.

*Apāyi*, *apyāyiṣṭa*. [The root] *pyai* becomes *pī* when referring to a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), according to Pāṇini VI.1.28; furthermore, by VIII.2.45, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the final consonant in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). According to the Vārttika on VI.1.28 stating "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] to *andhu* and *ūdhas*," we have *āpīno andhuḥ* (a well that has swelled) and *āpīnam ūdhaḥ* (a swollen udder). It does not apply here: *āpyānaś candramāḥ* (the moon has waxed). By VI.1.29, *liṭ* and *yaṅ* also take *pī*: *āpipye*, *āpepīyate*. Although *prapyānaḥ* would be expected by VI.4.29 (*kṛty-a-ca-...*), the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur by VII.4.34 (*na bhā-bhū-pū-kami-gami...*). (516, 517)

The root *tāyṛ* is used in the senses of continuity (*saṃtāna*) and protection (*pālana*). Continuity means a continuous series (*prabandha*). [From the root *tāy*] one forms *tāyate*, *atatāyat*. According to Pāṇini III.1.61, *dīpajanabudhapūri*, the suffix *ciṇ* is optionally applied in the sense of the agent: *atāyi* or *atāyiṣṭa*. [From the root] *taya* in the sense of protection (*rakṣaṇa*): *tayate*, *atītayat*. (518)

The root *śal* has the meanings "to move" and "to cover. One says *śalate* or *śalati*. Regarding *śal*, *hlad*, and *paṭl* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*) [Dhātupāṭha I, 896–898], as well as *śal* and *śvall* in the sense of "swift motion" (*āśugamane*) [I, 582–583]: By the rule *iṇ-bhī-kā-pā-* [Uṇādi-sūtra III, 43], *śalkaḥ* is formed, meaning "the bark of wood. By the rule *śali-paṭi-patibhyo niṭ* [Uṇādi-sūtra IV, 14], *śalākā* is formed (cf. Uṇādi-sūtra IV, 14). By the rule *kṝ-śṝ-śali-* [Uṇādi-sūtra III, 122], *abhac* is added, forming *śalabhaḥ* ("locust"). By the rule *śali-maṇḍibhyām ūkañ* [Uṇādi-sūtra IV, 42], [the word *śālūkam* is formed].

The words *śālūka*, *śalala*, and *śala* denote the porcupine; *sānasivarṇasiparṇasitaṇḍulāṅkuśacaṣālelvalapalvaladhiṣṇyaśalyāḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra IV, 107) [form the word] *śalya*, which refers to the porcupine (*śalyaka*). (519)

The root *val* means "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*). It forms *valate*. From it derive *trapodvalitaḥ*, *vālāḥ* ("hairs"), and *valmīkam* ("an anthill"). In the list beginning with *jval* (Dhātupāṭha I, 893), *bal* means "to breathe" (*prāṇane*); it forms *balati*. In the *curādi* class (X, 85), it is marked as *mit*, forming *balayati*. From *valka-* in the rule *śukavalkolkā* (Uṇādisūtra III, 42), we have *valkaḥ* ("bark"). From the suffix *in* (Uṇādisūtra IV, 117), we have *valiḥ* ("wrinkle," "contraction of the skin"). From the rule *valer guś ca* (cf. Uṇādisūtra I, 20), we have *valguḥ* ("beautiful"). From the rule *valimalitanibhyaḥ kayan* (Uṇādisūtra IV, 99), we have *valayaḥ* ("bracelets"). *Valīkam* (Uṇādisūtra IV, 25) refers to the edge of a roof-covering (*paṭalaprāntaḥ*).

This [root *bal*] begins with the dental and labial [consonant *b*]; however, they say that in the sense of "breathing" (*prāṇana*), it begins with the labial [consonant *v*]: *bala* (strength), *bali* (offering), *bāla* (child), *balākā* (crane), *balvaja* (a type of grass). Durga says *vala* and *vallā*; likewise, from the same [labial] beginning: *vallūra* (dried meat), *vallava* (cowherd), *vallabha* (dear to life), *vallī* (creeper), *vallarī* (small creeper), *vallā* (a type of grain).
(520, 521) 1 All manuscripts read this. 43 I.

The root *mala* is used in the sense of holding (*dhāraṇe*). From it are derived: *malate*, *malyate*; *mālā* (garland); *mālatī*, a specific type of tree; *mala* (impurity); *Malaya* (the mountain range); *mālayati*—Bhaṭṭi [uses this form] from the *curādi* class ending in *-a*, as in *malayati*; with the suffix *ghañ* (Pāṇini III.3.118), we have *parimalaḥ*, meaning a fragrant scent or perfume. From *mallate*: *mallaḥ* (wrestler); *mallikaḥ* (a vessel); *mallikā*, the *mallī* flower. (522, 523)

The root *bhala* is used in the senses of reproaching (*paribhāṣaṇa*), harming (*hiṃsā*), and giving (*dāna*). From *bhalate*, with the suffix *ūka* (cf. Uṇādi-sūtra IV.40), we have *bhalūka*, meaning "bear" (*ṛkṣaḥ*). From *bhallate*, with the suffixes *ulūka-* etc. (Uṇādi-sūtra IV.41), we have *bhallūka*, meaning "the bear *acchabhalla*"; *bhallah*, meaning "a crescent-headed arrow" (*kṣurapraḥ*); *bhalliḥ*; and *Bhallaṭaḥ*. In the *curādi* group, *bhala* is listed as meaning "mockery" (*ābhaṇḍana*) at X.161, taking the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings: *vibhālayate*; [also] *bhālūkaḥ* (vv. 524–525).

The root *kala* is used in the senses of sound (*śabda*) and counting (*saṃkhyāna*). It forms the following: *kalate*, *ākalate*, *saṃkalate*, *parikalate*, *pratyākalate*, *vikalate*. With the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini III.1.134): *kalaḥ*; with the suffix *ghañ* (Pāṇini III.3.19), from *kalyate*: *kālaḥ*. The gerundive forms are *kalanīyam* and *kalyam*. *Kālyam* means "dawn" (prabhāta), either as a primary derivative or because it is "suitable for the time" (*kāle sādhu*, Pāṇini IV.4.98). The past passive participle is *kalitam*. From the root *kali* with the suffix *in* (Uṇādi IV.117): *Kaliḥ*. With the suffix *ka* (Uṇādi IV.142): *kalikā*. With the suffix *am* added to *karda* and *kaḍa* (cf. Uṇādi IV.84): *kardamaḥ* and *kaḍamaḥ*. With the suffix *uṣac* added to *pṛ* and *kali* (cf. Uṇādi IV.75): *kaluṣaḥ*.

In the *uṇādi* [list], *kalmaṣam* (4) means "blackness" or "stain"; *kalmāṣaḥ* (4) means "variegated. *Kalyaḥ* occurs in the *aghyādi* group (*Uṇ.* IV, 111), or it means "skilled in the arts" (*kalāsu sādhuḥ*) according to *Pāṇini* IV, 4, 98. *Kalāyaḥ* is the "pigeon pea" (*satīnakaḥ*). *Kalilam* means "pervaded" or "thick with. *Kalalam* is the impurity of semen and blood. In the *curādi* [group], *kala* meaning "counting" is without a final *a* vowel (*adantaḥ*) (*X*, 319): *kalayati*, *kalanā*, *kalā*. By virtue of the rule for "excessiveness" (*bāhulakāt*) (*X*, 392), from the roots *kala*, *kila*, and *pila* meaning "to throw" (*X*, 64, 65), we derive *kālayati*, *kālaḥ*, *kālanam*, *kālanā*, and *kāliḥ*. *Kālikā*, however, refers to a mass of clouds, as found in the *manojñādi* group (*V*, 1, 133). (526)
*Kalla* means "soundless"; in the sense of being soundless, it refers to silence. It is used as *kallate*. *Kallaḥ*, *kallolaḥ*. (527)

The root *div* (in the sense of "playing" or "sporting") forms *devate* [present] and *adidevat* [perfect]; *devate* [present] and *adidevat* [perfect]. By the rule *atikamibhrami* (Uṇ. III.132), the suffix *ara* is added, yielding *devaraḥ*. By the rule *śakādibhyo ’ṭan* (Uṇ. IV.81), *devaṭaḥ* is formed. There is a repetition from the *ūrṇā* section. By the rule *vṛṣādibhyaś cit* (Uṇ. I.108), *devalaḥ* is formed. In the *divādi* group (IV.1), one says *dīvyati*; in the *curādi* group (X.166), *divu* in the sense of "cooing" (*parikūjana*) yields *devayate*, which takes the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings by the rule *ā kusmāt* (X.135); [the perfect is] *adīdivat*. Likewise, for *divu* in the sense of "wasting away" (*ardana*) (X.185), one says *paridevayati* (528, 529).

The roots *śevṛ*, *ṣevṛ*, *sevṛ*, *kevṛ*, *khevṛ*, *glevṛ*, *pevṛ*, *plevṛ*, *mevṛ*, and *mlevṛ* mean "to serve. [From *sev*: *sevate*, *siṣeve*, *asiṣevat*; for a root not taught with an initial *ṣ* (*aṣopadeśa*), it is *siseve*, *asisevat*. Regarding the rule *parinivibhyaḥ seva* (Pāṇini VIII.3.70), there is the substitution of *ṣ*: *niṣevate*. Regarding the rule *aḍvyavāye ’pi* (VIII.3.71), there is *paryaṣevata*. Although the restriction *stautiṇyor eva ṣaṇy abhyāsāt* (VIII.3.61) applies, in the case of *sthādiṣu abhyāsasya...* [the *ṣ* occurs].

1. P omits *puṣpam*. 2. P reads *taṅādau*. 3. Both K and P read *kardikaḍyor*; cf. Hemacandra’s *Uṇādisūtra* 347. 4. Cf. Hemacandra’s *Uṇādisūtra* 562 and 563. 5. All manuscripts read as follows: by [the rule] *sena cābhyāsasya* (Pāṇini VI.1.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]: *niṣiṣeviṣate*. In the *Uṇādi* section, [the form] *kevate* is appropriate; from roots such as *vṛṣ* etc., by [the rule] *cid* (Uṇādi I.108), the suffix *kalac* is applied: *kevalaḥ* (cf. entries 531a, 536, 530, 539, 537, 532, 533, 538, 534, 535).

*revṛ* [is used] in the sense of moving by leaps (*plutigati*); [it means] having gone by leaps. *revate*: *Revā* is the *Narmadā*. *revatī*, however, is a form of the root *rīṅ* (according to Pāṇini IV, 1, 30). (540) The roots with anudātta indicatory vowels ending in *m* (508): *mavya* in the sense of binding. From here up to the end of the section (631), there are eighty-eight roots that take the augment *iṭ* and are parasmaipada. *mavyati*. (541)

*sūrkṣya*, *īrkṣya*, *īrṣya*—these have the meaning of envy (*īrṣyā*). Envy is the inability to endure [another's] success born of desire. By the rule *krudhadruheṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ* (Pāṇini I.4.37), the recipient of the action is the *saṃpradāna* case: *caitrāyerṣyati* ("he envies Caitra"). Regarding the form *īrṣyate*, by the rule *tṛtīyasyaikāco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini VI.1.1–2), there is reduplication of the single consonant: *īrṣyiṣiṣati*. According to some, this applies to the consonant [cluster]: *īrṣyiyiṣati*.

And when there is *caṅ* following a causative (*ṇic*), because there is no third single-consonant (*ekāc*) [to undergo reduplication], reduplication occurs only of the second [syllable]; for, due to the absence of a third [single-consonant], the Vārttika does not apply. Consequently, by *halādiśeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini VI.4.60), only the letter *ṣ* is heard in the reduplicated syllable: *airṣiṣyat*. According to the view that "of a consonant" (*vyañjanasya*) applies, reduplication occurs only of the *y*: *airṣyiyat* (542–544). [The root] *haya* is used in the senses of motion and joy. *hayati*, *hayaḥ* (545).

*Śucyī* [denotes] the act of pressing (*abhiṣava*). Pressing is the extraction of non-liquid substances by means of a liquid; the Cāndras call it "bathing" (*snāna*) (cf. Ca. Dh. I, 161). The root *śuc* forms the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) as *śuśucya*. [The form] *śuktaḥ* results from the elision of *y* according to Pāṇini VI.4.49. Regarding *cucyī* 3, Durga [states] that the root *hary* means "motion" and "desire" (*gati-kāntyoḥ*) 4. It forms *haryati* [and *haryate*]. From the root *hary*, the suffix *kanyan* is applied with the replacement of the root by *hira* (Uṇ. V.44): *hiraṇyam* 547.

The root *al* is used in the senses of adorning (*bhūṣaṇa*), sufficiency (*paryāpti*), and warding off (*nivāraṇa*). It is nasalized (*sānunāsika*) for the purpose of receiving the technical designation *it* (Pāṇini I.3.2), as in the case of *pacati*. *Alati*: *Alakā*—the city [of Kubera]; *alakāḥ*—hair [curled locks]. [Derived from the root with] the suffix *kvun* in the senses of craft (*śilpa*) and name (*saṃjñā*) (Uṇādi-sūtra II.32). *Alindaḥ*—a porch or terrace. *Alikaṃ*—the forehead. *Alīkam*—falsehood. *Aliḥ*—a bee; and *āliḥ*—a female friend and a row. *Alarkaḥ*—a dog afflicted by rabies. *Alaktakam*—red lac-dye; however, it is called *arakta* because of the identity between the sounds *r* and *l* (Kāśikā on Pāṇini VIII.2.18). (548)

The root *ñiphaIā* means "to burst asunder. From it: *phalati*, *pratiphalati*, *utphalati*. According to *tṛphalabhajatrapaḥ* (Pāṇini VI.4.122), there is elision of the reduplication and the substitution of *e* for the root vowel in the perfect tense (*liṭ*): *pheluḥ*. By *kvun śilpisaṃjñayoḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra II.32), the suffix *kvun* is added to form *phalakaṃ*; however, *phalahakaḥ* refers to a quiver and similar objects. By *caraphaloś ca* and *ut parasyātaḥ* (Pāṇini VII.4.87–88), one forms *pampulyate*. By *ti ca* (VII.4.89), one forms *paṃphultaḥ*. In the sense of the present tense, the suffix *kta* is applied after a root ending in *ñī*: (Pāṇini III.2.187).

1 P adds *mavyaḥ* 2 P [interprets] as *asahiṣṇutvam* (intolerance/impatience) 3 All manuscripts read *śucī*, but cf. Hemacandra’s *Dhātupāṭha* I, 404 and Mādhava’s commentary I, 508 4 KC [interpret] as "in beauty and movement" (*kāntigatyoḥ*) 5 K [states it is so] because of oneness (*ekatvāt*) 6 cf. Hemacandra’s *Uṇādisūtra* 33, 45, 1.

*Praphullaḥ*: by the rule *anupasargāt phullakṣība* (Pāṇini VIII.2.55), the form *phullaḥ* is correct when formed with the suffix *kta*; by the vārttika *utphullasaṃphullau vaktavyau* (VIII.2.55, 1 Bh.), [the forms] *utphulla* and *saṃphulla* are also prescribed; however, when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), it is *praphultaḥ*. By the rule *āditaś ca* (VII.2.16), the augment *iṭ* does not occur; by the rule *vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ* (VII.2.17), one may say *phullam anena* or *phalitam anena*, and *praphūltaḥ* or *praphalitaḥ*. According to the *Uṇādi-sūtra* I.19, *phalipāṭi*, the word *phalguḥ* means "without essence" (*asāraḥ*), and there is also the feminine *phalgunī*.

From *phala* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) comes *phalitaḥ*; from *phulla* in the sense of "blooming" (*vikasana*) comes *phullitaḥ*. The roots *mīla*, *śmīla*, and *smīla* denote "closing," that is, the act of closing or contraction. One says *mīlati*. *Pramīlā* means drowsiness; it also denotes the act of closing. According to Pāṇini VII.4.3 (*bhrājabhāsadīpa-*), there is optionally a shortening of the penultimate vowel: *amimīlat* or *amīmilat*. From the common root *mila* (Dhātupāṭha VI.71), one says *milati*; the noun form is *melanam*. The Cāndra grammarians (Cāndra Dhātupāṭha I.163) read *kṣmīla* in place of *śmīla*. (549–553)

The root *pīl* means "to obstruct. Obstruction (*pratiṣṭambha*) is the act of blocking. [From the root: *pīlati*; the noun *pīlanam*. With the suffix *kvasu*: *pipīlvān* (by rule VII.2.8, *neḍ vaśi kṛti*). By the rule *kharu-śaṅku-* (Uṇ. I.37), which is an instance of the frequentative application (*bāhulaka*, III.3.1), we have *pīluḥ*. Also *pipīlakaḥ* and *pipīlikā* (554). The root *nīl* means "color. It refers to an action characterized by color, as in: "it becomes blue (*nīlati*) through the luster of an emerald"; *praṇīlati*. [Nouns derived from it are] *nīlam*, *nīlī*, *nīlaḥ* (3). *Kuṭṭimaḥ* (a paved floor); *nīlaṅguḥ* (a type of insect) (555).

*Śīla* means concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration is one-pointedness. [The root *śīl*] means to practice repeatedly. From the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of "practiced" (*anuśīlita*), according to Pāṇini III.2.1.7 (*śīlikāmibhakṣyācaribhyo ṇaḥ*): *māṃsaśīlā* ("one who habitually eats meat"), *śailūṣaḥ* ("an actor"). According to the rule of abundance (*bāhulakāt*) in III.3.1, some say it means "the descendant of Śilūṣa. In the *cur*-class (X.332), *śīlayati* (556). *Kīl* means to bind. [From this root: *kīlati*; *utkīlitaḥ* ("uprooted"), *kīlakaḥ* ("a peg"), *kīlā* ("a stake"), *kīlālam* ("nectar"); *kīliḥ* in the sense of the verbal root itself. With the causative suffix (*ṇic*): *kīlayati* (557). 4.

*kūla* [is used] in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*). It conforms [to this meaning]. From *kūl* in the sense of "being obstructed by water" (*ambhasā*), we have *kūla*. From *kula* in the sense of "congregation" (*saṃstyāne*) [DhP 1.895], we have *kula*. From *kṛ* [with the prefix *ku-*, according to Pāṇini VI.1.12 as cited in the Kāśikā], we have *kukūla* in the sense of "chaff-fire" (*tuṣāgni*). *Śūla* [is derived from] *śūl* in the sense of "paining" (*rujāyām*). It pains. By [the suffix] *ac* [Pāṇini III.1.134], we have *śūla* [in the sense of a "spear"]. *Tūla* [is used] in the sense of "extracting" (*niṣkarṣe*). Extraction is the removal of the core substance from an object. It extracts. Hence *tūla* ("cotton"). *Tūli* is a cotton bed; however, when referring to a brush-pen, it is *tūlikā*.
*Pūl* in the sense of "heaping together": *pūlati*. *Pūla*, *pūlī*—a heap of grass.

(561) *Mūl* in the sense of "establishing" or "foundation": *mūlati*. *Mūlam*; [as in] *unmūlayati kleśān* (he uproots the afflictions), *unmūlitaḥ* (uprooted). In the *curādi* group, *mūl* means "growing" (X, 63): *mūlayati*. (562) *Phal* in the sense of "accomplishment. Accomplishment (*niṣpatti*) means success (*siddhi*). *Phalati*. *Phalitaḥ*. Regarding the root *ñiphalā* (I, 549), there is the form *phullaḥ*. [The words] *phalam* and *palitam* are derived from *phal* with the suffix *itac* and the substitution of *pa* for the initial [phoneme]: *palitam*. (563)

1. *Phalgu* means worthless or insubstantial (*asāra*). 2. *Rodhaḥ* [means a bank or obstruction]. 3. *Om.* (omitted). 4. *KCom.* (Kāśikāvṛtti commentary). 5. *Saṃvaraṇe* (in the sense of concealing), according to K. 6. *Saṃphullaḥ* (fully blossomed). I.46: *Culla* is used in the sense of making a slight gesture (*hāvakaraṇa*) or indicating one's intention (*abhiprāyasūcana*). From the root *cullati*, we derive *culliḥ* (No. 564).

*Phulla* means to blossom. *Phullati*. *Phuliyaṃ* (I H, 1, 134); *phullitaṃ* (565). *Cilla* means looseness. *Cillati*. *Cillitaḥ*, *cillaḥ* (a bird) (566). *Tilla* means to go. *Tillati*. Durga also says *tila*: *telati* (567). *Vellṛ*, *celṛ*, *kelṛ*, *khelṛ*, *kṣvelṛ*—these [five] mean to move. From *vell*, it is reduplicated.

The verbal root *laka* (meaning "to move"): *vellati*; past passive participle *vellitaḥ*, imperfect *avivellat*. From the root *vel* in the sense of "instruction of time" (*velā tu vela kālopadeśe*, X. 334). From *cel* (VI. 63, meaning "to wear" or "clothing"): *celati*; *pāpacelī* ("one who wears evil clothes"). *Celā* (feminine). From *cil* (VI. 63, meaning "clothing"). From *kel* (meaning "to play"): *kelati*; *keliḥ* (play), *kelitam* (past passive participle). From *kīla* (557, meaning "to bind"): *kīlaḥ* (nail, bolt), *kīlakam*, *kīlitam*. From *khel* (meaning "to play"): *khelati*. By Pāṇini III. 3. 19 (*atra kṣepe*), *kheIam* (a place for playing). By Pāṇini III. 1. 134 (*khelā śiṅkhāṇake ca*), *khelā* (sport, practice). *Khilaṃ* (waste land) is derived by the rule of the *pṛṣodarādi* group (VI. 3. 109). From *kṣvel* (573, 569–572): *kṣvelati*; *kṣvelā* (spitting, sound).

*Pelṛ*, *phelṛ*, and *śelṛ* mean "to go. *Pelati*; *pelitam*, *apipelat*; *pelaṃ* means "testicles"; *pelavaṃ* means "thin" or "delicate"; *pelakaḥ* means "the smell of skin. *Phelati*; *phelā* means "that which is thrown away after eating"; by [Pāṇini III.1.135], *ke* [added], *phelaḥ* means "excrement. *Śelati*; *aśiśelat*. (574–576) *Skhala* means "to stumble" or "to move unsteadily. *Skhalati*; having stumbled (*skhalitvā*). (577)

[The suffix *ghan* is applied] after the root *khala* in the sense of "accumulation. By virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), it is also applied in the sense of "moving. According to the statement that "the words *khala*, *bhaga*, and *pada* [are formed with *ghan*]," the suffix *ghan* is used; [and by Pāṇini III.1.134, the feminine suffix] *ac* is added: *khalaḥ*, *khaliḥ* (oil-cake), *khalatiḥ*, *khalvāṭaḥ* (bald), *khalvam* (depth), and *khalīnam* (the bit in a horse's mouth). (578)

*Gala* means "to swallow" (*adane*). It swallows, hence *galaḥ*. Because it has multiple meanings, it also means "to flow" (*sravaṇe*) (Uṇādi X, 392). In the *uṇādi* [section], from the root *gal* we have *gallaḥ* (the cheek), *galvarkaḥ* (crystal), and according to Uṇādi V, 26, "and from *gale*" we have *gulphaḥ* (the ankle). In the *curādi* [section], *gala* means "to cause to flow" (*srāvaṇe*) (X, 160); with the *taṅ* [suffixes]: *udgālayate*. (579) *Sala* means "to go" (*gatau*). It goes, hence *salilam* (water) and *sālaḥ* (a tree) (580).

*dalaviśaraṇe*. It means "to burst open. From the roots *uṣi*, *kuṭi*, *dali*, *kaci*, and *khaji* [the suffix] *kapan* is applied (Uṇ. III.142): thus *dalapaḥ* and *dalam*. Because it is marked with *m* (I.856), one forms *dalayati*; in the *curādi* group (X.211), one forms *dālayati*. (581) *śala* and *śvalla* mean "to move swiftly. One forms *śalati*. By the rule *ato lrāntasya* (VII.2.2), there is *vṛddhi*: thus *aśālīt*. In the *ulvādi* group (Uṇ. IV.95), *śulvam* means copper and rope; *śulkam* (582. 583).

1 K *kvelṛ* 2 P I. *śelṛ*: *ṣelṛ*, *selṛ*. 3 P *selati*; [preterite] *asiṣelat*, *aselat*. 4 So all manuscripts. 5 See the footnote thereon. 6 KC omits. 7 C *gallakaḥ*. 8 P *sphaṭikā*. 9 P omits. 47 I *khorṛ*, *kholṛ*: in the sense of "obstruction of movement" (*gatipratighāte*). *khorati*. *khorādhamastrī* (a low woman), *khorikā* (a vessel), *khoraḥ* (a limping person). Durga reads *khoḍṛ*: *khoḍaḥ* (a person with a withered arm). *kholaṃ* (a helmet). (584)

*dhor* in the sense of skillful movement (*gaticāturye*). *Dhorati*; *adudhorat*. *Ādhoraṇaḥ* means an elephant driver (*hastipakaḥ*); *dhoritaṃ*, *dhoritakaṃ* refer to the gallop of a horse (*aśvagatau*). (585) *Tsar* in the sense of moving by stealth (*chadmagatau*), meaning a mode of secret movement. *Tsarati*. By the rule *bhṛmṛśī* (Uṇ. I.7), the suffix *u* is applied: *tsaruḥ* refers to the hilt of a sword or similar weapon (*khaḍgādimuṣṭiḥ*). Kauśika says that *tsadma* is also [used] here: *tsadmati*. (586) 3.

The roots *abhra*, *babhra*, *mabhra*, and *cara* have the meaning "to go. *Abhrati*; [the noun] *abhram*. *Babhraṭi*; by the rule *kṛño dve ca, kur bhraś ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra I.22–23), [we get] *babhruḥ*, meaning a mongoose (*nakula*). *Mabhrati*. *Carati*; *car* also means "to eat. By the rule *udaś caraḥ sakarmakāt* (Pāṇini I.3.53), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix is applied: *geham uccarate*, meaning "he oversteps the house" (*ullaṅghayati*). But not here: *uccarati dhvaniḥ* ("a sound issues forth"). By the rule *samas tṛtīyāyuktāt* (Pāṇini I.3.54): *aśvena saṃcarate* ("he moves along with a horse").

And from the roots *car* and *phal*, by [the rule] *ut parasyātaḥ* (VII, 4, 87–88): *cañcūryate*, *cañcuraḥ*. By [the rule] *ti ca* (VII, 4, 89): *cūrtiḥ*; and *caritam*, by [the rule] *gadamadacarayamaś cānupasarge* (III, [1, 100]).

1, 100) Regarding *yat*: by the rule *caryam, carer āṅi cāgurau* (III, 1, 100), we have *ācarya upadeśaḥ* (instruction); *ācāryaḥ guruḥ* (the teacher as a guru); and *āścaryam* is used in the sense of "wonderful" or "rare" (VI, 1, 147). From the *pacādi* group (III, 1, 134), we have *caraḥ*. *Paṭaccaraḥ* means a thief, because he "moves about in clothes" (*paṭaṃ carati*), or "moves about tearing [clothes]" (*pāṭayan carati*), hence *pāṭaccaraḥ*; or *paṭaccaram* refers to a worn-out garment. It may mean "acting like a cloth" (*paṭa ivācarat*) or "one who previously was [so]" (*bhūtapūrvam*). From the *prajñādi* group (V, 4, 38), we have *cāraḥ*. By the rule *kvun śilpisaṃjñayoḥ* (Uṇ. II, 32), we have *Carakaḥ muniḥ* (the sage Caraka). Regarding *careḥ*...

*ṭaḥ* (Pāṇini III.2.16): *kurucaraḥ*, *kurucarī*; by *bhikṣā-senādāyeṣu ca* (III.2.17), *ṭaḥ* [is applied]: *bhikṣācaraḥ*, *senācaraḥ*, *ādāyacaraḥ*; by *alaṃ-kṛñ-nirākṛñ* (III.2.136), *iṣṇuc*: *cariṣṇuḥ*; by *gocara-saṃcara* (III.3.119), two [forms] are correct; by *icchā* (III.3.101), *paricaryā* is correct here; from common usage (*loka*), *caryā* is the state of those such as wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) established in means such as meditation; *yuc* (III.2.148): [is applied].

*Carana*: [the suffix] *lyuṭ* (Pāṇini III.1.115), hence *caraṇam*; [the suffix] *itra* in the sense of "moving" (*arti-lū-dhū-sū-khana-saha-car-itra*, Pāṇini III.2.184), hence *caritram*; [the suffix] *ṇitran* in the sense of "conduct" (*careḥ vṛtte*, Uṇādi IV.171), hence *cāritram*; [the suffix] *i* in the sense of "a wall-top" (*khanikaṣyañjyasi*, Uṇādi IV.139), hence *cariḥ*; [the suffix] *iṇ*, hence *cāriḥ*; [the suffix] *uṇ* in the sense of "beautiful" (*dṝ-sanijani*, Uṇādi I.3), hence *cāruḥ*; [the suffix] *u* in the sense of "an oblation-cooking vessel" (*bhṛ-mṛ-śṝ-tṝ-cari*, cf. Uṇādi I.7), hence *caruḥ*.

1. *Kādhoraṇaḥ* means an elephant-driver. 2. Regarding *soC*: see Hemacandra’s *Dhātupāṭha* I, 405; Pāṇini reads *tsadeḥ* and *tsadati*. 3. Here, *kmarah* in the sense of "moving about" (*hūrchaṇe*) has likely been omitted by mistake. 4. Pāṇini reads *yākṛñoḥ*. 5. Pāṇini reads *taṅānau*. 6. Pāṇini adds: "one who goes to the house. 7. Pāṇini reads *caraṭ*. 8. See Hemacandra’s *Uṇādisūtra* 619. 9. Regarding *uṇ* and *ñuṇ*: all manuscripts [read this]. By the rule *careś ca* (Uṇādi V, 69), the suffix *amac* is applied to *car*, forming *caramaḥ*; by the rule for the suffix *ktin* (III, 3, 94), *cūrtiḥ* is formed, as in *brahmacūrtiḥ*; and *caritam* (as noted in the Kāśikā on III, 3, 2) becomes *carma* (see Uṇādi 588–591).

The root *ṣṭhivu* means "to spit. According to the rule *na subdhātuṣṭhivuṣvakkīnām* (cf. VI.1.64.1), the *ṣ* at the beginning of the root is not changed to *s*. By the rule *ṣṭhivuklamvācamāṃ śiti* (VII.3.75, Kāśikā), there is lengthening [of the vowel]: *ṣṭhīvaṭi*. Alternatively, when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution (cf. Candra-S. I.3.98): *ṣṭhevanam*, *ṣṭhīvanam*; *ṣṭhyūtvā*, *ṣṭhīvitvā* (VII.2.56). Regarding *tiṣṭheva*: some say that this *th* follows the *ṣ* (cf. VI.1.64, Kāśikā); thus, *tiṣṭheva* (592).

*Ji* means to conquer. Here, *jayaḥ* signifies excellence (*utkarṣaḥ*). By the rule *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ* (Pāṇini I.3.19), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are applied: *vijayate*, *parājayate*. This root is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) in its object of application (*lakṣye*): *jetā*. For this very reason, Kauśika did not study this [root] under the rule *ji jri abhibhave* (Dhātupāṭha I.993–994), as [the forms] would already be established by that alone. [Objection: That is not so; both [roots] are mentioned for the sake of distinguishing between intransitive and transitive uses. From the rule *kṛvāpājimisvadisādhyaśūbhya uṇ* (Uṇādi-sūtra I.1), we derive *jāyuḥ* (medicine); and *jaitram*, meaning "belonging to the victor" (*jetuḥ*), by the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini IV.3.120). (593)

The root *jīv* means "to sustain life. It forms *jīvati* ("he lives") and *jīvaḥ* ("living being"); the short vowel [of the suffix] is applied by the rule *bhrājabhāsabhāṣadīpajīva* (Pāṇini VI.4.3). From it are derived: *ajijīvat* and *ajījivat* (the reduplication varies); *yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhuyāt* ("one should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice as long as one lives"), where the suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *yāvati vindajīvoḥ* (Pāṇini III.4.30); *jīvakaḥ* ("a bird"); *jīvañjīvaḥ*, a specific kind of bird; *jīvātuḥ* ("life-restoring medicine"), formed by the rule *jīver ātuḥ* (Uṇādi I.80); *jīvitam* ("life"); and *jīvitam* again, formed by the rule *jīver ātṛkan vṛddhiś ca* (Uṇādi I.81).

*Jaivātṛka* means the moon; *jīmūta* is a cloud, being the source (*mūta*) of life (*jīvana*). Regarding the rule *jīvikā saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini III, 3, 109): the roots *pīva*, *mīva*, *nīva*, and *tīva* denote stoutness. *Pīvati*; *pīvaḥ* means "thriving" or "well-nourished"; by the rule *chitvaracchatvara* (Uṇādi-sūtra III, 1), we have *pīvaraḥ*. *Nīviḥ*; *nīvī* means "capital" or "principal wealth. *Tīvaram*, *tīvram*. (594. 595. 596. 597. 598. 599)

In the sense of "vomiting" (*nirasana*): *kṣīvati*, *kṣīvitaḥ*, *acikṣivat*. From the root *kṣībṛ* in the sense of "intoxication" (*mada*) [DhP I.407], one has *kṣībate*, *kṣībaḥ*, and *acikṣībat*. According to Candra [DhP I.191], there is the root *kṣivu*: *kṣevati*, with gerunds *kṣyūtvā* and *kṣevitvā*; and in the *divādi* class [DhP IV.4], there is *kṣīvyati* (599).

The roots *urvī*, *turvī*, *durvī*, and *dhurvī* have the sense of "to injure. *urvati*; [the past participles are] *ūḥ* and *ūrṇaḥ*. *tūḥ*, *tūrṇaḥ*. *dūḥ*, *dūrṇaḥ*, *dūrvā*. *dhūḥ*, *dhūrṇaḥ*; by the rule *hasimṛgriṇ* (Uṇādi-sūtra III.86), the suffix *tan* is applied: *dhūrtaḥ*. Candra lists *thurvī* (Candra-dhātupāṭha I.195); the followers of Durga list *jurvī*: *jūrvati*, *juh*, *jūrṇaḥ* (rules 600, 601, 603, 604, 602). *gurvī* means "to lift up" (*udyame*). [Present: *gūrvati*. [Past participles: *gūḥ*, *udgūrṇaḥ*. In the *curādi* group, *gūrī* means "to lift up" (X.155): *āgūrayate* (rule 605).

1 *Pīvañjīvaka* and *cakora*. 2 Cf. *Uṇ.* III,91 and *Hem.* *Uṇ.* 216. 3 Thus all manuscripts. 4 *P* adds: "It is neuter. 5 *P*: "In the sense of injury" [49]. 1 *Murvī* in the sense of binding. It binds (*mūrvati*). *Mūrvā* is a grass; its derivative (according to IV,3,134) is *maurvī*; also *mūḥ*, *mūrṇaḥ* (606).
*Pūrv* and *parv* mean "to fill. From *pūrv*: *pūrvati*, *pūrvaḥ*. From *parv*: *parvati*, *parvataḥ* (607–609).

*Carv* means "to chew. *Carvati*. *Carvitaḥ*; *Cārvākaḥ*. In the *cur*-class (*curādi*), it is *carvayati* (1). *Arba* and *barba* end in labials (see sūtras 442 and 445) (610). *Bharv* means "to injure. *Bharvati*, *bharvaḥ* (611).
*Garva* means to humble or diminish pride. Some say that the repeated recitation of the six roots beginning with *carv* is for the sake of distinguishing their meanings.

*Arva* and *śarva* mean to injure. *Arvaḥ* and *śarvaḥ* [are used] in the sense of pervading. [In the form] *invati*, because the letter *v* is dental-labial (*dantyoṣṭhya*), it lacks the status of a *jhal* consonant; therefore, by Pāṇini VIII.3.24, there is no substitution of *anusvāra*. (618)

The roots *pivi*, *mivi*, and *nivi* mean "to sprinkle" (*secana*). They form *pinvati* and *minvati*. Some say they mean "to serve" (*sevana*) (619–621). The roots *ivi*, *jivi*, *divi*, and *dhivi* have the meaning "to please" (*prīṇana*). [From *ivi*: *invati*; *invakāḥ* refers to the stars of Mṛgaśiras. [From *jivi*: *jinvati*. [From *dhivi*: by the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyor a ca* (Pāṇini III.1.80), there is the *uv*-suffix: *dhinoti*. The followers of Candra also include *hivī* (Ca. Dh. I.204): *hinvati* (622–625).

The roots *rivi*, *ravi*, *davi*, and *dhavi* have the meaning "to go" (*gati*). [They form: *riṇvati*, *raṇvati*. [The roots] *abi* and *rabī* end in labials (403, 401): *rambate*; *karambaḥ*, *karambitam*. [From *dhanv*: *dhanvati*; *dhanvā* (626–628).

The root *kṛvi* is used in the senses of "injury" and "doing. By the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyor a ca* (Pāṇini III.1.80), [the suffix *u* is added and the vowel is replaced by *a*]: *kṛṇoti* (629). The root *mava* is used in the sense of "binding. By the rule *jvaratvarasrivyavimavām upadhāyāś ca* (VI.4.20), *ūṭh* is substituted for the penultimate vowel: *mūḥ*, *muvau* (630).

The root *ava* is used in eighteen senses: protection, motion, beauty, pleasure, satisfaction, understanding, entry, hearing, lordship, requesting, action, desire, radiance, attainment, embracing, injury, giving, and increase. It has eighteen meanings. It means "he protects" (*avati*). From this root, the forms *ūḥ*, *uvau*, and *ūtiḥ* are derived. The form *ūtiḥ* is established by Pāṇini III.3.97: *ūti-yūti-jūti-*. The word *otuḥ* ("cat") is formed by Uṇādi-sūtra I.70: *sitanigami-*, with the suffix *tun*. The word *om* is formed by Uṇādi-sūtra I.141: *avateṣ ṭilopaś ca*. The word *oniḥ* is formed by Uṇādi-sūtra II.103: *artisṛdhṛdhamyaśi-*.

*Avaniḥ*: from the roots *iṇ*, *sīdīṅ*, *uṣ*, and *vi*, the suffix *nak* is applied (cf. Uṇ. III.2): *ūnaḥ*. From the roots *avi*, *tṛ*, *stṛ*, and *tantri*, the suffix *īḥ* is applied (Uṇ. III.158): *avīḥ*, meaning "a menstruating woman. From the root *in* (Uṇ. IV.117): *aviḥ*. [The words] *avaṭaḥ* and *avinaḥ* (631) have acute accents on the first syllable (*udāttā udāttetaḥ*). 596. 1 Cf. Hem. Dh. I.453. 2 All manuscripts read thus. 3 P reads *cety uvikaraṇaḥ* I.50.

The root *dhāv* means "to cleanse. It is marked with the acute (*udātta*) accent on its final vowel. Because it is marked with the circumflex (*svarita*) accent and has the augment *iṭ*, the Atmanepada suffix is applied according to Pāṇini 1.3.72 (*svaritettvāt svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*), as in: *dhāvate pādau* ("he washes his feet") or *dhāvati*. From it are derived: *dhāvitvā* / *dhautvā* (gerund), *dhautaḥ* (past passive participle), and *dhāvakaḥ* (agentive noun). Regarding the root *dhāv* (DhP 1.982), they say it denotes "swift motion" (632). The roots *dhukṣ* and *dhikṣ* mean "to kindle," "to afflict," and "to live. From here until the end of this section (682), forty-six roots are marked with the augment *iṭ* and take the Atmanepada endings. Examples include: *dhukṣate* (present), *saṃdhukṣitaḥ* (past passive participle) (633, 634).
The root *vṛkṣ* means "to cover. *Vṛkṣaḥ*.

(635) The root *śikṣ* means "to acquire knowledge. Regarding *śikṣer jijñāsāyām* (Pāṇini I.3.21), the ātmanepada endings and the suffix *āna* are applied: one practices with the bow (*dhanuṣi śikṣate*), whereas elsewhere one practices (*śikṣati*), meaning "he desires to be able" (*śaktum icchati*) by means of the desiderative suffix *san* (Pāṇini III.1.7). [The forms] *śikṣitaḥ* and *śikṣā*. (636)

*Bhikṣ* is used in the sense of begging (*yācñā*), whether there is lack of gain or gain, and in the sense of affliction (*kleśa*) or manifest speech (*vyaktā vāk*). There is a separate enumeration of these meanings as they are established in various regions and so forth. From *bhikṣate*: by the rule *jalpabhikṣa* (Pāṇini III.2.155), the suffix *ṣākan* is applied, yielding *bhikṣākaḥ* (masculine) and *bhikṣākī* (feminine). By the rule *sanāśaṃsa* (Pāṇini III.2.168), the suffix *u* is applied, yielding *bhikṣuḥ*. Regarding the inclusion of "affliction" (*kleśa*), the refined scholars (*sabhyāḥ*) read it separately; accordingly, there is the Cāndra-sūtra *kleśa bhāṣaṇe* (Cāndra Dhātupāṭha I.445), and according to Durga, *kleśa* means "to oppress" (*bādhana*): thus *kleśate*, *kleśati*.

*Śitaḥ*; in the *divādi* group (cf. IV.52a) it is *kliśyati*, in the *kryādi* group (IX.50) it is *kliśnāti*, and in the *curādi* group (? it is *kleśayati* (637, 638). *Dakṣa* [is used] in the sense of growth and speed. It takes the form *dakṣate*. *Dakṣaḥ* (masculine); in the feminine, by the rule *Āsuridākṣibhyāṃ ṣphaḥ* (cf. IV.1.19, 1), we have *Dākṣāyaṇī Tārā*. From the roots *dru* and *dakṣi*, by the suffix *inan* (*Uṇ.* II.50), we have *dakṣiṇaḥ*. From *śru*, *dakṣi*, and *spṛhi*, by the suffix *āyyaḥ* (cf. *Uṇ.* III.96), we have *Dakṣāyyo Garuḍaḥ*; his offspring is *dākṣāyyo gṛdhraḥ* (639).

In the cases of *dīkṣā*, shaving (*mauṇḍya*), sacrifice (*ijyā*), initiation (*upanayana*), restraint (*niyama*), and the instruction of vows (*vrata-ādeśa*). Shaving is the act of tonsure; sacrifice is the performance of a ritual; initiation is the tying of the girdle of muñja grass; restraint is self-control; and the instruction of vows is the proclamation of the purificatory rites. [The root] *dīkṣ* is used: "he undergoes initiation" (*dīkṣate*). Regarding the forms *dīkṣitvā* and *dīkṣā*, the suffix *yuc* does not apply by the rule *sūda-dīpa-dīkṣaś ca* (Pāṇini III.2.153); thus we have *dīkṣitā*. Others say that *dīkṣ* occurs in the sense of shaving and *jyā* in the sense of initiation and so forth: *jyavate*, *jīnaḥ*. (640)

The root *īkṣ* means "to see. By the rule *rādhīkṣyor yasya vipraśnaḥ* (Pāṇini I.4.39), [Caitra] becomes the recipient (*saṃpradāna*): *caitrāyēkṣate* ("he gazes at Caitra"). By the rule *īkṣikṣamibhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini III.2.1,8), the suffix *ṇa* is applied: *grāmekṣā* ("the act of looking at the village") as a feminine noun; likewise *prekṣā*. The root *īṣ* is used in the senses of "motion," "injury," and "seeing" (*gati-hiṃsā-darśaneṣu*). He moves (*īṣate*). By the rule *ac* (Pāṇini III.1.134), the suffix *ac* is applied: *īṣā* ("pole" or "shaft"). 1. P: *vegita-gatau* ("in rapid motion"); 2. All manuscripts; 3. KC: *jyopanayanādau*; 4. All manuscripts, cf. also Hemacandra Dhātupāṭha I.881 and Vopadeva 11.2; 5. P: *°dāneṣu*.

51. 1. *kīlikā*; from the root *īṣ* with the suffixes *halanasa*, there is a single substitute (*pararūpa*): *halīṣā* (the pole of a plow), *manīṣā* (wisdom). From the root *īṣ*, with the suffix *kiṅ* (Uṇ. I.14): *iṣuḥ* (an arrow). From the root *īṣ*, with the suffix *ikaḥ* and the vowel shortened (Uṇ. IV.21): *iṣīkā* (the tip of a blade of grass). The root *bhāṣ* means "to speak clearly. It forms *bhāṣate*. Due to the rule *bhrājabhāsa-* (Pāṇini VI.1.15), the vowel may be shortened: *ababhāṣat* or *abībhaṣat*. [The derivatives are] *bhāṣyam* (that which is to be spoken), *bhāṣitam* (spoken), and *bhāṣā* (speech). (642–643)

The root *parṣ* means "to moisten. It forms *parṣate*. According to *Uṇādi-sūtra* IV.52, *pārṣṇiḥ* [is derived from this root] as well as *ghṛṇi* and *prṣṇi*. *Parṣat* and *pariṣat*, however, are derived from the root *sad* (I.907). (644) *Geṣṛ* means "to seek. Seeking (*anvicchā*) is searching. It forms *geṣate*; the aorist is *ajigeṣat*. (645) *Yeṣṛ* means "to strive. It forms *yeṣate*. (646) *Jeṣṛ*, *ṇeṣṛ*, *eṣṛ*, and *hreṣṛ* mean "to go. [From *jeṣṛ*] it forms *jeṣate*. [From *ṇeṣṛ*] it forms *neṣate*, and [the agent noun] *naptṛ* and *neṣṭṛ* [are derived from it].

In this regard [Uṇ. II, 96], the form *iṣ* is not desired. From the root *iṣ* (meaning "to seek") belonging to the sixth class (*tudādi*, VI, 59), we have *anveṣate* and *anveṣitaḥ*; however, from the same root belonging to the fourth class (*divādi*, IV, 19), meaning "to go," we have *anviṣyati*. From the root *iṣ* meaning "desire" belonging to the sixth class (*tudādi*, VI, 59), we have *anvicchati*. From the root *iṣ* meaning "repetition" belonging to the ninth class (*kryādi*, IX, 53), we have *anviṣṇāti*. From the tenth class (*curādi*), we have *anveṣayati*. As for the form *anveṣṭī*, it is a usage based on error. (647–650) The root *heṣṛ* (meaning "inarticulate sound") is used as follows: *heṣate aśvaḥ* ("the horse neighs"). The past participle is *heṣitam*, and the abstract noun is *heṣā*. Candra also lists the root *reṣṛ* (Candra Dhātupāṭha I, 455). (652, 651)

The root *kās* is used in the sense of "sound" and "contempt. Contempt for sound arises from being afflicted by disease. [Examples: *kāsate*; by rule III.1.35 (*kāspratyayād ām*), [the perfect form is] *kāsāñcakre*. [Nouns derived from it are] *kāsaḥ* ("cough") and *vikāsaḥ* ("expansion"), [the latter] from the root *kas* (DhP I.913). (654)

The root *bhāsṛ* means "to shine. By the rule *bhrājabhāsa-* (VH 4.3), the vowel may be shortened: *ababhāsat*, *abībhasat*. By the rule *bhañjabhāsamido ghurac* (III.2.161), the suffix *ghurac* is added: *bhāsuraḥ*. By the rule *stheśabhāsa-* (III.2.175), the suffix *varac* is added: *bhāsvaraḥ*. By the rule *bhrājabhāsa-* (III.2.177), the suffix *kvip* is added: *bhāḥ*. From *bhāti* (Dhātupāṭha II.42), the form is *bhā*; by the rule *cintipūji-* (III.3.105), the suffix *aṅ* is added due to the inclusion of the letter *ca*; and by the rule *guroś ca halaḥ* (III.3.103), the suffix *ap* is added: *bhāsā* (655).

*rāsṛ* in the sense of sound: *rāsate*. From *rās* and *valli*, [the suffix *abha* is added] according to Uṇādi III.125, thus *rāsabhaḥ*; also *rāsnā* and *rāsakaḥ*. (657) *ṇāsṛ* in the sense of sound: *nāsate*. (656) *ṇasa* in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilye*): from this [root], *nasate*; thus *nāsā* and *nāsikā*. (658) 1. There is a substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) for the root *īṣ*. 2. P adds that it is also used in the sense of "a blade" (*halārtha*). 3. This rule is found in later recensions of the *śakandhvādi* group under Pāṇini VI.1.94, but not yet in Bhartṛhari or the Kāśikā. 4. P reads *iṣikā*. 5. KC reads *preṣṛ*. 6. P adds *rāsaḥ*. 7. P reads *asmāt*.
I 52 *bhyasa* means "to fear. *bhyasate*. Regarding *bheṣṛ*, Candra (Ca. Dh. I, 607) states: *bheṣate* (659).

The root *ā-śas* is used in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*). [Examples: *āśaṃsate*, *āśaṃsyate*. [The noun] *āśaṃsā*; and by the rule *sanāśaṃsabhikṣām uḥ* (cf. HI 2, 168), [the agentive suffix] *u* is applied: *āśaṃsuḥ*. Regarding the root *śaṃs* in the sense of "praise" (*stuti*) [DhP I, 764], [the forms] *śaṃsati*, *śasyate*, and *śastam* are derived. Durga states that [the root here is] *ā-śās*: [examples are] *āśāsate*, *āśāsyate*, *āśāsitvā* / *āśāstvā*, *āśāsā*, *āśāstaḥ*. In the *adādi* class, *ā-śās* is used in the sense of "desire" (II, 12); with the *taṅ* suffixes: *āśāste*, *āśīḥ*. Likewise, for *śās* in the sense of "instruction" (*anuśiṣṭi*) [DhP II, 66]: *śāsti* (660).

*Gras* and *glas* mean "eating. [From the root *gras*: one eats (*grasate*). Having eaten (*grastvā*, *grasitvā*), [the past passive participle] *grastaḥ*. [The noun] *grāmaḥ* is formed by the rule *grasater ā ca* (Uṇ. I, 142); likewise *grāsaḥ*. [The word] *grīṣmaḥ* is formed according to Uṇ. I, 149. (661, 662) *Īh* means "exertion" or "striving. One exerts oneself (*īhate*); [perfect] *īhāṃcakre*; [future] *īhitā*. [Past passive participle] *īhitam*; [abstract noun] *īhā*. (663) *Bahi* and *mahi* mean "increase. [Present] *baṃhate*. [The word] *bahu* is formed according to the rule *laṅghibaṃhyor nalopaś ca* (Uṇ. I, 30). [Present] *maṃhate*. [The word] *mahat* is formed in the sense of the present tense according to *pṛṣadbṛhad* (Uṇ. II, 84). However, *mahī* is derived from the root *mahi* in the sense of "worship" (DhP. X, 321). (664, 665)

The root *ahi* means "to go. From the root *aṃh*, [we derive] *aṃhas* (sin), according to the rule *āhanter ḍo hrasvaḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra IV.137): thus *ahiḥ* (snake) and *aṃhriḥ* (foot). Three roots beginning with *cur* (tenth class) have the sense of shining (*bhāsārtha*): *aṃhayati*, *baṃhayati*, *maṃhayati*. (666) *garha* and *galha* mean "censure" (*kutsana*). One censures (*garhate*); [the noun] *garhā*. *garha* in the sense of "blaming" (*vinindana*) belongs to the *cur*-class (tenth class) or optionally takes *ṇic*: *garhayati*, *garhati*. (667, 668)

The roots *barh* and *balh* signify preeminence (*prādhānya*). From *barh*, with the suffix *vun* (Pāṇini III.1.150), we have *Barhakaḥ* and *prabarhaḥ*. *Balhaḥ*; from the place-name *Balhi*, by rule IV.3.53, we have *Bālhikaḥ*. The roots *vehr̥*, *jehr̥*, and *bāhr̥* denote effort (*prayatna*). From *vehr̥*: *vehati*; "a cow that miscarries" (*saṃścattṛpadvehad*) is called *vehad* (Uṇ. II. 85); some say it means "she destroys" (*vihanti*). From *bāhr̥*: by [the rule] *kṣubdhasvānta* (Pāṇ. VII. 2. 18), from *bāhr̥* we have *bāḍham* and *bāhitam*. From *vah* in the sense of "carrying" (*prāpaṇa*) (DhP. I. 1053): *vahati*, *vahate*, *voḍhā* (674–676).
From *drāhr̥* in the sense of "throwing down" (*nikṣepa*): *drāhate*, *drāhyam*. Durga says that *drāha* means "the cessation of sleep" (*nidrākṣaya*). (677)

The root *kāś* means "to shine. It forms *kāśate*; and how does it form *cākaśīti*? Here, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) must be stated. [Examples: *kāśaḥ*, *prakāśaḥ*, *akāśaḥ*, *pratīkāśaḥ*, *nīkāśaḥ*. 1 KC *bhesṛ* and *bhesate*; 2 P adds *āśāstiḥ*; 3 P *bahuḥ*; 4 KC *kutsāyām*; 5 KC *plīha*; 6 KC omits; 7 P *nidrākṣaye*; 53 I.

In the word *kāśe*, there is lengthening by [Pāṇini] VI, 3, 123. From the rule *hani-kuṣi-nī-rami* (Uṇ. II, 2), we have *kāṣṭham*; and from *in* (Uṇ. IV, 117): *Kāśiḥ* is a country (678). The root *ūh* means "to reason" (*tarka*). Reasoning (*tarka*) is conjecture (*utprekṣā*). One reasons (*ūhate*). By the rule *upasargād asyatyūhyoḥ* (I, 3, 29, 3), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings or *āna* (the present middle participle suffix) may optionally apply: *samūhati*, *samūhate*. [The nouns] *samūhaḥ* [and *samūhaḥ*]. By the rule *upasargād dhrasva ūhateḥ* (VII, 4, 23): *samuhyate*, *parisamuhya*, *samuhyo 'gniḥ* (679).

The root *gāh* means "to stir" (*viloḍane*). Stirring is agitation (*parimalanam*). One stirs the water; [the forms] are *gāḍhā* and *gāhitā* (Pāṇini VII.2.44). *Gāḍhaḥ* (VII.2.15). (680) *glah* means "to seize" (*grahaṇe*). [One] seizes (*glahate*); [the forms] are *glāḍhā* and *glahitā*. Candra and Durga read the root as *gṛh* (Candra-Dhātupāṭha I.472). (681) *ghas* means "to do" (*karaṇe*). [One] does (*ghaṃsate*). Candra says it is *ghaṣ*: [one] does (*ghaṃṣate*). Durga says *ghuṣ* means "to produce luster" (*kāntikaraṇa*): [one] produces luster (*ghuṃṣate*). (682) 2.

Those beginning with *udātta* and ending with *anudāttet* (643), starting from *ghuṣir* in the sense of "making sound," up to *arha*, are eighty-eight roots that take the augment *iṭ* and are *parasmaipada*. Examples: *ghoṣati*; *aghuṣat*; *aghoṣīt*. By the rule *ghuṣir aviśabdane* (Pāṇini VII.2.23), the augment *iṭ* is not added to the *niṣṭhā* suffixes: *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope has been sounded"), but not here: *saṃghuṣitaṃ vākyam* ("the sentence was articulated"). In the *curādi* class, *ghuṣir* is used in the sense of "articulating" (*viśabdane*) [X.187]: *ghoṣayati*; by the *uṇādi* suffix *itnuc* (Uṇ. III.29): *ghoṣayitnuḥ* (683).

The root *akṣū* means "to pervade" and "to collect. By [Pāṇini III.1.75], *śnu* is optionally applied: *akṣati*, *akṣṇoti*; past participle *aṣṭa*, *akṣita*. *Akṣam*, *akṣaram*. The roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* mean "to make thin. By [Pāṇini III.1.76], *śnu* is applied when meaning "to make thin": *taksati*, *takṣṇoti*. But not here: *saṃtakṣati vāgbhiḥ* ("he refines with words"); past participle *taṣṭa*, agent noun *takṣitā*; *taṣṭaḥ*, *takṣā*, *Takṣakaḥ*. *tvakṣati*; *tvaṣṭā*, *tvakṣitā*. *Tvakṣ* is used for the purpose of distinguishing the meaning from *tvac* ("skin") [VI.1.685, 686]. [KC add *grahū*]

2. Hemacandra, I.856, apparently following Kṣīrasvāmin: *ghasuḍ* in the sense of "making" (*karaṇe*), [the form] *ghaṃsate*. Candra states that this root ends in a retroflex nasal (*mūrdhanya*): *ghaṃṣate*. Candra himself (I.473): *ghuṣir* (read as *ghuṣi*) in the sense of "making. Maitreya (I.653): *ghuṣi* in the sense of "making beautiful" (*kāntikaraṇe*), [the form] *ghuṃṣate*. Mādhava (I.642), like Maitreya, adds: "Candra and Kāśyapa read it with an *it*-augment and a short penultimate vowel (*itupadha*), as *ghiṣ*, while Svāmī (i.e., Kṣīrasvāmin) reads it as *ghas*."

(He read it as *ghasīti*, ending in a dental and with *a* as the penultimate vowel. Just as we do, so too did Deva, Maitreya, and Durgā. Thus, this is a verb that circulated in several forms (*ghaṃsate*, *ghaṃṣate*, *ghiṃṣate*, *ghuṃṣate*), appearing to be a word from the lower vernacular (the *kāntikaraṇe*—according to them, in the sense of "covering," i.e., *pāmśukaraṇe*).
A verb with the same meaning was *dhuṣ* (X, 98), and this too exhibits a similar fluctuation from a phonetic standpoint: 3rd person singular *addit*, 4th person singular *taṣṭ̣am* (I, 54).

The root *ukṣ* means "to sprinkle. [From it derive] *ukṣatī*, *ukṣitaḥ*, and by Uṇādi-sūtra I.158, *ukṣan* with the suffix *nity*, forming *ukṣā* (687). The root *rakṣ* means "to protect. [Examples: *caurād rakṣati* ("he protects from a thief"). By Uṇādi-sūtra IV.188, with the suffix *asun*: *rakṣaḥ* (688). The root *ṇikṣ* means "to kiss. Kissing is the contact of the mouth. [Examples: *praṇikṣati*. Regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the forms *praṇikṣitā* and *pranikṣitā*, Pāṇini VIII.4.33 states: "The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs after *pra* in the case of the roots *nikṣ*, *niṃs*, and *nind*" (689).

The roots *tṛkṣ*, *stṛkṣ*, and *ṇakṣ* mean "to go. From *tṛkṣ* comes *Tārkṣya*, meaning "the offspring of Tṛkṣa" (Pāṇini IV.1.105). It is correct that *stṛkṣ* is taught with an initial *ṣ*; thus the followers of the Cāndra school read: *tṛkṣa*, *ṣṭṛkṣa*, *ṇakṣa* (cf. Ca. Dh. I.215). From the rule *aminakṣi* (Uṇādi III.105), the suffix *atran* is applied to form *nakṣatram*. Regarding the rule *nabhrāṭ* (VI.3.75), the fact that this word is listed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) is for the purpose of indicating that the etymological derivation of nouns is not fixed. (690–692) The root *makṣ* means "to injure. It forms *makṣati*. With the suffix *ghañ* (I.3.121), it forms *makṣaḥ*. *Makṣikā* ("fly") is mentioned in the phrase *yūkā-makṣī-kamaṅkuṇam* (694), which is Vedic (*cchāndasa*).
The root *vakṣ* means "to strike" (*saṃghāte*). By [the rule] *asun* (Uṇ. IV.188), *vakṣaḥ* is formed.

(693) The root *tvakṣ* means "to cover" (*tvacane*). Covering is the grasping of the skin, or "concealing," according to Durga. (695) The root *tvaṣṭ̣ā* [is derived from] *sūrkṣya*, meaning "to disregard. It forms *sūrkṣyati*. According to Candra (Ca. DII. I.219), this root ends in *ṣ*: *sūrkṣati*; non-disregard is *asūrkṣaṇam*, which is non-contempt. Even though it ends in *y*, by [the rule] *yasya halaḥ* (Pāṇini VI.4.49), there is the elision of *y*. (697) 3.

The roots *kāṅkṣi*, *vāṅkṣi*, *māṅkṣi*, *drāṅkṣi*, *dhraṅkṣi*, and *dhvāṅkṣi* are used in the sense of longing (*kāṅkṣā*). Examples: *kāṅkṣati*; *drākṣā* (grape); *dhvāṅkṣaḥ* (crow). According to Durga, *drāṅkṣi*, *dhraṅkṣi*, and *dhvāṅkṣi* are also used in the sense of a terrible cry (*ghoranirvāśita*).

Some say that *pakṣi* means "to accept" (*parigraha*) (696). *Cūṣa* means "to drink" (*pāna*): *cūṣati*; *cūṣitaḥ*; having drunk (*cūṣitvā*) (704). *Tūṣa* means "to be satisfied" (*tuṣṭi*): *tūṣati*. However, in the *divādi* group (IV.75), it is *tuṣyati* (705). *Pūṣa* means "to grow" (*vṛddhi*): *pūṣati*. *Puṣa* means "to nourish" (*puṣṭi*) (I.732): *poṣati*.

In the *divādi* class (IV. 73), it is *puṣyati*; in the *kryādi* class (IX. 57), *puṣṇāti*; and in the *curādi* class (X. 210), *poṣayati*. By the rule *śvan-ukṣan* (Uṇ. I. 158), *pūṣā* [is formed]. The root *mūṣa* means "stealing" (*steye*). It forms *mūṣati*. *Mūṣā* is a crucible for melting metals; it is listed in the *gaurādi* group (IV. 1. 41) as *mūṣī*. With the suffix *ṇvul* (III. 1. 133), we have *mūṣakaḥ* (mouse). In the *kaṣādi* group, *muṣ* has the meaning of "injury" (*hiṃsārtha*) (I. 723): *moṣati*. In the *kryādi* class (IX. 58), *muṣ* means "stealing": *muṣṇāti*. By the rule *muṣer dīrghaś ca* (Uṇ. II. 42), the suffix *ika* is added with a long vowel, yielding *mūṣikaḥ* (mouse). Durga states that *lūṣa* is also [used in this sense] (707, 708).
*Ṣūṣa* means "in procreation. It forms *sūṣati* and *suṣūṣa*. According to Caraka, it begins with the palatal (*tālavya*): *śūṣā* is a type of herb.

The roots *yūṣ* and *jūṣ* mean "to injure. *Yūṣaḥ*, *yūṣam*; *jūṣitaḥ*; *jūṣā*. (711) *Bhūṣ* means "to adorn. *Bhūṣati*; *bhūṣā*. In the *curādi* class (X, 190), it is *bhūṣayati*. Regarding the suffix *tasi*, Durga says it is *bhūṣeti*: *taṃsati*; *uttaṃsaḥ*, *avataṃsaḥ*. (712, 713) *Ūṣ* means "injury" or "heat. *Ūṣati*. *Ūṣaḥ* is alkaline soil; *ūṣmā* is heat; *ūṣaṇam* is black pepper; *tryūṣaṇam* is the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*). (714)
The root *īṣ* means "to glean. It forms *īṣati*. From it come *īṣā* ("a probe for seeking wounds") [Uṇ. I, 14], *iṣuḥ* ("an arrow") [Uṇ.

I, 14], and *iṣīkā* ("a blade of grass") [Uṇ. IV, 21]. (715) The roots *kaṣ*, *śiṣ*, *jaṣ*, *jhaṣ*, *śaṣ*, *vaṣ*, *maṣ*, *muṣ*, *ruṣ*, and *riṣ* have the meaning "to injure. *Kaṣati*. *Nikaṣaḥ* ("a touchstone") is a stone. By [Pāṇini] VI, 3, 54 and III, 2, 42, the suffix *khac* is applied: *kūlaṃkaṣaḥ* ("one who destroys the bank"). By VII, 2, 22, when the suffix *kta* follows, there is no *iṭ* augment for *kaṣ* used with the words *kṛcchra* and *gahana*: *kaṣṭaḥ agniḥ* ("a distressing fire"). By III, 4, 34, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after *nimūla* and *samūla* with *kaṣ*; according to the rule *kaṣādiṣu tair evānuprayogaḥ* (III, 4, 46), the same verb is used in the subsequent construction.

According to Uṇādi-sūtra I.86, *kaṣeś cha ca*, we have *kacchūḥ*, meaning "scabies" or "itching. According to Uṇādi-sūtra III.62 (*vṝtṝvadi*), the suffix *sa* is applied: *kakṣaḥ* means "grass," as well as "the armpit" or "the root of the thighs. However, near a house, it means "a fence" or "a girdle" (*kakṣyā*). From the roots *kaṣ* and *dūs*, with the suffix *īkan* (Uṇādi IV.16), we have *kaṣīkā*. According to Kaṇṭha, there is also [the root] *khaṣ*: *khaṣati*, *khaṣaḥ* (cf. 716–725). *bhaṣ* means "to scold. It has sound as its object, meaning to make a contemptible sound. III.42), *ulmukam* (Uṇ. III.84), *ulapaḥ* (denoting a fine creeper), *ulvam* (Uṇ. IV.95) meaning the placenta (*jarāyuḥ*). From the rule *uṣikuṣigartibhyas than* (Uṇ. II.4): *oṣṭhaḥ* (lip). By [the rule] *bhyāṃ kit* (Uṇ. IV, 161): *uṣṭrali*, *uṣṭrī*; by *uṣaḥ kit* (Uṇ. IV, 233): *uṣāḥ*; by *asun* (Uṇ. IV, 188): *uṣaḥ* meaning dawn.

(727) The roots *jiṣu*, *viṣu*, and *miṣu* mean "to sprinkle. [From *viṣu*] one forms *pariveṣati*. In the *hvādi* group, *viṣḷ* means "to pervade" (III, 13): *veveṣṭi*. [From *miṣu*] one forms *meṣati*; in the *pacādi* group (III, 1, 134), *meṣaḥ*. In the *tudādi* group, *miṣa* means "to vie" (VI, 60): *miṣati*. [The roots] *miśa* and *maśa* mean "sound"; they end in palatals (tālavya) (I, 759–760). (728–730)

The root *puṣ* means "to nourish. [Present tense: *poṣati*; [future: *poṣitā*; [aorist: *apoṣīt*. By the rule *puṣaḥ kit* (Uṇ. IV.4), [the suffix *ara* with the *kit* marker] yields *puṣkaram* ("lotus"); by *kalaś ca* (Uṇ. IV.5), [the suffix *ala* with the *ka* marker] yields *puṣkalam* ("abundant"). By *stanihṛṣipuṣi* (Uṇ. III.29), [the suffix *itnu*] yields *poṣayitnuḥ* ("one who nourishes"). By *sve puṣa* (Pāṇ. III.4.40), [the suffix *ṇamul*] yields *svapoṣaṃ puṣṭaḥ* ("he was nourished according to his own capacity"). In the *divādi* group (IV.73), it is *puṣyati*. By *puṣādidyutādi* (III.1.55), [the suffix *aṅ* is used] in the *luṅ* tense: *apuṣat*. In the *kryādi* group (IX.57), it is *puṣṇāti*. In the *curādi* group, *puṣa* in the sense of "supporting" (X.210) yields *poṣayati* (732).

The roots *śriṣ*, *śliṣ*, *pruṣ*, and *pluṣ* mean "to burn. *Śreṣati* and *śleṣati*; [aorist] *aśreṣīt*, *aśleṣīt*; [gerund] *śriṣṭvā*, *śliṣṭvā*, *śreṣitvā*, *śleṣitvā* (Pāṇini VII.2.56). *Śliṣ* in the sense of "embracing" belongs to the *divādi* group (IV.77): *śliṣyati*; [noun] *śleṣmā*. *Śliṣ* in the sense of "causing to adhere" belongs to the *curādi* group (X.38): *śleṣayati*. *Ploṣati*; in the *divādi* group (IV.8, 107) [we have] *pluṣyati*; [gerund] *ploṣitvā*, *pluṣṭvā*; [past participle] *pluṣṭaḥ*. In the *kryādi* group, *pruṣ* and *pluṣ* mean "to sprinkle with oil" or "to fill" (IX.55, 56): *pruṣṇāti*, *pluṣṇāti* (733–736).

The roots *pṛṣu*, *vṛṣu*, and *mṛṣu* mean "to sprinkle. [From *pṛṣu*: *parṣati*. In the sense of the present tense, *pṛṣat* is derived by *Uṇ.* I.84: "In *pṛṣad-bṛhad*," etc.; and by *Uṇ.* III.111: "After *pṛṣi* and *rañji*, [the suffix *at* is] *kit*": thus *pṛṣataḥ* means both a deer and a drop. In the *Uṇādi* section: *pṛṣṭham* (*Uṇ.* II.12), *pārṣṇiḥ* (*Uṇ.* IV.52), *Parjanyaḥ* (*Uṇ.* III.103), and *pṛṣṇiḥ* (1) means a ray. However, from the root *spṛś* [by *Uṇ.* III.103], *pṛśniḥ* (VI.128) means one with a small body (*alpa-tanuḥ*) [*Uṇ.* IV.52]. [From *vṛṣu*: *varṣati*. By *Pāṇini* III.1.120, "Optionally after *kṛ* and *vṛṣ*, [the suffix] *kyap* [is applied]."

*vṛṣya* means "rainy" (*varṣyam*). By [Pāṇini] III.1.135, *vṛṣaḥ*; by III.2.154, *laṣapatapadasthābhūvṛṣa*, [the suffix *u* is added] to form *varṣukaḥ*. By the rule III.3.56 (Kāśikā), "there is an addition of *bhaya* and others in the prescription of *ac*," [the suffix *ac* is added] to form *varṣam*. By III.1.134, *aci*, *varṣā* refers to the season. From the gerundive suffixes *ktvā* and *lyap*, we have *vṛṣṭvā* and *varṣitvā*. From the past passive participle suffix *kta*, *vṛṣṭam*. When the agent is intended, as in "the god has rained," it is *vṛṣṭo devaḥ*. By Uṇādi-sūtra I.156, *kanin yuvṛṣi*, *vṛṣā* refers to Indra. Also, from the rule *ṛṣivṛṣibhyāṃ kic ca* (cf. Uṇādi-sūtra).

Thus he said: from *vṛṣa* with the suffix *ala*, according to Uṇādi I.108 (*vṛṣādibhyaś cit*), we have *vṛṣala*; from *sṛ* and *vṛṣi* with the suffix *kit*, according to Uṇādi IV.49, we have *vṛṣṇi*; from *vṛṣ* with the suffix *ṛt*, according to Pāṇini VI.3.116 (*nahivṛtivṛṣi...*), with lengthening, we have *prāvṛṭ*. From *mṛṣu* in the sense of enduring (*sahane*), we have *marṣati*; having endured, *mṛṣṭvā* or *marṣitvā*; because of the rule *mṛṣas titikṣāyām* (Pāṇini I.2.20), this root does not take the *kit* designation [in the gerund], since the phrase *na ktvā seṭ* (I.2.18) is understood to apply there: hence *mṛṣṭam*.

In the sense of "enduring" (*mṛṣyati*) or "speaking words that have been endured" (*apamṛṣitaṃ vākyam āha*), the suffix *yuc* is applied according to Pāṇini III.3.130 (as cited in the Kāśikā) for verbal roots used in common speech (*bhāṣāyām*). Thus, from the root *śās*, we have *durśāsanaḥ*; from *yudh*, *duryodhanaḥ*. From the root *bhṛṣu*, meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*) and "to strike together" (*saṃghāta*), we derive *bharṣati*. 1. Compare Hemacandra’s *Uṇādisūtra* 635.57.1. *Durmarṣaṇaḥ* (737–739). *Bhṛṣu* (739a): to injure and to strike together. *Bharṣati*. (See Hemacandra’s *Uṇādisūtra* 635). 57.1.

*Ghr̥ṣu* [is used] in the sense of rubbing (*saṃgharṣe*). It forms *gharṣati*. From the gerundives *ghr̥ṣṭvā* and *gharṣitvā*, and from the past passive participle *ghr̥ṣṭaḥ*; by [the rule] *lyuḥ* (Pāṇini III, 1, 134), one has *saṃgharṣaṇaḥ* (740). *Hr̥ṣu* [is used] in the sense of being false or feigning (*alīke*). It forms *harṣati*. From the gerundives *hr̥ṣṭvā* and *harṣitvā*, and from the past passive participle *hr̥ṣṭaḥ*; by [the rule] *hṛṣer lomasv* (Pāṇini VII, 2, 29), one has *hṛṣitāni lomāni* ("the hairs are bristling"); and in the senses of being astonished or struck back (as noted in the Kāśikā on VII, 2, 29): *hṛṣṭaś Caitraḥ*, *hṛṣitaḥ*. By [the Uṇādi rule] *hṛṣer ulac* (Uṇādi I, 98), one has *harṣulaḥ*; by [the Uṇādi rule] *stanihṛṣi* (Uṇādi III, 29), one has *harṣayitnuḥ*. In the *divādi* group, *hr̥ṣa* is used in the sense of being pleased (*tuṣṭau*) (IV, 119): it forms *hṛṣyati* (741).

The verbal roots *tuṣ*, *hras*, *hlās*, and *ras* have the meaning of "sound. *tuṣati*; *Tosalaḥ* (name of a king), *Tosalā* (name of a region). *hrasati*; *hrasitaḥ*, *hrasvaḥ*. *hlāsati*. *rasati*, *rasitam*; in the *curādi* group (*X*, 385), *ras* with the suffix *-ā* means "to taste": *rasayati*, *rasanā*, *rasyate*: *rasaḥ*; in the *uṇādi* group (*III*, 15), *rāsnā*; in the sense of "possessing" (*astyarthe*), *rasālā* (*sūtra V*, 2, 125).
(742–745) *lās* [is used] in the senses of "adhering" and "playing. *lāsati*. *alasaḥ*, *vilāsaḥ*, *hāsaḥ*, *lāsyam*, *lasikā* (a disease). (746)

Some say that *ghas* means "eating. By the suffix *ghañ* (Pāṇini 3.3.19), we have *ghāsaḥ*; by *kmarac* (3.2.160), we have *ghasmaraḥ*. (747) *jarca*, *jharcha*, and *jharjha* mean "to revile. Regarding these, Candra and Durga read *jartsati* (Ca. Dh. I, 241); some read *carcati*; others read *jarjati*; and still others read *jharcati*. What is the truth here? The gods will know. It is the same in the *tudadi* class as well (6.17). (748–750) 1.

The roots *pisṛ* and *pesṛ* mean "to go. From *pesati*, the suffix *varac* is applied by rule III.2.175 (*stheśabhāsapisa*), resulting in *pesvaraḥ*. In the *curādi* group, *pisa* means "to go" (X.32): *pesayati*. According to the learned authorities, there are also the forms *piśṛ*, *peśṛ*, and *vesṛ*; from *vesṛ* comes *vesaraḥ*, meaning a mule (as in entries 751, 752, 755, 756, and 754).

*Has* (to laugh) is used in the sense of laughing. Regarding *hasati*, there is a prohibition of [the substitution of] *ha* and other roots in the case of reciprocal action (cf. Pāṇini I.3.14–15): *vyatihasanti*. Because of the rule *hmyantakṣaṇa* (Pāṇini VII.2.5), which prescribes *e* as an *it*, there is no *vṛddhi*: *ahasīt*. According to *svanahasor vā* (Pāṇini III.3.62), the suffix *ap* is applied: *hasaḥ* and *hāsaḥ*. By the rule *sphāyi* (Uṇādi II.13), the suffix *rak* is applied: *hasraḥ* (day). By the rule *hasimṛgriṇ* (Uṇādi III.86), the suffix *tan* is applied: *hastaḥ* (hand). *Niśa* (in the sense of concentration/fixing): *praṇiśati*; *niśā* (night).

The root *miś* is used in the sense of sound and the act of anger; that is, in the sense of making a sound and performing an act of wrath. By [Pāṇini III.1.135] *ke*, there is the suffix *vyāṅ*. By [Uṇādi II.32] *kvun*: *maśakaḥ* (759, 760). The root *śav* means "to go. The root *śavati* is a verb denoting motion; it is spoken among the Kāmbojas, while the Āryas call this same word a derivative form (cf. *Paspaśā* p. 9 and Yāska II.2). It goes (*śavati*). *Śavaraḥ*; *śavaḥ*, *śavam* (761).
1. Judging from its position in the Dhātupāṭha, *śas* appears to be the oldest form, which was later replaced by various Prakrit transformations and neologisms (I 58).

[The root] *śas* [is used] in the sense of "leaping" (*plutigatau*); [it is used] in the sense of "moving by leaps" (*plutibhir gamane*). [It forms the present tense] *śaśati*. [The nouns] *śaśaḥ*, *śaśakaḥ* [are derived from it] (762).

The root *kava* means "to sound. Kauśika says it is *kaś*. *Kāśa* is a type of grass; *Kāśi* [is a city]; *Kaśmīrāḥ* [are a country]. The root *śasu* has the meaning "to injure. One says *śasati*. By the rule "na śasadadavādi" (Pāṇini VI.4.126), the substitution of *e* for *a* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur: *śaśasatuḥ*, *śaśasuḥ*. By the rule "hmyantakṣaṇaśasa" (Pāṇini VII.2.5), one says *aśasīt*. From the gerundive suffix *-tvā*: *śastvā*, *śasitvā*. By the rule "dliṛṣaśasī vaiyātye" (Pāṇini VII.2.19), it is *aniṭ* [in the sense of "shamelessness"]: *viśastaḥ*; otherwise, *viśasitaḥ*. By the rule "dāmnīśasv" (Pāṇini III.2.182), the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied: *śastram*. [The agent] *viśasitā*. In the *uṇādi* group, [the word] *śastā* [is formed]. (762a, 763)

The root *śaṃs* is used in the sense of "praising. One praises (*śaṃsati*), or it is praised (*śasyate*). From the rule stating that the suffix *kyap* is optionally applied after the roots *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh* (Pāṇini III.1.109, Kāśikā), we have *śasya* (that which is to be praised). Furthermore, the suffix *ṇyat* is also desired after *śaṃs*, yielding *śaṃsya*. The word *nṛśaṃsaḥ* means a cruel person. According to the *Uṇādi* list (II.94), *śaṃstā* refers to one who slaughters animals. For this very reason, Durga states that *śansu* is used in the sense of "praising" (764). The root *cah* is used in the sense of "deceit" (*kalkana*); deceit is guile. One deceives (*cahati*). It belongs to the *curādi* class as a *mit* root (X.83): *cahayati* (765). 4.

*raha* means "to abandon. From it we have *rahati*, *arahīt*. *Virahaḥ* and *Rāhuḥ* (Uṇ. I, 1 comm. are derived with the suffix *asun* (Uṇ. IV, 188): *rahas*. In the *cur*-class (X, 312), there is *rahayati* (767). *rahi* means "to go. From it, *raṃhati* and *raṃhaḥ* (768).

The roots *dṛh*, *dṛhi*, *bṛh*, and *bṛhi* mean "to grow strong" (*vṛddhau*). *darhati*; *dṛḍhaḥ* is correct [in the sense] of "thick" (*sthūla*) or "strong" (*bala*), according to Pāṇini VII.2.20. *dṛṃhati*. *bṛhati*. In the sense of the present tense, *bṛhat* is formed by Uṇādi-sūtra II.84: *pṛṣadbṛhad*. It is also correct [in the sense] of "sovereign" (*prabhu*), according to Pāṇini VII.2.21: *parivṛḍhaḥ*. By Uṇādi-sūtra II.110: *bṛṃher nalopaś ca*, the suffix *isi* is added: *barhiḥ*. By Uṇādi-sūtra IV.145: *bṛṃher no 'c ca*, [the suffix *man* is added and] *na* is substituted for *ṛ*: *brahmā*. *bṛndaṃ*. *bṛhi* also means "to sound. *bṛṃhati*, *bṛṃhitam*. Durga states that the root is *bṛh*. *abṛhat*, *abarhīt* (by Pāṇini III.1.57). Regarding *bṛṃheḥ*, because of the elision of *na*, there is *bṛhaḥ* in the sense of the present day (sūtras 769–772).

The roots *tuh* and *uh* mean "to afflict. From *tuh*, we have *tuhati*; [the forms] *atuhat* and *atoḥīt* are derived according to Pāṇini III.1.57. According to Uṇādi-sūtra II.52, *vepituhyor hrasvaś ca*, the word *tuhina* ("snow") is formed. From *ūh*, we have *ohati* and *apohati*.

1. In the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*); 2. *so* is found in all manuscripts (*alleHss.*), cf. also II, 60; 3. cf. Hem. Uṇ. 857; 4. *maha* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*) [Uṇ. 766], which is missing in all manuscripts, may have been omitted by accident since it is mentioned at X, 321, although it is also absent in Śākaṭāyana; 5. thus in K and C, and occasionally elsewhere, in order to mark stems ending in *-as*, *-is*, and *-us* as such and to distinguish them from the nominative.
To distinguish the *a*, *i*, and *u*-stems: 6 *praṃhas* (cf. the preceding note). 7 All manuscripts read thus.
59 I (VI, 1, 94), *auhāt*, *auhīt*. Regarding *tuhi* and *duhi*, Candra and Durga [state] (Ca. Dh. I, 257) (773, 775, 774).

The root *arh* is used in the sense of "to deserve" (*pūjāyām*). It forms *arhati*. By the rule *arha* (Pāṇini III.2.12), the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), which supersedes the suffix *aṇ*: thus, *pūjārhā* ("one who deserves honor"). By the rule *arhaḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini III.2.133), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied: *arhan* ("deserving"). Due to its inclusion in the *nyaṅkv-ādi* group (Pāṇini VII.3.53), it becomes *arghaḥ*. By the rule *halaś ca* (Pāṇini III.3.121), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). *Arghi* is a separate verbal root: *kalāṃ nārghanti ṣoḍaśīm* ("they are not worth even a sixteenth part"). *Arghaḥ* means "price. By the rule *śakadhṛṣajñā* (Pāṇini III.4.65), the suffix *tumun* is applied: *arhati bhoktum* ("he deserves to eat").

The root *arh*, meaning "to worship," belongs to the *cur*-class (see X, 192) and takes the suffix *ṇic*: *arhayati*. It does not occur in the sense of "fitness" and so forth. (776, 776a) These [roots] have an acute accent on the first syllable (*udāttetaḥ*). 731.

The root *dyut* means "to shine. From this point on, thirty-seven roots ending in *r* or *ā* are *seṭ* (taking the augment *iṭ*) and *ātmanepadin* (taking the middle voice endings). *dyotate*. By the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi* (Pāṇini I.3.91), the *parasmaipada* (active voice) optionally applies; in that case, by the rule *puṣādidyutādi* (III.1.55), the suffix *aṅ* is applied: *vyadyutat*. In the *ātmanepada*, it is *vyadyotiṣṭa*. In the *liṭ* (perfect tense), by the rule *dyutisvāpyoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (VII.4.67), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*): *vididyute*. Due to this specific statement, the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant) does not apply. In the *caṅ* (periphrastic aorist), it is *vyadidyutat*. The word *dyotanaḥ* is formed with the suffix *kvip* (III.2.177).

*Vidyut*: from the root *dyut*, with the substitution of *j* for the initial [consonant] (cf. Uṇ. II.111): *jyotiḥ*. The group beginning with *ghaṭ* (800) precedes the group beginning with *dyut* (777).

*Śvit* in the sense of "color": *śvetate*; *aśvitat*; *aśvetiṣṭa*. By the rule *āditaś ca* (VII.2.16), it is *aniṭ* [in the perfect]: *śvittaḥ*. By the rule *vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ* (VII.2.17): *śvittam anena*, *śvititam anena*; *praśvittaḥ*, *praśvititaḥ*. From *ktra* (Uṇ. IV.163): *śvittram*. (778)

The root *mid* means "to lubricate" (*snehane*). Lubrication is the application of oiliness. [From *mid*: *minnaḥ*, *minnam*, *meditam*. Because of the rule *śīṅ-svidi-midi-dhṛṣaḥ* (Pāṇini I.2.19), there is no *kittva* [of the suffix]; thus we have *praminnaḥ* and *prameditaḥ*. From the rule *bhañja-bhāsa-mido ghu-ra-c* (Pāṇini III.2.161): *meduraḥ*. From the rule *amicimi-di-śasi-bhyaḥ ktraḥ* (Uṇādi IV.163): *mitram*. From the rule *asun* (Uṇādi IV.188): *medas* (fat). With the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini III.1.134): *Meda* is the name of a Mleccha tribe, and *medinī* (the earth).

In the *divādi* class (*I* V‚ 133), there is *medyati*; in the *curādi* class (*X*, 8), *mida* means "to moisten": *medayati* (779). *Ñikṣvidā* means "moistening" and "delusion. [From this root: *kṣvedate*; *kṣviṇṇaḥ*. According to the Arhat, it is *ñikṣviḍā*: *kṣveḍaḥ* means "poison," *kṣveḍā* means "sound. According to Nandī, it is *ñiṣvidā*: *svedate*, *asvidat*, *asvediṣṭa*; *svinnaḥ*. By the rule *saḥ svidisvadisahīnāṃ ca* (*VIII*, 3, 62), the *s* is substituted [for the *ṣ*]: *sisvedayiṣati*. *Ṣvidā* means "oozing from the body" (*gātraprakṣaraṇe*) (*I* V‚ 79); from this [root], *svidyati* (780).

1. All manuscripts. 2. Nominative singular of *śatṛ*; P: *śatṛ*. 3. Cf. Hemacandra’s *Dhātupāṭha* I, 564, and furthermore Manu II, 86, where the editions read *arhanti* instead of *arghanti*, as likewise in the Pañcatantra ed. Kielhorn II, 58. 4. According to Kunda and P, *śvetitam* and *praśvetitaḥ*; cf. I, 2, 19. 5. P adds *arśaḥ* (I 60).

The root *ruc* is used in the senses of "to shine" and "to find pleasure in. "Finding pleasure in" (*abhiprīti*) means "desire" (*abhilāṣa*). According to the rule *ruccarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini I.4.33), the one who finds pleasure is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*): *caitrāya rocate rocanaḥ* ("The light finds pleasure in Caitra"). In the forms *arucat* and *arociṣṭa*, the Ātmanepada suffix *taṅ* is applied by the rule *na pādam* (Pāṇini I.3.89). In *parirocayate*, the same applies. By the rule *rājasūyasūrya-* (Pāṇini III.1.114), the word *rocya* is formed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), meaning "one who is pleasing. In the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), the suffix *ṇyat* (III.1.124) is applied to form *rocyam*. By the rule *yajayācaruca-* (VII.3.66), the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*) does not occur here. [The suffix] *ghañ* (I.3.18) is also applicable.

19): *rokaḥ* [is derived] by means of the suffix *lyuṭ* (Pāṇini III.3.117); *rocanī* "a grinding stone" [is derived from the same root]; *rocanā* [is derived] from the causative (*ṇyantāt*) by means of the suffix *lyuḥ* (III.1.134); *rociṣṇuḥ* [is derived] by means of the suffix *iṣṇuc* according to *alaṃkṛñ-nirākṛñ-* (III.2.136); *rukmam* [is derived] by *yujirucitijāṃ kuś ca* (Uṇādi I.145); *rociḥ* [is derived] by the suffix *isiḥ* (Uṇādi II.112); *ruciḥ* [is derived] by *ik kṛṣyādibhyaḥ* (cf. Uṇādi IV.119); *ruciram* [is used] in the sense of "possessing beauty" (*astyarthe*), according to Uṇādi I.52. (781) *Ghuṭ* in the sense of "turning around. [The verb] *ghoṭate*; [the aorist forms] *aghuṭat*, *aghoṭiṣṭa*. *Ghoṭakaḥ* "horse"; *ghuṭikā* "the bone of the ankle" (782).

*ruṭ* means "to shine" (*dīptau*). It forms *roṭate*. *Ruṭha* and *luṭha* mean "to strike against" (*pratīghāte*). From the form *loṭhate*, we have *aluṭhat* and *aloṭhiṣṭa*. Because it is observed in usage that [the root] *luṭhati* exists, it should be recited in the *tudadi* class (cf. VI.87). Some authorities read *ruṭa* and *luṭa*; this is supported by the evidence of the rule *bādhṛ roṭane* (I.5) [as seen in the commentary on sūtras 783, 785, and 784].

The root *śubh* means "to shine. It forms *śobhate* (he shines), *aśobhata* (he shone), and *aśobhiṣṭa* (he has shone). From it come *śobhanaḥ* (beautiful), *ke* (Pāṇini III.1.135) *śubham* (the auspicious); from the evidence of grammatical rules (*jñāpakāt*) comes *śobhā* (beauty); with the suffix *rak* (Uṇādi II.13) comes *śubhram* (white/bright); in the Uṇādi list, *śukaḥ* (parrot, III.42), *śukraḥ* (semen, bright), and *śuklaḥ* (white; cf. Uṇādi II.28). In the *tudādigaṇa*, *śubha* and *śunbha* are listed as meaning "to beautify" (VI.33): *śubhati* (786).

The root *kṣubh* means "to move. Moving is the alteration of form (*rūpānyathātva*). [Conjugations: *kṣobhate*, *akṣubhat*, *akṣobhiṣṭa*. According to Pāṇini VI.1.18, *kṣubdha* is used in the sense of "churning" (*mantha*), while otherwise it is *kṣubhita*. In the *divādi* class (IV.129), it is *kṣubhyati*; in the *kryādi* class (IX.47), it is *kṣubhnāti*. (787) The roots *ṇabha* and *tubha* mean "to injure. [Conjugations: *nabhate*, *tobhate*. In the *kryādi* class (IX.48–49), they are *nabhnāti* and *tubhnāti*. By the suffix *asun* (Uṇ. IV.188), we have *nabhaḥ*. (788–789)

The roots *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu*, and *bhraṃśu* mean "to fall" (*avasraṃsane*). *sraṃsate*; by the rule *nīg vancusransv* (Pāṇini VII.4.84), the form *sanīsrasyate* occurs; by the rule *vasusransudhvansvanaḍuho daḥ* (VIII.2.72), we have *ukhāsrat*. The gerunds are *srastvā* and *sraṃsitvā*; the feminine noun *srastiḥ* is formed according to *ktin ābādibhyaḥ* (III.3.94, 1). *dhvaṃsate*; the intensive form is *danīdhvasyate*; the past passive participle is *parṇadhvat*; the feminine noun is *dhvastiḥ*; the gerunds are *dhvastvā* and *dhvaṃsitvā*; and the past passive participle is *dhvastaḥ*. *bhraṃśate*; [the intensive form is *banībhraśyate*].

*bhraṣṭiḥ*, *banībhraśyate*, *bhraṣṭvā* / *bhraṃśitvā*, *bhraṣṭaḥ*; [the root] *bhraś* belongs to the *divādi* group (DhP IV.115). [The root] *dhvaṃs* [is used] in the sense of "going" and so forth (790–793). 1 All manuscripts. 2 P reads *pratighāte*. 3 Perhaps a corruption for *nipātanāt*; cf. VI.33. 4 P reads *manthaś cet*. 61 I.

*Sranbhū* means trust. [The forms] *visrambhate*, *vyasrabhat*, and *vyasrambhiṣṭa* [are derived from it]. Kauśika says that *sranhv* [is the root]: [the form] *sraṃhate* [is used], because it begins with a sibilant (*ūṣman*) at its end (794).

The root *vṛt* means "to turn" (*vartana*). Turning is staying (*sthiti*). [Examples: *vartate*, *vartanaḥ*¹; *avṛtat*, *avartiṣṭa*; by the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanor vā* (I, 3, 92), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is optionally used; and by the rule *na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ* (VII, 2, 59), the augment *iṭ* is not applied in that very context: *vartsyati*, *vartiṣyate*; *avartsyat*, *avartiṣyata*; *vivṛtsati*, *vivartiṣate*. [Gerund: *vṛttvā*, *vartitvā*; [past participle: *vṛttaḥ*; [derivative nouns: *vṛttiḥ*, *vṛtyaḥ* (III, 1, 110); [possessive suffix *matup*: "that in which turning exists" (cf. V, 2, 101, 1). ¹ *vartanaḥ* is derived from the root *vṛt* with the suffix *-ana*. It refers to one who turns or stays. The form *vartanaḥ* is provided here for comparison with the subsequent grammatical analysis. The text uses *vartanaḥ* as a noun meaning "one who turns/stays. The commentary explains that the root *vṛt* signifies staying (*sthiti*). The forms *vartate* and *vartanaḥ* illustrate the present indicative and the agentive noun respectively. The rules cited govern the formation of future, conditional, desiderative, gerund, past participle, and derivative nouns from this root. The specific mention of the prohibition of *iṭ* after the four roots beginning with *vṛt* (namely *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *syand*, *mṛj*) is crucial for the correct formation of these forms. The final example demonstrates the application of the possessive suffix *matup* (*vat*) to form an adjective meaning "possessing turning/staying. The reference to V, 2, 101, 1 indicates that this formation follows the general rules for such suffixes. The text thus provides a comprehensive grammatical overview of the root *vṛt*.

From the root *vṛt*, by [Uṇādi-sūtra] II, 107, the suffix *ani* is applied: *vartaniḥ*. By [Uṇādi-sūtra] IV, 144, the suffix *manin*: *vartma*. Regarding the substitution of *vṛtta* for the causative (*ṇi*) in the sense of "studying," see Pāṇini VII, 2, 26. With the suffix *ṇamul* after *vṛt* and *grah* when combined with *hasta*, according to Pāṇini III, 4, 39: *hastavartaṃ vartayati* ("he turns it with his hand").
