From this [root], *kelayati* and *keliḥ* [are derived]. In the *tudādi* group (VI, 61), *kila* is used in the senses of whiteness and playing (*śvaityakrīḍana*): *kilati*. [From this,] *pelayati*; and *pelam*. Regarding the suffix *aṇic* in the sense of state or object (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), Candra (64. 65) states that from *pelṛ* in the sense of going (I, 574), one has *pelyate*.

*bila* means "to split. *belayati*. *bilam*, *bilvaḥ*, *bilmam*. In the *tudādigaṇa* (VI.67), *bilati*. Kauśika says *bhila*: *bhelayati*; *bhelaḥ*, *bhilmam* (66). *tila* means "to oil. *telayati*. *tilāḥ*, *tilakam*. In the *tudādigaṇa* (VI.62), *tilati* (67). *cala* means "to move" (*bhṛti*). *cālayati*. In the *bhvādigaṇa* (I.850), it is marked as *mit* for "shaking": *calayati*; in the *tudādigaṇa* (VI.64), *cala* means "to sport": *calati* (68).

The root *pal* is used in the sense of protecting (*rakṣaṇe*). It forms *pālayati*. *Palam*, *palalam* (sesame paste), *kravyam* (raw meat), and *palālam* (chaff). According to Candra (Ca. Dh. X, 50), it also means "he protects" (*pāleti*); hence *pālī*. (69) The root *lūṣ* is used in the sense of harming (*hiṃsāyām*). It forms *lūṣayati*; [the past passive participle] *lūṣitaḥ*. (70) The root *śulb* is used in the sense of measuring (*māne*). It forms *śulbayati*. *Śulbam* is a rope (*rajjuḥ*). According to Candra (71), it is also used in the sense of measuring with a winnowing basket (*śūrpa-māna*). (71)

1. All manuscripts. 2. P adds *dāhe caike*. 3. P reads *tilaḥ*. 4. P reads *tāmrarajaḥ*. X 176. The root *chuṭ* [is used] in the sense of cutting (*chedane*). One says *ācchoṭayati*; *choṭikā* means a snap of the fingers (*yucchā*), as well as the act of snapping (*choṭanam*). It belongs to the *tudadi* class (Dhātupāṭha VI.84) as *chuṭati*. Candra (Ca. Dh. X.52) gives *cuṭeti*, and Durga (72) gives *muṭeti*.

*Puṭ* in the sense of crushing: *poṭayati*; *poṭā* means a woman possessing the characteristics of both male and female. It also has the meaning of "shining" (*bhāsārtha*). In the *tudādi* class, *puṭ* is used in the sense of joining together (*saṃśleṣaṇa*): *puṭati*, *puṭaḥ*, *puṭam*. (73) *Pasi* in the sense of destruction: *paṃsayati*. From the rule *arjidṛśi* (Uṇ. I, 28), the suffix *u* is added and the vowel is lengthened: *pāṃsuḥ*. (74) Regarding *bhadi*, Durga says it means "auspiciousness. [The form is *bhandayati*. (74a)

*Vaja* [is used] in the senses of path (*mārga*) and formation (*saṃskāra*); that is, in the sense of path and in the sense of formation. Some say it means "in the sense of path" and "in the sense of formation," while others say there are two roots. [The form] *vājayati* is derived from *vraj*. Candra [says] it is *vraj*, and for this very reason, since it is established by the *bhvādi* class (DhP I, 272), he did not record it [separately]. [He says] *mārgayati*, [and the noun] *mārgaḥ*. Durga [says] *vaja* [means] "searching" (*mārgaṇa*) and "formation" (*saṃskāra*). (75)

The root *śulka* is used in the sense of "releasing" (*asarjana*). It forms *śulkayati*. Some say that *śulba* is also used in the sense of "not releasing. (76) *Chap* is used in the sense of "going" (*gati*); it forms *champayati*. (77) *Kṣap* is used in the sense of "patience" (*kṣānti*); it forms *kṣampayati*. (78) *Kṣaj* is used in the sense of "living in hardship" (*kṛcchrajīvana*); it forms *kṣañjayati*. In the *Ghaṭādi* group, *kṣaj* is used in the senses of "going" and "giving" (DhP I. 806); (79) *svarta* is used in the sense of "going," and by the word "and" (*ca*), also in the sense of "living in hardship"; it forms *svartayati*. [Objection: The phrase "in the sense of going" is incorrect, because the word *svarta* itself is impossible [as a base]. Nandī says it is a *ṣopadeśa* [root with initial *ṣ*]; thus, *siṣvartayiṣati*. The followers of Durga say *śvabhra* is used in the sense of "going"; it forms *śvabhrayati*; [the noun] *śvabhram*. (80)

The root *jñap* is used in the senses of making known (*māraṇa*), satisfying (*toṣaṇa*), and sharpening (*niśāna*). Although its status as a *mit* is established by its inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group (Pāṇini I.849), it is listed here for the sake of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in its own meaning (*svārtha*). This is so that the *parasmaipada* ending may apply according to Pāṇini I.3.72 (*kartrabhiprāyakriyāphale*). Alternatively, it serves a restrictive purpose: "Except for *yam* and others, no other roots ending in the causative suffix (*ṇi*) are *mit*. Some maintain that the *mit* designation for *yam* and others must necessarily be stated, whereas for *jñap*, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of ease.

He causes the animal to be known [slaughtered] (*saṃjñapayati*), he informs the teacher (*vijñapayati*), he makes the weapon known [prepared] (*prajñapayati*). [The forms] *ājñaptaḥ* and *ājñapitaḥ* [are used]. Having informed the teacher (*vijñapya guruṃ*), having made known the Dharma (*prajñāpya dharmaṃ*), having commanded the servant (*ājñāpya bhṛtyam*)—in these cases, the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of pleasing in some way. Likewise, one who wishes to cause [something] to be known is expressed as *jijñapayiṣati* or *jñīpsati*. Some say that the *ṇic* suffix is applied even in the sense of "making known" because the root has multiple meanings; others say it is because *jñapti* and *jñāna* have the same meaning. (81) *Yam* in the sense of serving food: *yamayati*. Durga says that there is also a root *yama*; the particle *ca* is said to be intended to draw in the *mittva* (the property of causing the vowel to be short) of this very root, so that it does not apply to *cam* and the others. *Yam*.
1. *P* [records] *choṭane*; 2. *P* [records] *śulka-asaṃsarjana*.

*X* [states] *cameti Candraḥ Pārāyaṇe*. For this very reason, he did not study *na kamya-camām*, nor did he study *yamo 'pariveṣaṇe* (I, 869–871), due to the contradiction; here too, some read *yamo 'pariveṣaṇe* (82).

The root *cah* is used in the sense of deceiving (*kalkana*). One says *cahayati* or *cāpayati*; so says Candra (83). Some say that *rah* means "abandoning" (*tyāga*), but that is not correct, because [the meaning] is established through narrative and other means (X.312) (84). The root *bal* is used in the sense of strengthening (*prāṇana*). One says *balayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.893), one says *balati* (85). The root *ci* is used in the sense of piling up (*caya*). One says *cayayati*. This is because the chapters possess authoritative evidence (*pramāṇavattva*). [Regarding the rule] *cisphuror ṇau* (VI.1.54), which prescribes the substitution of *ā* for the vowel in *ci* and *sphur* before the causative suffix *ṇi*, if the root were marked with the mute letter *m* (*mittva*), what would be the purpose? [The answer is: it is for the sake of the continuation of the *mittva* designation up to this point; thus one says *capayati*. The fact that the root is marked with the mute letter *ñ* (*ñittva*) is an indicator (*liṅga*) that the *ṇic* suffix is not invariably present; thus one says *cayate* or *cayati*. In the *svādi* class (V.5), one says *cinoti* or *cinute*; and in the sense of causation (*hetu*), one says *cāyayati* (86).

Others [are not *mit*] even when followed by *ṇi* in the sense of non-causative (*ahetu*). Other roots than the five beginning with *syam*, *śam*, *ghaṭ*, *naṭ*, and *śraṇ*—such as *yoj* and others belonging to the *cur-ādi* class—are not designated as *mit* when followed by *ṇi* in the non-causative sense: *niśāmayate* (X, 156); *udghāṭayati* (X, 183). Candragomin did not accept this, because for roots such as *ghaṭ*, the designation *mit* applies only in the sense of "effort" (*ceṣṭā*) and so forth, and thus there would be no application [of the rule] in senses such as "joining" (*yojana*): "The Creator, having become intent, quickly brings about the desired [result]" (*jhaṭiti ghaṭayati vidhir abhimatam abhimukhībhūtaḥ*). [Similarly: *ghaṭṭa* in the sense of "moving/shaking": *ghaṭṭayati*; *ghaṭṭanā*; *ghaṭṭaḥ* = a place for crossing a river; *araghaṭṭaḥ*. (87)

*Khada* in the sense of covering: *khaṭṭayati* "he covers his face" (89). *Saṭṭa* in the sense of injury: *saṭṭayati*; *saṭṭakaḥ* (90). *Vyaya* in the sense of destruction: *vyāyayati*. Candra considers this to be derived from *vyeñ* (DhP I, 1056). Kauśika says *vyapa-vyayeti*, while Nandī says *vyudi-vyayeti*. *Pravyundayati* (96). *Pūla* in the sense of a mass or heap: *pūlayati*; *pūlā*. Some say *pūrṇa* (94). *Puṃsa* in the sense of crushing: *utpuṃsayati* (95). *Musta* in the sense of a mass: [*mustayati*] (88). *Ṭaki* in the sense of binding: *ṭaṅkayati*. [The derivatives are] *ṭaṅkanā*, *ṭaṅkanam*, *ṭaṅkaḥ*.

*Viṭaṅka* (97): *dhūṣ* in the sense of making radiant. It forms *dhūṣayati*. Some say the final consonant belongs to the palatal class (*tālavya*), while the followers of Durga say it belongs to the dental class (*dantya*); [the derivative is] *dhūsara*. *Kīṭa* (98): *varaṇa* in the sense of covering. It forms *kīṭayati*; [the derivative is] *kīṭa*. *Cūṇa* (99): in the sense of contraction. It forms *cūṇayati*. Some say it is *cūrṇa*, while Candra says it is *tūṇa*; [the derivative is] *tūṇīra*.
*Pūja* (100): in the sense of worship. It forms *pūjayati*. By the rule *cintipūji* (Pāṇini III.3.105), the noun *pūjā* is formed.
Worthy of worship, honored by kings; (101) 1 P from the *Pārāyaṇavyākhyāna* 2 P omits 3 88 after 95 4 96 before 94 5 all manuscripts read thus X 178.

In the context of praising the sun (*arka*): *arkayati*. According to some, [it means] "the burner" (*tapana*). (102) *śuṭha* in the sense of laziness (*ālasya*): *śoṭhayati*. According to some, [it means] "deceitful" (*śaṭha*). (103) *ś-u-ṭ-h-i* in the sense of drying (*śoṣaṇa*): *śuṇṭhayati*; *śuṇṭhī* is another name for *viśvā* (ginger). Candra derives [this] from the *bhvādi* class (I, 367). (104) *juḍa* in the sense of impelling (*preraṇa*): *joḍayati*. (105) *gaja*, *marca*, and *mārja* have the meaning of sound (*śabda*). *gājayati*; [these belong to] the *bhvādi* class.

(I, 265) *gajati*. *mārcayati*¹. *mārjayati*; *mārjitā* (106, 107). *ghṛ* in the sense of flowing: *ghārayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I, 985), *gharati*; in the *hvādi* class (III, 14), *jigharti*. The predecessors read *ghṛ sṛ* in the sense of covering, while Durga reads *ghara* in the sense of flowing (108). *paci* in the sense of expansion: *prapañcayati*; *prapañcaḥ*. In the *bhvādi* class, *paci* in the sense of making manifest (I, 187): *pañcate*, *pañcikā*, *vipañcī*, *paṅkaḥ* (109).

The root *tij* means "to sharpen. It forms *tejayati*; [the nouns] *tejanā* and *tejanī*. In the *bhvādi* class (I. 1020), with the sense of "endurance," it takes the desiderative suffix (*san*): *titikṣate*. They say that "sharpening" is expressed by *tejataḥ* (110). The root *kṛt* means "proclamation. Proclamation is a loud utterance. It forms *kīrtayati*; [the noun] *kīrtiḥ* is formed by rule III. 3. 97 (111). The root *vardh* means "cutting" and "filling. It forms *vardhayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I. 796), it forms *vardhate* (112).

*Kupi* means "to cover. From *kump*—according to *cintipūji* (Pāṇini III.3.105)—comes *kumpā*. Kauśika says: *kubī* means "a very dense enclosure" (*kumbā sugahanā vṛtiḥ*, Amarakośa II.7.18). *Lubi* and *tubi* mean "to crush. From *lubi*: *lumbayati*; [as in] "with clusters of young shoots and fruits" (*pravālaphalalumbibhiḥ*). From *tubi*: *tumbayati*; [the nouns] *tumbī* and *tumbakaḥ*. *Tupī* is according to the followers of Durga; all three are established in the *bhvādi* class in the system of Candra. (114, 115) *Hlapa* means "in distinct speech. (116)

*cuṭa* in the sense of cutting (*chedane*). *coṭayati*. In the *tudādigaṇa* (VI. 84), it is *cuṭati*. Nandī says *cuṭīti*; Durga says *cuṇṭayati*, *cuḍīti* (117). *ila* in the sense of impelling (*preraṇe*). *elayati*. In the *bhvādigaṇa* (? cf. VI. 65), it is *elati* (119). *mrakṣa* in the sense of smearing (*mlecchane*). *mrakṣayati* (120). *mlecha* in the sense of indistinct speech (*avyaktāyāṃ vāci*). *mlecchayati*. In the *bhvādigaṇa* (I...).

220) *mlecchati*. Since [the roots] *mrakṣ* in the sense of "concealment" (*roṣe*) and *mlecha* in the sense of "indistinct sound" (*avyakte śabde*; cf. CandraDh. I, 217, 53) are already established, Candra did not accept these two [as belonging to the *cur*-class]. [This is because of the rule: "This [application of suffixes] is manifold" (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*, X, 392); thus, all [roots] should be recited in the *cur*-class—this is the intention (*abhiprāya*) of Candra (121). *marja* and *marjayati*; cf. I, 1, 47, 3. 2 P: "he turns back. *cuḍīti* according to Nandī: *cuṇḍayati*; *cuṭīti* according to Durga. 3 P: This is the intention of Candra. 179 X.

The root *brīs* is used in the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*). One says *brīsayati*; some say *brūseti*. [In the sense of] overcoming (*barhayati*), one overcomes the enemy. In the *bhvādi* class (I, 669), *barh* is used in the sense of preeminence (*prādhānye*): "the village-dweller excels" (*barhate*). (122, 123) The root *gard* is used in the sense of sound (*śabda*). One says *gardayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I, 58), *gardati*. Some say *garjeti*. (124) The root *gardh* is used in the sense of longing (*abhikāṅkṣā*). One says *gardhayati*. In the *divādi* class (IV, 136), *gṛdhyati*. (125)

*gurda* means "in the former abode. *Pūrvaniketana* means the original dwelling. In the *Pārāyaṇa*, there are two verbal roots: *gurdayati* and *pūrvayati*. In the *Bhvādi* class, *pūrva* is used in the sense of filling (*pūraṇe*, I, 607): *pūrvati* (126, 127). *Jas* is used in the sense of protecting (*rakṣaṇe*), and also in the sense of burning (*dahī*). [From these, one forms] *jaṃsayati* and *daṃhayati* (128, 128a). *Īḍ* is used in the sense of praising (*stutau*); [from this, one forms] *īḍayati*. In the *Adādi* class (II, 9), [one forms] *īṭṭe* (129).

The root *jasu* is used in the sense of "injuring. By the rule *jāsiniprahaṇa* (Pāṇini II.3.56), the genitive case is employed: *caurasyojjāsayati* ("he causes the thief to be injured"). In the *divādi* class (IV.102), it is *jasyati* (130).

*Piḍi* is used in the sense of "compression" (*saṃghāte*). *piṇḍayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.293), *piṇḍate*; [the nouns] *piṇḍaḥ*, *piṇḍī*. Some say the root is *paḍī*: *paṇḍayati*; [the nouns] *paṇḍitaḥ*, *paṇḍā*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.301), *paṇḍate* (131).

*Ruṭa* is used in the sense of "anger" (*roṣe*). *roṭayati*; [the noun] *grāmaroṭaḥ*. Candra, considering this to be *ruṣ*, states that its formation is established by both the *bhvādi* and *divādi* classes (I.724, IV.120). Some say *ruṭa* is used in the sense of "injury" (*upaghāte*), and others say *ruṭh* (132).

*ḍap* and *ḍip* mean "to strike together": *ḍampayati*, *ḍimpayati*. According to Daurga, *ḍabhi* and *ḍibhī* [mean]: *ḍambhayati*, *dambhaḥ*; *ḍimbhayati*, *ḍimbaḥ* (138). *Dabha*, *dibhi*, *vipa*, *ṭipa*, *ḍipa*, *stipa* mean "to throw. [Examples: *dābhayati*, *dimbhayati*. According to Nandī, *dabhī* [means]: *dambhayati*. *Vepayati*, *ṭepayati*, *ḍepayati*, *stepayati*. According to Candra, *ḍabi* and *ḍibī* [mean]: *viḍambayati*, *āḍambaraḥ*; *ḍimbayati*, *ḍimbaḥ* (a conflict of weapons). *Stūpa* means "to raise up": *stūpayati*. [This root belongs to] the *divādi* group (IV, 127).

He performs the act of *stūpyati*. Candra (cf. Ca. Dh. I V, 70) states that *ṣopadeśa* is [the form] *tuṣṭūpayiṣati*. (134) In the 23rd *paryaṭṭaka* of the 100th *sūtra*, there are 142 verbal roots (*dhātu*). From the beginning, there are 1,677 [roots]. [Note: All manuscripts read "so" (thus). P reads *dabhi* and *dambhayati*, but cf. Hem. Dh. X, 142. So [is it] in Kṣ.; there is a gap in P. The sections containing classes I through IX contain 1,505 roots according to Kṣ.’s count. Since the numbers mentioned for the tenth class (123 *sūtras*, 142 roots) do not match...]
The more precisely one examines it, the more likely it is that "1677" has been erroneously written for "1647.

[Note: X 180] Regarding "ā kusmād ātmanepadī": he will state [in X, 171], "or from the root *kusma*"; thus, from this point onward, the group [of roots] is *ātmanepada*, whether it be a specific root or the entire class. The particle *ā* is used here in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*)—as seen in Pāṇini I, 4, 89 (Kāśikā) and II, 1, 13—for if it were intended as an exclusive limit (*maryādā*), he would have said "prāk kusmāt" (before *kusma*).

*cita* means "to perceive" (*saṃcetane*). It forms *cetayate*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.39), *citī* means "to know": *cetati* (135). *dāśṛ* means "to give" (*dāne*). It forms *dāśayate*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.931), *dāśati* and *dāśate* (135a). *daṃśi* means "to bite" (*daṃśane*). It forms *daṃśayate*. In the sense of "shining" (*bhāsārtha*) [class X.224], it forms *daṃśayati*; in the *bhvādi* class (I.1038), *danśa* means "to bite": *daśati* (136).
The root *das* is used in the senses of seeing and biting: *daṃsayate*; *daṃsitaḥ*. It has the sense of shining (*bhāsārtha*) [DhP. X, 246]: *daṃsayati* (137).

*Tantr* is used in the sense of maintaining a family (*kuṭumbadhāraṇe*). "Family" (*kuṭumba*) means retinue; this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). [Examples: *tantrayate*. *Tantra*: *svatantraḥ*. From the rule *avitṛstṝtantribhya īḥ* (Uṇ. III, 158): *tantrīḥ*. From *aca iḥ* (Uṇ. IV, 138): *tantriḥ*. *Tandrā* and *tandrī* are derived according to the rule for words beginning with *pṛṣodara* (VI, 3, 109). Considering these to be two distinct roots, the followers of Candra also cite *kuṭumbayati* as an example (139). (139) 3.
The root *matri* is used in the sense of speaking secretly: *mantrayate*; *mantraḥ*.

(140) The root *spaś* has the senses of seizing and joining: *spāśayate*; by [the rule] *atsmṛdṝtvara* (Pāṇini VII.4.95), we have *apaspaśat*. By [the rule] *vā dānta* (Pāṇini VII.2.27), we have *spaṣṭaḥ* and *spāśitaḥ*. In the *bhvādi* class, *spaś* means "to harm" (cf. I.936): *spaśati*; *spaśaḥ* means "a spy. (141)

The roots *bharts* and *tarj* are used in the sense of threatening (*saṃtarjana*). One sees them used as *bhartsayate* and *tarjayate*. In the object of the action (*lakṣya*), they are seen as *bhartsayati* and *tarjayati*. Similarly, there are forms such as *niśāmayati*, *bhālayati*, *koṭayati*, *vañcayati*, and *nivedayati*; for this very reason, he did not include those roots beginning with *cur* that are accompanied by vowels. In the *Bhvādi* class, *tarj* is listed as "threatening" (I. 245): *tarjati* (143. 142). *Bast* and *gandh* are used in the sense of striking (*ardana*). From *bast*: *bastayate*; *bastaḥ*, *bastiḥ*. From *gandh*: *gandhayate*; *gandhaḥ*, *gandharvaḥ*, *ghoṭakaḥ* (144. 145).

The root *kiṣk* is used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*). It is conjugated as *kiṣkayate*. *Kiṣku* means "a cubit" (*hasta*) or "a span" (*vitasti*); [it is also the name of] *Kiṣkindhā*. Durga says it is *hiṣk*; *hiṣkita* is observed [as its form]. In the *Bhvādi* class (I, 914), *hikkati* is found. (146) *Niṣka* is used in the sense of "measure. It is conjugated as *niṣkayate*; *niṣka* [is a noun]. (147) *Lal* is used in the sense of "desire" (*īpsā*). It is conjugated as *lālayate*. From *ku* and *lālayate*, *kulālaḥ* ("potter") is derived. In the *Bhvādi* class, *laḍa* is used in the sense of "play" (*vilāsa*) (I, 381): *laḍati*. (148)

*kūṇ* means "to contract. He contracts his face (*mukhaṃ vikūṇayate*). (149) 1. *sūtrayet* 9P; they cited [this]; cf. Ca. Dh. X, 65 3 138 s.v. 133. From here, there is a gap in K and C until 189 181 X.

*tūṇ* in the sense of filling: *tūṇayate*; *tūṇaḥ*, *tūṇīraḥ*. Candra [states] *tūla* [in this sense]. (150) *bhrūṇ* in the sense of hope (*āśā*): *bhrūṇayate*; *bhrūṇaḥ* means "embryo" (*garbhaḥ*). Some say [it is used] in the sense of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*). (151) *śaṭh* in the sense of boasting (*ślāghā*): *śāṭhayate*; *śāṭhaḥ*. Nandi says *śaṭa*, while Kauśika says *śala*. (152)

The root *yakṣ* is used in the sense of worshiping a yakṣa: *yakṣayate*. [The noun] *yakṣaḥ* is formed with the suffix *manin* (Uṇ. IV, 150). [The root] *syam*, meaning "to conjecture," is *syāmayate*. In the *bhvādi* class, *syamu* is listed alongside *svana* (I, 878) and is marked as *mit*; thus [the forms] are *syamati* and *syamayati* (154). [The root] *gūrī* is used in the sense of exertion (*udyama*). [In the Ātmanepada: *udgūrayate*; [the noun] *āgūraṇā*. In the *tudādi* class, *gurī* is also listed in the sense of exertion (VI, 103): [the form] *udgurate*. Regarding the rule *apaguro ṇamuli* (VI, 1, 53), there is optionally an *āttva* (vowel substitution) in this case: [the forms] *apagāram* and *apagoram* (155).

The root *śam* is used in the sense of "perceiving" (*ālocane*). In the form *niśāmayate*, or as in *dānta-śānta* (VH 2.27), it means "calmed" (*śāntaḥ*); when not meaning "perceiving," it is *niśāmitaḥ*. In the *divādi* class (I 4.72), one says *śāmyati*; by the rule *śamo 'darśane* (I 3.23), there is the substitution of *m* for *n*: *śamayati rogam* ("he calms the disease"). It means "to characterize" (*lakṣayate*) or "to be characterized" (*lakṣate*). In other cases (X 5), as in *ghaṭaṃ lakṣayati* (156. 157), it means "to mark.
The root *kuts* is used in the sense of "reviling" (*avakṣepaṇe*). One says *kutsayate*. By the rule *cintipūjī* (III 3.105), the noun *kutsā* is formed (158).

*truṭ* means "to break. In the causative, *troṭayate* (he breaks) a rope. In the *tudādi* class (VI. 82), it is *truṭyati*; or, by the rule *vā bhrāśa* (III. 1. 70), it is *truṭati*. Some say *truḍ*: *uttroḍayate* (he pulls up) a blade of grass. *gal* means "causing to flow. *galayate*, *udgālayate*. In the *bhvādi* class (I. 579), it is *galati*. *bhal* means "investigation. Investigation (*ābhaṇḍana*) is examination (*nirūpaṇa*). *Nibhālayate*.

*Kuṭ* [is used] in the sense of heating (*pratāpane*). It means "to strike" (*koṭayate*). In the *tudādi* class (DhP VI.73), in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilye*), it is *kuṭati*. Candra says *truṭeti*; for this very reason, it is established by the root *truṭ* "cutting" (159). Durga says *kūṭa* [is used] in the sense of non-bestowal (*āpradāne*) (162).

The root *vañcu* is used in the sense of "deceiving" (*pralambhana*). Deceiving is the false proclamation of a result. The connection of these and other such roots [with the *cur*-class] is for the purpose of recognition, so that it may be understood: "this very same root belongs to the *cur*-class in a different meaning. Regarding the rule *gṛdhivañcyoḥ pralambhane* (I.3.69), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used: *vañcayate bālam* ("he deceives the child"), whereas in another sense, *vañcayati* ("he avoids the snake"). In the *bhvādi* class, *vañcu* means "to go" (cf. I.204): *vañcati* (163).

*vṛṣ* is used in the sense of "binding power" (*śaktibandhana*). Binding power is the incapacity for procreation. *Varṣadharaḥ* means "one who causes to rain. In the *Bhvādi* class, *vṛṣu* is listed as "to sprinkle" (I, 738): [he sprinkles]. Some say that the root beginning with the fourth letter of the dental class (*tavarga*) is for the purpose of "maintaining capacity": he overcomes the enemy (*dharṣayate 'rim*). *mad* is used in the sense of "satisfaction" (*tṛpti*) and "purification" (*śodhana*). Purification is "attainment" (*saṃpatti*). According to Nandin, it means "connection with satisfaction. He gladdens (*mādayate*). In the *Divādi* class, *madī* is listed as "joy" (IV, 99): he becomes intoxicated (*mādyati*). In the *Ghaṭādi* class, *madī* is listed as "joy and languor" (I, 853): he makes intoxicated (*madayati*). (165)

*div* is used in the sense of cooing (*parikūjana*). It is a *gantrī* [verb] for one desiring the gods (*devayate*). In the *div-ādi* class (I V, 1), it is *dīvyati*; in the *bhv-ādi* class (I, 529), in the sense of playing (*devana*), it is *paridevate* (166).

*gṝ* is used in the sense of perceiving (*vijñāna*). It is *gārayate*. In the *tud-ādi* class (VI, 117), in the sense of swallowing (*nigaraṇa*), it is *nigirati*; in the *kry-ādi* class (IX, 28), in the sense of sound (*śabda*), it is *gṛṇāti*. According to Candra (167), *kṝ* means "perception" (*vijñāna*). *vid* is used in the senses of consciousness (*cetana*), narration (*ākhyāna*), and dispute (*vivāda*). It is *vedayate sukham*, *āvedayate kathām*, *pravedayate vādinam*. In the *ad-ādi* class (H, 55), it is *vetti*; [the root] *div*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "div–". The translation reflects the available portion.)
In the first [class] (I V, 62), *vidyate* occurs; in the sixth class (VI, 138), *vindati* and *vindate*; in the seventh class (VII, 13), *vinte*.

[The root] *man* means "to be stiff" (*stambha*). Stiffness is pride (*garva*). [Example: *mānayate vṛṣalaḥ* ("the low-born man is arrogant"). According to Candra, in the alternative form, *manati*. In the fourth class (IV, 67), *manyate*; in the eighth class (VIII, 9), *manute*. [The root] *yu* means "contempt" (*jugupsā*). [Example: *yāvayate brāhmaṇān jālmaḥ* ("the scoundrel treats the Brahmins with contempt"); [derivative form: *yāvyam*. In the second class (II, 23), *yauti* in the sense of "mixing"; in the ninth class (IX, 9), *yunāti* in the sense of "binding. Some say that *yuji* means "contempt": [example] *yojayate* (170).

Or [the suffix] occurs after the name *kusma*. *Kusma* is observed [as a word]; from this nominal stem (*prātipadika*) *kusma*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) optionally occurs. Alternatively: *kusma* is observed as a distinct verbal root (*prakṛti*); from the root *smi-* preceded by *ku-*, the suffix *ḍa* occurs according to Pāṇini III.2.101 (*parikhādiṣu ca*), as seen in other cases as well: *kusmayate*, *kusmayati*.

One might object: "Is it not already established that *smiṅ* is derived from the root *ku-* as in *kusmayate*? Furthermore, since the suffix *kvip* applies after the name *kusma*—as it does after all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*) according to Pāṇini III.2.11—the form *kusmatī* will be established. Therefore, for what purpose is it stated, 'or after the name *kusman*'? Having raised this objection, he provides the following resolution: "The verb *kusmayati* is not one that has a causative marker (*akārita*)."

There is an obligatory compound with a particle (*kṛt*) name [according to Pāṇini II.2.18], but not with a finite verb (*tiṅ*), as in the case of *kutsitaṃ smayate* [which would fall under II.2.19: *atiṅ*]. Consequently, there would be no restriction on the word order, such that one could also use *smayate ku*, which is not desired. Now, even if this form were to occur in the common language (*bhāṣā*) as a different verbal root (*prakṛti*) ending in *-aṇ* [i.e., *kusmayate*], by what would it be prevented? To this he says: "The status of the prefix (*upasarga*) is held to be external; thus we have *prakusmayate*, *vikusmayate*, etc."...

According to the rule *te prāg dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini I.4.80), in the case of *kusmayate*, the prefix (*upasarga*) would be external [to the verbal root], and the erroneous interpretation that "only *ku-* is the prefix" would be incorrect. Furthermore, when the suffix *yak* follows a sārvadhātuka [affix], after the elision of the causative marker *ṇi*, the form *kusmyate* is desired, whereas [according to your view] it would be *kusmīyate*; likewise, [the perfect forms] would be either *kusmayāṃcakre* or *kusmiyāṃcakre*, or *kusiṣmiye*, or *acukusmata*; [and the desiderative] would be *cukusmayiṣate* or *kusismayiṣate*; [the nominal derivatives] would be *kusmanā*, *kusmitiḥ*, *kusmayitvā*, or *prakusmya*. Therefore, it is only the causative [marker *ṇic*] that applies, and not [the alternative interpretation]. Why? Because...

Since there is no status as a verbal root (*kriyāvācin*) without the indication of its own meaning (*svārthanirdeśa*), the case-terminations (*kāraka-pratyaya*) based on action must be applied. Now, if the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is desired even in the sense of "he causes that to be done," as in the case of *sūtrayati* and so forth (Pāṇini III.1.26), is it not already established by the rule "from a nominal stem [is derived] the meaning of a verbal root" (X.368)? True; however, the purpose of listing this separately is the occurrence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the cessation of the form of the original root. But Durga read *kusmayate*, and he states that *kusma* is a verbal root seen by the wise which expresses a meaning produced by the intellect (171).
In thirty-four sūtras, the section on *ākusmīya* consists of thirty-seven verbal roots (*dhātu*).
[The following are examples: *carc* in the sense of study; one studies the Veda (*vedam carcayati*). According to Pāṇini III.3.105, *cintipūji*, the form is *carcā*.
[Next,] *bukk* in the sense of barking; a dog barks (*bukkayati*). In the *bhvādi* class (Pāṇini I.1.122), it is *bukkati*.

Regarding the rule *śabda upasargād āviṣkāre*: "The mountain *pratiśabdayati*" means it manifests an echo (*pratiśrutkā*). [He] *viśabdayati*. According to Nandī, because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), [the suffix applies] even without a prefix (*anupasargāt*) in the sense of manifestation (*āviṣkāre*): [he] *śabdayati*. For the followers of Durga, there is a single rule: *śabda*, meaning "in the act of making sound" (*śabdakriyā*); from that, [it follows] "after a prefix, in the sense of manifestation. Candra establishes this by the very rule: *prātipadikād dhātvartha* (X.368). (174)

*kaṇ* in the sense of closing the eyes: it makes the eye one-eyed (*kāṇayati*); one who is one-eyed (*kāṇaḥ*). In the *bhvādi* class (I.476), it is *kaṇati*; because of its status as a *mit* root (I.831), it is *kaṇayati*.

(175) *jabhi* in the sense of destroying: *jambhayati*, *jambhyate*. In the *bhvādi* class, *jabha* and *jṛbhi* are used in the sense of gapping (cf. I.415, 416): *jabhate*, *jabhyate*. Candragomin says *jabh*. By the rule *radhijabhor aci* (VII.1.61), the nasal augment (*num*) is applied: *jambhayitum*. (176) *ṣūda* in the sense of flowing: *sūdayati*. Some [authorities] say it also means "killing": *nisūdayati*. In the *bhvādi* class, it is used in the sense of trickling (I.25): *sūdati*; *sūdaḥ*, *nisūditaḥ*. (177)

In the sense of "striking" (*tāḍane*), [the form] *ujjāsayati* is used according to *jāsiniprahaṇa* (Pāṇini I.3.56). In the *divādi* class (IV.102), it is *jasyati*. It is stated as *jasī* (X.128): *jaṃsayati*. In the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*), [the forms are] *pāśayati* (according to Pāṇini VI.1.60) and *paśati* or *paśate* in the *bhvādi* class (I.936). Regarding both of these, Durga states that they end in the retroflex nasal (*mūrdhanyānta*). In the sense of "disease" (*roge*), [the form is] *āmayati*. In the *bhvādi* class, *ama* is used in the sense of "motion" and so forth (I.493):

*amati*. In the *ghaṭādi* group, *ama* is used in the sense of "disease" (cf. I.869): *amayati*. From the word *ati*, the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel should be understood. Thus, *āmayaḥ* and *āmayate* (180).

*caṭa* and *sphuṭa* mean "to split. [The causative forms] *uccāṭayati* and *sphoṭayati* mean "to cause to split" or "to tear asunder. In the *bhvādi* class (I, 352), there is *sphoṭati*; in the *tudādi* class (VI, 80), there is *sphuṭati* (181, 182). [The root *pra-vaṇ*] in the sense of "inclination" belongs to the tenth class (X, 184).

The roots *caṭ*, *sphuṭ*, and *ghaṭ* have the meaning of "killing" (*hanti*). These [roots] take the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of killing: *uccāṭayati*, *āsphoṭayati*, *vighāṭayati*. Others, however, explain that *caṭ* is a *curādi* root meaning "to burst open" (*āsphuṭa*) or "to strike" (*āsphoṭana*), while elsewhere it belongs to the *bhvādi* class (Dhatupatha I, 316, not according to Kṣīrasvāmin): *uccaṭati*. Some, however, say they have the meaning of "killing" and also express their own inherent meaning (*svārtha*): *ghātayati*, *todayati*; or, because of its recitation in another group, it means "to strike" (*tudati*) according to the *tudadi* class (VI, 1).

In this way, the reading of *tud* in the sense of "to strike" (*hiṃsā*) is for the sake of the *ātmanepada* endings. Regarding *ghaṭ* in the sense of "joining together" (*saṃghāṭa*), Durga says: *saṃghāṭayati*. The reading of *ghaṭ* in the *bhvādi* class (I, 800) is for the sake of the *dyutadi*-group meaning, for the sake of the *taṅ* (middle voice) endings, and for the sake of the designation *mit* (183–184). *Div* means "to injure. One says *paridevayati*; elsewhere, one says *dīvyati* (IV, 1). Candragomin states that [the form] is established by *divu* in the sense of "warbling" (*parikūjana*) (X, 166) (185). *Arj* means "effort toward acquisition" (*pratiyatna*). *Pratiyatna* is refinement (*saṃskāra*). One says *arjayati*. In the *bhvādi* class, *arj* and *sarj* are listed in the sense of "acquisition" (I, 242–243): one says *arjati* (186).

*Ghuṣir* is used in the sense of "making a sound" (*viśabdane*). "Making a sound" means producing a distinct sound. One *udghoṣayati*. According to some, it is used in the sense of "not making a sound": one *apaghoṣayati* evil, meaning "one conceals" (*apahnute*) it. The fact that the root ends in *ṛ* is a sign that it is not invariably followed by the causative marker (*ṇic*): *aghuṣat*, *aghoṣīt*, *ajūghuṣat*. Kauśika states that *ghuṣa* is used in the sense of "making a sound. In the *Bhvādi* class (I. 683), *ghoṣati* is listed. *Āṅaḥ krand* is used in the sense of "continuity"; it belongs to the *Curādi* class: one *ākrandayati*. In other cases, one *krandati* (I. 71).

*Laṣ* is used in the sense of applying oneself to an art or craft (*śilpopayoga*). *Lāṣayati* means he carves or fashions by means of a lathe and so forth. Elsewhere, it is *laṣati* or *laṣyati* (Dhātupāṭha I, 937). Kauśika says that it ends in a palatal: *lāśayati*. *Bhūṣa* is used in the sense of adorning (*alaṃkāra*). *Bhūṣayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (Dhātupāṭha I, 712), it is *bhūṣati*. Regarding the suffix *tasi*, Durga says it is *bhūṣeti*: *uttaṃsayati*, *avataṃsayati*; *uttaṃsaḥ*, *avataṃsaḥ*. *Mokṣa* is used in the sense of releasing (*asana*). *Mokṣayati* [means he releases] arrows. Elsewhere, it is *mokṣate* (Dhātupāṭha VI, 136).

The root *arh* is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). [In the Causative: *arhayati*, [Aorist] *ārjihat*; [Past Passive Participle] *arhitam*, [Feminine Abstract Noun] *arhaṇā*. In the *Bhvādi* class (I, 776), *arhati* is used in the sense of commanding (*jñāniyojanā*). [Examples: *ājñāpayati bhṛtyān* ("he commands the servants"); [Past Passive Participle] *jñāpitaḥ*, [Feminine Abstract Noun] *jñāpanā*. Elsewhere (IX, 36), *jānāti* is used in the sense of knowing. *Bhaj* is used in the sense of bestowing (*viśrāṇana*). Bestowing is giving. Others say that in the sense of bestowing it means "separating" (*viṣecana*). [Examples: *bhajayati*; [Noun] *bhājī* (Pāṇini IV, 1, 42). Elsewhere (I, 1047), *bhajati* and *bhajate* are used.

1. *pantyaktajana* (!); 2. *KP sahane*; 3. *P adds abhilāṣī*. 185. X. *śṛdha* in the sense of *aprasahana*. *Aprasahana* means lack of forbearance (*amarṣaḥ*). Some say that in the sense of *prasahana* it means overcoming (*abhibhava*). One causes the enemy to be bold; [forms: *aśaśardhat*, *aśīśṛdhat*. In the *Bhvādi* class, *śṛdhu* is listed as "making a contemptuous sound" (I, 797): *śardhate*; likewise, from *śṛdhu* and *mṛdhu* in the sense of "moistening" (I, 922, 923): *śardhate*, *śardhati* (195).

Regarding *nikāra* and *upaskāra*: *nikāra* means affliction. One torments the enemy (*yātayaty arim*); *yātanā* is intense suffering. A king "torments" a vulnerability, meaning he conceals it; *pratiyātayati* means he reflects [it]; *pratiyātanā* is a reflection. In the *bhvādi* class, the root *yat-* is used in the sense of effort (*prayatne*): *yatate*. And with the prefix *ni-*, it is used in the sense of returning grain or wealth: one "returns" a debt (*niryātayaty ṛṇam*), meaning one clears it; grain and wealth are mentioned as illustrative examples (196).

[The root] *vas* [is used] in the senses of dwelling, causing to dwell, cutting, and removing: *vāsayati*, *vāsanā*; it causes a tree to dwell (*vāsayati vṛkṣam*); it causes an enemy to dwell (*vāsayaty arim*), meaning "he kills him. In the *Bhvādi* class (I, 1054), it is *vasati*; in the *Adādi* class (II, 13), it is *vaste*; and *vastra* (204). [The root] *car* [is used] in the sense of doubt: *vicārayati*. For deliberation (*vicāraṇā*) occurs when there is doubt. Durga says that *car* is used in the sense of non-doubt. Elsewhere (I, 591), it is *carati* (205). [The root] *cyu* [is used] in the sense of enduring: *cyāvayati*. In the *Bhvādi* class (I, 1004), it is *cyavate*. [The form] *cyusa*...

According to some, [the prefix] *sa-* is used; according to others, *ha-*. [The root] *cyu* takes *ṇiC* in the sense of "mixing" (*avakalkana*). Mixing (*avakalkana*) means blending. He mixes rice with curd (*bhāvayati dadhnaudanam*). The fifth case ending is used for the purpose of indicating that the causative form (*ṇyant*) is not invariably present: Nandī says "in the sense of deliberation" (*vikalkana*). He causes the Brahmin to deliberate upon austerity (*bhāvayed brāhmaṇaṃ tapaḥ*); [the result is] "deliberated upon" (*bhāvitam*). The root *bhū* in the sense of "attainment" is *ātmanepada* (X, 300), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) optionally applied: he causes himself to become (*bhāvayate*), or he becomes (*bhavate*). The root *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (I, 1): he exists (*bhavati*). [The root] *kṛp* takes *ṇiC* in the sense of "purpose" (*tādarthya*). Purpose refers to the object of an aim. He prepares [it] (*kalpayati*).

One intends the oblation for the deities. In the *Bhvādi* class, the root *kṛpū* means "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) [DhP I.799]: *kalpate*. According to some, it means "preparation" (*avakalkana*) when it has the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*); for this very reason, Durga states that the roots *bhū* and *kṛp* mean "preparation. Candragomin explained both as meaning "consideration" (*cintana*) in the sense of preparation: *saṃbhāvayati*, *avakalpayati* (208).

*raga* and *laga* are used in the sense of "tasting" (*āsvādane*): *rāgayati*, *lāgayati*. In other senses, *rage* (in the sense of "doubt") and *lage* (in the sense of "attachment") belong to the *ghaṭādi* group (DhP I. 822–823): *ragati*, *lagati*, *ragayati*, *lagayati*. Candra [records] *raka* and *laka*; Durga [records] *āsādana* (197).

*Anca* is used in the sense of "qualifying" (*viśeṣaṇe*). Qualification means excellence (*atiśaya*). *Añcayati* means "he qualifies objects," i.e., "he makes them manifest. In the *bhvādi* class, *ancu* is used in the sense of "motion" (cf. I. 203): *añcati* (198).
1. *nikāra* and *upasaṃskāra*; 2. *sneha*, *cheda*, and *avahananana*; 3. 197–203, after 208; 4. *hāni*; 5. *sāmarthya* [is] *uddhṛta*; 3. *ācchādana*; *āsvādana*; X 186:

*ligi* in the sense of *citrikaraṇa* (making a mark or distinguishing). [One] *liṅgayati*, *ulliṅgayati*; *liṅga*. In the *bhvādi* class, *ligi* has the meaning of motion (*gatyartha*) (I, 165): *āliṅgati* (199).

*Mud* means contact. *Modayati* means to moisten groats with ghee; hence *modaka*. In the *bhvādi* class (*muda harṣe*, I.16), one finds *modate* (200). *Udhrasa* means to glean. This root is read specifically in the *kryādi* class (IX.52) for the purpose of adding the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in its own sense; because it is marked with *u* as an *udit*, it takes the augment *iṭ*: *udhrāsayati*, *udhrasnāti*. Some say that *u* is part of the actual form of the root: *udhrāsayati*, *udhrasnāti*. Others say that *ut* precedes both: *uddhrāsayati*, *uddhrasnāti* (202). 1.

*Muca* [is used] in the sense of releasing (*pramocane*). It causes arrows to be released (*mocayati śarān*). In the *Bhvādi* class, *muc* is used in the sense of deceit (*kalkane*)—as stated in [Pāṇini I, 185]: *mocate*. In the *Tudādi* class, *mucḷ* is used in the sense of liberation (*mokṣaṇe*)—as stated in [Pāṇini VI, 136]: *muñcate*, *muñcati*. (203) [The rule applies] up to *svada*, provided the root is transitive (*sakarmakāt*). He will state [later] that *ṣvada* means "to conceal" (*saṃvaraṇa*) [in Pāṇini I, 187]; from this point onward, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to transitive roots. Śākaṭāyana, however, maintains that the causative is formed after *svada* preceded by the prefix *ā*: *āsvādayati dadhi* ("he causes the curd to be tasted"); otherwise, because it belongs to the *Bhvādi* class [as per Pāṇini I, 18], it is *svadate*, meaning "he experiences the taste" (*svādam anubhavati*).

*Gras* means seizing; it causes [the fruit] to be seized (*grāsayati*). *Tras* means warding off, according to Durga: it terrifies the deer (*trāsayati mṛgān*). According to Nandi, it means supporting; some say it means seizing. Elsewhere (*I V, 10*), one finds *trasati* and *trasyati*. *Puṣ* means supporting; it nourishes an ornament (*poṣayaty ābharaṇam*). In the *Bhvādi* class (*I, 732*), it is *poṣati*; in the *Divādi* class (*IV, 73*), it is *puṣyati*; in the *Kryādi* class (*IX, 57*), it is *puṣṇāti*. *Dal* means splitting; it splits wood (*dālayati dāru*). [Derivatives include] *dālapaḥ* and *dālmiḥ*. In the *Bhvādi* class (*I, 581*), where *dal* means falling apart (*viśaraṇe*), it is *dalati*; because of its designation as having an indicatory *m* (*mittvāt*) (*I, 856*), it is *dalayati*.

*paṭ*, *puṭ*, *ruṭ*, *luṭ*, *tuji*, *piji*, *laji*, *luji*, *aji*, *kusi*, *kuśi*, *trasi*, *dasi*, *daśi*, *ghaṭi*, *raghi*, *laghi*, *ahi*, *bahi*, *mahi*, *gupū*, *dhūpa*, *vicha*, *cīva*, *barha*, *balha*, *putha*, *lokṛ*, *locṛ*, *ṇada*, *kupa*, *tarka*, *vṛtu*, *vṛdhu*—these roots have the sense of "shining" (*bhāsārtha*) and, being transitive (*sakarmaka*), they take the causative suffix (*ṇic*). [Examples: *pāṭayati*; from *phalipāṭi* (Uṇ. I, 19), *paṭuḥ*; in the *Bhvādi* class (I, 318), *paṭati*.

Their inclusion among other groups, even though they are transitive, is for the purpose of allowing the optional addition of the causative suffix *ṇic*; however, they cite as counter-examples those roots read in this very [divādi] class which take the regular verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*): *trasati*, *kuṃsati*. *Poṭayati*: in the *tudādi* class (VI.74), it is *puṭati*. *Roṭayati*, *loṭayati*: in the *bhvādi* class (I.783–784), it is *roṭate*, *loṭate*; in the *divādi* class (IV.113), *luṭ* meaning "to strike," it is *luṭyati*. *Tujjayati*: in the *bhvādi* class (I.264), it is *tuñjati*. *Piñjayati*: in the *adādi* class (II.18), it is *piṅkte*.

*lañjayati*, *lañjati*; *luñjayati*, *luñjati*. *añjayati*; in the *rudhādi* group (cf. VII.21), *aṅkte*, *vyanakti*. *kuṃsayati*, *kuṃsati*; *bhrukuṃsaḥ*, *bhrakuṃsaḥ*. *kuṃśayati*, *kuṃśati*. *traṃsayati*, *traṃsati*. *daṃs-* (see 209); *daṃśayati*, *daṃśati* (see 204–208); *daśati* (see before 197). [Root] *daṃś* (9P) in the sense of "moving away" (visaraṇe). [Root] *daṃś* (X).

*sayati*, *daṃsati*. *daṃśayati*; in the *bhvādi* class (*I*, 1038), *daṃśa* means "to bite": *daśati*. *ghaṇṭayati*, *ghaṇṭati*; *ghaṇṭā*. *raṅghayati*, *laṅghayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (*I*, 107, 108), *raṅghate*, *laṅghate*. *aṃhayati*, *baṃhayati*, *maṃhayati*; in the *bhvādi* class, *ahi* means "to go," and *bahi*, *mahi* mean "to increase" (*I*, 666, 664, 665): *aṃhate*, *baṃhate*, *maṃhate*. *gopayati*, *dhūpayati*, *vicchayati*; in the *bhvādi* class (*I*, 422, 423).

VI. 129) *gopāyati*, *dhūpāyati*, *vicchāyati*; [the suffix] *-āya-* is applied according to the rule *gupū-dhūpa-vichi* (cf. III. 1. 28). *Cīvayati*; in the *bhvādi* class, *cīva* means "to take" (cf. I. 928): *cīvati*. *Barhayati*, *balhayati*; in the *bhvādi* class, *barha* and *balha* mean "preeminence" (I. 669, 670): *barhate*, *balhate*. *Pothayati*; in the *divādi* class, *putha* means "injury" (IV. 12): *puthyati*. *Vilokayati*, *ālocayati*; in the *bhvādi* class (I. 76, 177): *lokate*, *locate*.

*nādayati* (he causes to sound), in the *bhvādi* class (I, 55); [the root] *nad* is *nadati*. *kopayati* (he makes angry), in the *divādi* class (IV, 122); [the root] *kup* is *kupyati*. *tarkayati*; [the nouns] *vitarkaḥ* (reflection) and *tarkitaḥ* (conjectured). *vartayati* (he turns/rolls) and *vardhayati* (he increases); [the roots] *vṛt* and *vṛdh* are in the *bhvādi* class (I, 795–796); [the roots] *vṛt* and *vṛdh* are *vartate* and *vardhate*. Others recite [the roots] *bhaji*, *pisi*, *laḍi*, *bṛhi*, *taḍi*, *naṭi*, etc.: *bhañjayati* (he breaks); [the root] *bhañj* is in the *rudhādi* class (VII, 16) as *bhanakti*; *piṃsayati* (he grinds) and *piṃsati*; *laṇḍayati* (he leaps) and *laṇḍati*; *bṛṃhayati* (he strengthens); [the root] *bṛh* is in the *bhvādi* class (cf. I, 772).

*Nandī* states that *bṛṃhati*, *tāḍayati* (taḍati), *nāṭayati* (naṭati) are *ātmanepada*-verbs in the *bhū-ādi* class: [thus] *naṭate*. According to the *Pārāyaṇa*, roots such as *paṭ* and others, when transitive and having the sense of "shining," take the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in their own meaning: *bhāsayati diśaḥ* (he illuminates the quarters), *dīpayati*, *indhayati*, *prakāśayati*. However, their recitation in other classes of roots is for the sake of other grammatical operations (212, 213, 243, 214, 215, 217, 244, 218, 245, 223, 225, 221, 246, 224, 227, 253–257, 231–234, 229, 230, 235–242, 219, 222, 258, 228, 259, 250).
The root *pūr* is used in the sense of filling (*āpyāyane*). It forms *pūrayati*. In the *divādi* class (I. 4. 52), it forms *pūryate* (261).

The root *ruj* is used in the sense of injuring (*hiṃsāyām*). It forms *rojayati*. In the *tudādi* class (VI. 4. 95), *ruj* is used in the sense of breaking (*bhaṅge*): *rujati* (262). The root *ṣvad* is used in the sense of covering (*saṃvaraṇe*). It forms *svādayati* and *sisvādayiṣati* (VIII. 3. 62). In the *bhvādi* class (I. 1. 18), *ṣvad* is used in the sense of tasting (*āsvādane*): *svadate* (263).
The section on transitive roots (*sakarmaka-paryāṭṭaka*). Here, within forty-two sūtras, there are seventy-seven verbal roots.

Regarding the rule *ā dhṛṣād vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.47), he will state that *dhṛṣ* means "to overpower" (306); from this point forward, the option of adding the causative suffix *ṇic* is established. In the alternative case, the regular conjugational suffix *śap* applies. In this context, the application of *ṇic* is restricted by rule to an option; however, its non-constant status as having a causative form (*ṇyantatva*) follows the specific usage of the texts, being intended as an option in certain instances.

The root *pṛcī* means "to join" or "to connect. It forms *yojayati* and *yojati*. In the *divādi* group (*divādau*), *yuj* means "to concentrate" (*samādhau*)—as in *yujyate*; in the *rudhādi* group (*rudhādau*), *yujir* means "to join" (*yoge*)—as in *yunakti*. [From *pṛcī*] one forms *saṃparcayati*. In the *rudhādi* group (*rudhādau*), it forms *saṃpṛṇakti*; in the *adādi* group (*adādau*), *pṛcī* means "to join" (*saṃparke*)—as in *saṃpṛkte* (cf.
264, 265). The root *arca* means "to worship" (*pūjāyām*). It forms *arcayati* and *arcati* (cf. 266).
The root *sah* means "to endure. It forms *sāhayati* and *sahati*, as in: "This very same elephant endures the insults from young elephants" (*Subhāṣitāvalī* 631).
In the *Bhvādi* class (I, 905), it is *sahate* (267).
The root *īr* means "to cast away"; casting away is impelling. It forms *īrayati* and *īrati*. In the *Adādi* class (II, 8), it is *īrte* (268).

The root *lī* means "to liquefy" (*dravīkaraṇe*). From it, one forms: *vilālayati*, *vilāpayati*, *vilāyayati*, *vilayati*; as well as the nouns *vilayaḥ* and the past passive participle *vilāyitam*. Regarding the rule *liyo vā* (VI, 1, 51), because it is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions), the substitution of *ā* for *i* does not occur except in the senses of "delaying," "honoring," and "overpowering. Therefore, in other cases, the substitution of *ai* and *au* takes place. However, only in the sense of "delaying" and so forth does the substitution of *ā* occur along with the augment *puk*: *kas tvām ullāpayate?* ("Who is making you delay?"). In the reflexive sense, one forms *ālāpayate* and *apalāpayate*. Furthermore, according to the rule *liyaḥ saṃmānanaśālīnīkaraṇayoś ca* (I, 3, 70), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used in the senses of "honoring" and "making modest. In the sense of "liquefying through affection" (*snehavipādane*), the augment *nuk* is added [according to the rule *līyater alpaviṣaye nuk*]. 1. Note: *vilālayati* is derived from the causative stem *vilāla-*. 2. Note: *snehavipādane* refers to the softening or melting of something through affection or heat.

(VII, 3, 39): *ghṛtaṃ vilīnayati* (he causes the clarified butter to melt). In the *divādi* class (IV, 31), *lī* means "to adhere": *līyate*. In the *kryādi* class (IX, 31), *lināti*. (269) *vṛjī* means "to avoid": *varjayati*, *varjati*. In the *adādi* class (II, 19), *vṛkte*. In the *rudhādi* class (VII, 24), *vṛṇakti*. (270) *vṛñ* means "to cover": *āvārayati*, *āvarati*, *āvarate*. In the *svādi* class (V, 8), *vṛṇute*, *vṛṇoti*. In the *kryādi* class, *vṛṅ* means "to choose" (IX, 38): *vṛṇīte*. (271)

The root *jṝ* means "to lose vitality. It forms *jārayati*, *jarati*, and *jāraṇā*. In the *divādi* class (*IV*, 22), it is *jīryati* and *jīrṇaḥ*; in the *kryādi* class (*IX*, 24), it is *jṛṇāti*. According to Nandī, there is also the form *jri*: *jrāyayati*, *jrayati*, and in the *kryādi* class, *jriṇāti*. The root *ric* means "separation" and "mixing. It forms *recayati* and *recati*. In the *rudhādi* class (*VII*, 4), it is *riṇakti*. (272–273)

The root *śiṣ* is used in the sense of "not employing entirely. Not employing entirely means not being utilized. [It forms] *śeṣayati* and *śeṣati*. With the prefix *vi*, it signifies excellence (*atiśaya*). Excellence means preeminence. [It forms] *viśeṣayati*, *viśeṣati*, and *vyaśeṣīt*. In the *rudhādi* class, *śiṣḷ* is listed in the sense of distinguishing (*viśeṣaṇe*): [it forms] *viśinaṣṭi* and *vyaśiṣat* (274). The root *tap* is used in the sense of burning (*dāhe*): [it forms] *tāpayati* and *tapati* (275).

The roots *tṛp* and *dṛp* mean "to inflame. [In the curādi class: *tarpayati*, *tarpati*. In the *divādi* class (*divādau*), *tṛp* means "to please" (*prītau*) [Pāṇini I.4.86]: *tṛpyati*; in the *svādi* class, *tṛpnoti* (cf. V.2.25 with reference to I.4.86). [In the curādi class: *darpayati*, *darpati*. In the *divādi* class [I.4.87], *dṛpyati*. Some say [the roots] *cṛt* and *chṛd*: *cartayati*, *cartati*; *chardayati*, *chardati* (cf. 276, 277). *dṛbhī* means "fear": *darbhayati*, *darbhati*. In the *kryādi* class, *dṛbhī* means "to tie" (*granthe*) [cf. VI.1.34]: *dṛbhṇāti* (278).

1. So K and P; C reads *viṣīṇayati*. 2. So K and G; P reads *snehavipāṭane*. 3. P adds: *riṅkte* in the sense of giving (*adādau*). 189. *Chada* in the sense of covering (*saṃvaraṇe*): *chādayati*, *chadati*. In the sense of strengthening (*ūrjane*), it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group (I, 851): *chadayati* (290).

Now, *śrath* in the sense of "injury": *śrāthayati*, *śrathati*. Some say *śranth*: *śranthayati*, *śranthati*. (280) *mī* in the sense of "thought"; in the sense of "thinking": *māyayati*, *mayati*. In the *divādi* group (IV.29), it is *mīyate*; in the *kryādi* group (IX.4), it is *mīnāti*. (281) *krath* in the sense of "injury": *krāthayati*, *krathati*. In the *bhvādi* group (I.838), it is *mit*: *krathayati*. (282)

*Śīka* in the sense of "endurance" (*āmarṣaṇe*): *śīkayati*, *śīkati*; [the reduplicated aorist] *aśīśikat*. In the *Bhvādi* class (*I*, 75), *śīkṛ* means "to sprinkle" (*secane*): *śīkate*; [the reduplicated aorist] *aśiśīkat*. (283) *Arda* and *hiṃsa* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyām*): *ardayati*, *ardati*; *hiṃsayati*, *hiṃsati*; in the *Rudhādi* class (*VH*, 19), *hinasti*. (285, 286) After the prefix *āṅ*, the root *ṣad* has the meaning of "going" (*padyarthe*). The meaning of *padyati* is "motion" (*gati*). [Thus: *āsādayati*, *āsadati*; some say *āsīdati*. Elsewhere (*I*, 907), *sīdati*. (288)

*Śundha* means "to purify. [The forms] *śundhayati*, *śundhati* (289). *Juṣa* means "to satisfy. [The form] *joṣayati*. In the *tudādi* class (*juṣī* in the sense of "affection" and "service," VI.8), [the form] *juṣate* (291). 1. *Dhūñ* means "to shake. [The forms] *dhūnayati*; according to some, *dhāvayati*; [also] *dhavate*, *dhavati*; [the past passive participle] *dhūnitaḥ*. In the *svādi* class (V.9), [the forms] *dhunoti*, *dhūnoti*; in the *tudādi* class (VI.105), *dhuvati*; in the *kryādi* class (IX.17), *dhunāti* (292).

The root *prī* (in the sense of "to satisfy") forms *prīṇayati*. Because of its association with *dhū*, the augment *nuk* is added [by Pāṇini VII 3.37, vārttika 1], resulting in *prāyayatīti* according to some; [it also forms] *prayate* and *prayati*; [the past passive participle is] *prīṇitaḥ*. In the *divādi* class (*prīṅ* in the sense of "to love," IV 36), it forms *prīyate*; in the *kryādi* class (IX 2), it forms *prīṇāti* and *prīṇīte* (293).

In the context of *śrantha* and *grantha*, *saṃdarbha* means binding (*bandhana*). [The roots] *śranthayati*, *granthayati*, *śranthati*, and *granthati* belong to the *bhvādi* class: *śrathi* in the sense of loosening (*śaithilye*) and *grathi* in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilye*) (I, 35–36): *śranthate*, *granthate*. In the *kryādi* class (IX, 39–41), there are *śrathnāti* and *grathnāti* (294). *Āpḷ* is used in the sense of obtaining (*lambhana*), where obtaining is acquisition (*prāpti*): *āpayati*, *āpati*; *āpitam*. In the *svādi* class (V, 14), in the sense of pervading (*vyāpti*), there is *āpnoti*; *āptam* (295).

*tanu* [is used] in the sense of faith (*śraddhā*) and instrument (*upakaraṇa*). It means "to stretch" or "to extend" (*tānayati*, *tanati*); having stretched (*tatvā*, *tanitvā*), it is "excessively" (*nitāntam*). In the list beginning with *tan*, *tanu* means "extension" (*vistāre*)—[as in] *tanute*, *tanoti*, *tataḥ*. [The rule] "and after a prefix, there is lengthening" (*upasargāc ca dairghye*) includes the particle *ca* placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakramam*): [examples are] *pratānayati*, *ātānayati*, *pratanati*. *vana*... [in the sense of] faith and instrument... [all manuscripts read thus]. (Note: The numbers and letters refer to grammatical references and manuscript variants.)

Regarding the two [roots] meaning "to injure," this is the *Cāndra* *Pārāyaṇa*: *vānayati*; however, with a prefix, it is *udvānayati*. That is already established by the root *vana* "to sound" in the *Bhvādi* class (I, 490). (296) *Vad* in the sense of "informing": *vādayati*, *vadati*, *vadyate*. In the *Bhvādi* class (I, 1058), there are *vadati* and *vadate*; due to its belonging to the *yajādi* group (VI, 1, 15), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*):

*udyate*. Candra read the root as *vac* (297). *Mān* in the sense of "honoring": *mānayati*, *mānati*. In the *Bhvādi* class (I, 1021), there is *mīmāṃsate* (299). *Bhū* in the sense of "attaining," which takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*): *saṃbhāvayate*, *saṃbhavate*.

"Being in such a state. Regarding *bhuvo 'vakalkane* (X, 207): *bhāvayati* [is used] in the first class (*bhvādi*, I, 1) as *bhavati*. Although [the form] is established by the mere recitation [of the root], the mention of the option (*vā*) is for the sake of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings even when combined with the suffixes *aṇ* and *ic*:

"May we have supplicants, and may we be givers" (300). Regarding *vaca* in the sense of speaking: *vācayati*, *vacati*, *vācyate*, *vacyate*. Candragomin states that it belongs to the *curādi* group in the sense of sending a message. In the second class (*adādi*, II, 54): *vakti*, *ucyate*, *sva-*...

By the rule *piśācācaryāt* (VI.1.15), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for roots beginning with *ā*. *garh* in the sense of censuring: *garhayati*, *garhati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.667), it is *garhate* (301).

*mārg* in the sense of searching: *mārgayati*, *mārgati*. *mṛg* in the sense of searching (X.352): *mṛgayate* (302). *kaṭh* in the sense of longing: *utkaṇṭhayati*, *utkaṇṭhati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.283), [it is *utkaṇṭhate*].

The root *utkaṇṭh* means "to long for. (303) The root *mṛj* means "cleansing" and "adornment. From it come *mārjayati* and *mārjati*; the world [uses] the words *mārjanā* and *mārjitā rasālā*. It belongs to the *ad*-class (H, 57), hence *saṃmārṣṭi*; because the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (I, 1, 63) is not universally obligatory, there is the substitution of *āt* for *mṛj* (304). The root *mṛṣ* means "endurance. From it come *marṣayati* and *marṣati*. In the *div*-class (IV, 55), one says *mṛṣyati*. Some read this [root] by transposing it for the sake of relying on its having a final *a*: *mṛṣayati* and *mṛṣati* (305).

*dhṛṣ* is used in the sense of "not being overcome" (*aprasahana*). Non-overcoming is subjugation (*abhibhava*); for this very reason, it is appropriate that it is [also] called "overpowering" (*prasahana*). [Examples: *dharṣayati*, *dharṣati*; *pradhṛṣṭaḥ*, *pradharṣitaḥ*. In the *svādi-gaṇa*, *ñi-dhṛṣā* is used in the sense of "boldness" (*prāgalbhya*): *dhṛṣṇoti*. In these thirty-seven rules, the group of forty roots beginning with *ā-dhṛṣ* forms the *ādhṛṣīya* section. [These roots] end in *a*. From here until the end of the *gaṇa*, the fact that they end in *a* is prescribed for the purpose of prohibiting the designation of *it*. Consequently, by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini VI.4.48), there is the elision (*alopa*) of the [final] *a*. Regarding the *sthā-* [of the elided sound...]

1. *saṃvādayati*, *saṃvadati*. 9. *addit* [is used] in the sense of deliberation (*vicāre*). 3. After rule 298, [the following is added] after 300. 4. All manuscripts read thus (without *vā*). 5. P adds *saṃskāre ca*: *mārgayati vāsasī*. 3. It has been stated [at] 191 that because of the prohibition of *nivṛtti*, there is an absence of *vṛddhi* and other such changes: *kathayati*, *kathakaḥ*. Because of the mention of the plural, the Dramiḍas hold that for roots beginning with *vaṭila* and *lañji* (372, 374), there is the addition of the letter *a* at the end: *vaṇṭāpayati*, *lañjāpayati*.

The root *kath* is used in the sense of "connection of speech. "Connection" (*pratibandha*) here means the continuity [of speech] through uninterrupted utterance; for this very reason, some read the term as *vākya-prabandha*. It forms the word *kathā*: because of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*allopāt*), there is no subsequent *vṛddhi* replacement, since the word *para* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭavācitvāt*). By the rule *cintipūji* (III.3.105), the suffix *aṅ* is applied: thus *kathā*. In *kathaka*, there is the elision of the causative marker *ṇi* before a suffix that does not require *iṭ* (VI.4.51). In *saṃkathayya*, the suffix *lyap* is applied, and by the rule *lyapi laghupūrvāt* (VI.4.56), the *ay* substitution occurs.

He said: according to the rule *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini VI.1.93), [the substitution of *guṇa*] does not occur because the root lacks an *aglopa* (elision of a penultimate vowel). How then is *acīkathat* formed? Another root must be sought. *Var* in the sense of "desiring" (*īpsā*): he chooses a maiden (*kanyāṃ varayati*); [the noun] *varaḥ*. Or, from the *curādi* class, from the root *vṛñ* (X.271): *vārayati*, *varati*, *varate*. In the *svādi* class, *vṛ* (V.8) in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*): *vṛṇoti*, *vṛṇute*. In the *kryādi* class, *vṛṅ* (IX.38) in the sense of "sharing" (*saṃbhaktau*): *vṛṇīte*. *Gaṇ* in the sense of "counting" (*saṃkhyāne*): *gaṇayati*. By the rule *ī ca gaṇaḥ* (VII.4.97), [the forms] *ajīgaṇat* and *ajagaṇat* are obtained. [The derivatives are: *gaṇakaḥ*, *gaṇikā*, *gaṇaḥ*, *gaṇanā*, *gaṇanam*. (309)

*Śaṭha* and *śvaṭha* are used in the sense of speaking improperly. [In the causative: *śaṭhayati*, *śvaṭhayati*. In the *Bhvādi* class, *śaṭha* is listed under "deceit" (*kaitave*, I.363): [in the simple form] *śaṭhati*; in the causative, *śāṭhayati*. Regarding *śvaṭha* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*, cf. X.29), the form here is *śvāṭhayati* (310). *Paṭa* and *vaṭa* are used in the sense of "tying" (*grantho veṣṭanam*). [Examples: *paṭayati rajjum* (he ties a rope), *vaṭayati*. In the list beginning with *paṭa* (X.212), one finds *pāṭayati*. In the *Bhvādi* class, *aṭa*, *paṭa* are listed in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), and *vaṭa* in the sense of "tying" (*veṣṭane*, I.317, 318, 322): [in the simple form] *paṭati*, *vaṭati*; in the causative, *pāṭayati*, *vāṭayati* (311).

*raha* means "to abandon. *Rahayati* is "separation" (*viraha*). In the *bhvādi* class (I, 767), *rahati*; with a causal suffix, *rāhayati* (312). *Rahi* in the sense of "going": *raṃhayati*, *raṃhāpayati*. In the *bhvādi* class (I, 768), *raṃhati* (312a).

The roots *stan* and *gad* are used in the sense of "sound. *Deva* means "cloud. Regarding the forms *gadiḥ* and *iti-ktic-ktau dhātunirdeśe* (Pāṇini III.3.108–109), the designation [of the root] as having an indicatory *ī* (*īdit*) is inappropriate, because in the alternative view where the suffix *ṇic* is not applied, forms such as *gattā* are not observed; for this very reason, Candra states: *stan gada śabda* (Candra Dhātupāṭha X.83). [Examples: *stanayati*, *gadati*, *ajagadat*. By the rule *stani-hṛṣi-puṣi-gadi* (Uṇādi-sūtra III.29), the suffix *itnuc* is applied after the causative (*ṇi*): *stanayitnuḥ* ("thunder"), *gadayitnuḥ*. In the *Bhvādi* class (I.489, 53): *stanati*, *gadati*; in the sense of causing another to act (*hetu*), *stānayati*, *gādayati*; *ajīgadat* (I.313, 314).

Or *pata-gatau* (in the sense of "going"). [The forms] *patayati*, *patati*, *apapatat*, and *apātīt* [are derived from this]. By the rule *spṛhi-gṛhi-pati* (Pāṇini III.2.158), the suffix *āluc* is applied: *patayāluḥ*. In the *bhvādi* class (Dhātupāṭha I.898), [the root is] *patati*, [with the preterite] *apaptat*. Others have read *pata aiśvarye* ("to possess power"); however, the word *vā* is for the sake of including the subsequent portion [of the root], as in the case of *vāvṛtu-vat* (Pāṇini IV.52). (315) X 192.

The root *paś* [takes the suffix *ṇic*] when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). This is because the meaning [of the root] has not been specified [in the rule], and thus [the application of *ṇic*] occurs in the sense of "going" (*gatau*). Candra says this [root] is non-Vedic (*anārṣa*). Some say that for the root *paś*, belonging to both the *bhvādi* and *curādi* classes, there is a rule regarding its becoming vowel-ending (*adanta*) when followed by *ṇic* and not preceded by a prefix. Thus: *paśayati*. When preceded by a prefix, it does not occur: *prapaśati*. Some say that for *paś*, when not preceded by a prefix, it optionally becomes vowel-ending: *paśayati*, *pāśayati*. Nandī says this [root] ends in a retroflex nasal (*mūrdhanya*). Regarding *svar* in the sense of "throwing" (*ākṣepa*): *svarayati*. In the *bhvādi* class, *svṛ* is listed as "sound and affliction" (*śabdopatāpayoḥ*, I, 979): *svarati*; in the sense of "causing" (*hetu*), *svārayati* (317). Regarding *rac* in the sense of "effort toward perfection" (*pratiyatna*): *racayati*; *racanā* (318).

The root *kal* is used in the senses of "going" and "counting. 1. In the *bhvādi* class (*kala* in the sense of sound and counting, I.526): *kalate*; in the causative sense (*hetau*), *kālayati*. From the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepa*, X.64): *kalayati gām* (he drives the cow). The root *cah* is used in the sense of "deceit" (*kalkana*). Deceit (*kalkana*) means hypocrisy (*dambhana*). [Causative: *cahayati*; [Aorist: *acacahat*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.765): *cahati*; [Aorist: *acīcahat*.

In the sense of "great worship" (*mahāpūjā*): *mahayati*. It belongs to the *bhvādi* class (cf. I, 766) as *maha*; in the *kaṇḍvādi* class (III, 1, 27) it is *mahīṅ*: *mahīyate*. From the roots *ava* and *mahi*, the suffix *ṭiṣac* is applied (Uṇ. I, 46): *mahiṣaḥ*. From *maha* with the suffix *ina* (cf. Uṇ. II, 56): *mahinaḥ*. By the rule for *śvan*, *ukṣan*, etc. (Uṇ. I, 158), we have *maghavan*. In the sense of "present," from *pṛṣad* and *bṛhat* (Uṇ. II, 84): *mahat*. When used as a masculine noun in the sense of a name, the suffix *gha* is applied (III, 3, 118): *mahī* (321).

The roots *śāra* and *kṛpa* mean "to weaken" or "to become weak. From *śāra*: *śārayati*, *aśaśārat*; in the *kryādi* class (IX, 18), from *śṝ*: *śṛṇāti*, *aśīśarat*. According to Nandī, the reading with the short vowel (*śara*) implies that there is no elision of the penultimate *n* (referring to Pāṇini VI.4.93): thus *aśaśarat*. Durga reads it as *sāra*. From *kṛpa*: *kṛpayati*, *acakṛpat*; [the derivatives] *kṛpaṇaḥ* and *kṛpaṇā*; in the rule for the formation of the suffix *aṅ* (III.3.104), we have *kṛpā*; by the rule *kṛpes tādarthye* (X.208), the suffix *la* is applied: *kalpayati*; in the *bhvādi* class (I.799), from *kṛpū* meaning "capability": *kalpate*.

*śrathayati*; because it belongs to the *kapirikādi* group (cf. Pāṇini VIII.2.18 Bh.), it is *ślathayati*. *śratha* in the sense of "to delight" (cf. X.13): *śrāthayati* (322–324). *spṛha* in the sense of "desire. By the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini I.4.36), that which is desired is the *saṃpradāna* (dative): *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati* ("he desires flowers"). By the rule *spṛhi-gṛhi* (Pāṇini III.2.158), there is the suffix *aluc*: *spṛhayaluḥ* (325). *bhāma* in the sense of "anger": *bhāmayati*, *ababhāmat*. In the *Bhvādi* class (I.468), *bhāmate*, *abībhamat* (326).

The root *sūca* means "to betray" (*paiśunya*). [Conjugations: *sūcayati*, *asusūcat*; [derivative nouns: *sūcakaḥ*, *sūcaṭ* (cf. 1H, 1, 134): *sūcī*, *sūciḥ*; from *sūceḥ kṣman* (cf. Uṇ. IV, 176): *sūkṣmam*; from *sūcisūtri* (Pāṇini III, 1, 22, 3 Bh.): the intensive (*yaṅ*) form *sosūcyate*. Grammarians state that only monosyllabic roots beginning with *smi* and others are designated as having a *ṣ* in their upadeśa (original teaching), due to their association with those specific roots. Therefore, for the following words, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur: *sūca*, *sūtra*, *saṃgrāma*, *sāntva*, *sāma*, *sabhāj*, *sthūla*, *stana*, *stena*, and *stoma*. [Examples include] *viṣūcikā* and *suṣāman* etc. (Pāṇini VIII, 3, 98). (327)

1. P adds *diśam* and *tārāḥ*. 2. P [adds] *smiṅ-* and so forth. 193. *kheṭa* in the sense of devouring (*bhakṣaṇe*). One devours: *kheṭayati*, *acikheṭat*; *kheṭaḥ* means a village. In the *Bhvādi* class, *khiṭ* is used in the sense of fear (*uttrāse*) (I, 324): one fears, *kheṭati*, *acīkhiṭat*; *ākheṭaḥ*. *Kheḍeti*—these belong to Durga (328).
In the sense of throwing (*kṣepa*): *khodayati*. There is a variant reading: *khoṭa*, *khoḍeti*.

(329) In the sense of smearing (*upalepana*): *gomayati* the earth; [the result is] *gomaya*. Since the division between base and suffix is conceptual, at some time the derivation of *gomaya* from *gomāt* was established; however, nowadays, by Pāṇini IV.3.145, *mayaṭ* is added after *go-* in the sense of "cow-dung. This same principle should be inferred for *kumāra* and others. (330) In the sense of playing (*krīḍā*): *kumārayati*. One who plays is a *kumāra*; or, one whose *māra* (death/danger) is contemptible (*kutsita*) is a *kumāra*. (331)

*Śīla* is used in the sense of "maintaining" (*upadhāraṇa*). Some say that "maintaining" means "practice" (*abhyāsa*) or "familiarity" (*paricaya*). [The forms] *śīlayati*, [and] *aśiśīlat*. In the *Bhvādi* class, *śīla* is listed under concentration (*samādhi*) (I, 556): *śīlati*, *aśīśilat* (332). *Sāma* is used in the sense of "consoling" (*sāntvana*). Consoling is pleasing. [The forms] *sāmayati*, *asasāmat*. Regarding the root *sāma* in the sense of "the employment of conciliation" (cf. X, 33), there is *asīsamat*; and *nāmansāman* (333).

The root *vel* is taught for the sense of "time. From it are derived *velayati* and *avivelat*. In the *Bhvādi* class, *velṛ* is listed as "motion" (cf. I, 573): *velati*, *velā*; and because this root also has *ṛ* as its *it*-marker (VII, 4, 2), we have *avivelat*. For this reason, Candra did not teach this [root] here [in his list]. (334) *palyūla* is used in the senses of "cutting" and "winnowing. Durga says: "in the senses of cutting and falling. One winnows the field; the wind winnows the bank. The followers of Durga read *valyūla*. (335)

Or [it is used] in the senses of motion (*gati*) and serving (*sevana*). *Vāpayati*; because it ends in a dental, there is lengthening and the elision of *a* before *lyap* (Pāṇini VI.4.56): *nirvāpya*. In the *adādi* class (II.41), in the senses of motion and scenting: *vāti*. According to some: *vāteti*; *vātayati*, *avavātat*. *Gaveṣa* in the sense of seeking (*mārgaṇa*):

*gaveṣayati*; *gaveṣaṇā*. *Vāsa* in the sense of service (*upasevā*): *vāsayati*, *avavāsat*; *vāsakaḥ*, *vāsanā*. In the *bhvādi* class (I.1054), *vasati*, *avīvasat*; in the *adādi* class (II.13), *vaste*; here, *vasa* in the sense of affection (*sneha*), etc. (X.204): *vāsayati*. (338)

*Nivās* [is used] in the sense of clothing. [From the root *vas* with prefix *ni-*: *nivāsayati*, *nivāsayitvā*, *aninivāsat*; however, *nyavavāsat* alone would be more appropriate, because the prefix is external [to the root]. *Bhāj* [is used] in the sense of dividing. [From the root *bhaj* with prefix *vi-*: *vibhājayati*, *ababhājat*. [Past participle: *bhājitam*, [gerund: *vibhājya*. In the *Bhvādi* class, *bhaj* means "service": *bhajate*, *bhajati*, *abībhajat*. In the tenth class (*curādi*), *bhaj* means "giving away": *bhājayati*. (339) [Note: Both of these [roots *vas* and *bhaj*] are short according to Candra. (340) [Note: Kṣīrasvāmin says: "Both of these are short. P adds: "Both of these are short according to Candra."
X 194: *sabhāja* in the sense of showing affection or honoring. *sabhājayati*, *sabhājyate*. *sabhājanam*, *sabhājanā*, *sabhājakaḥ*, *sabhājaḥ*.

After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied diversely (*bahulam*) in the sense of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and it behaves like the desiderative suffix (*iṣṭhavad*). From whichever nominal (*nāman*) it is derived, *ṇic* occurs according to usage in the sense of a verbal root—that is, in the sense of a specific action (*kriyāviśeṣa*). He oversteps the bank: *utkūlayati*. He goes against the bank: *pratikūlayati*. He goes along the bank: *anukūlayati*. He crushes clods of earth: *avaloṣṭayati*. Having uprooted the grass, he cuts it down: *uttṛṇayati*. She gives birth to a son: *putrayati*. He climbs a tree: *vṛkṣayati*.

He causes [something] to be like a tree (*vṛkṣayati*). To illustrate this very point, it is said: "From that [base], in the sense of 'he does it,' 'he describes it,' or 'he surpasses by means of it,' there is the *ṇic* suffix, and [the resulting form] is the verbal root. That is to say, the *ṇic* suffix occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the accusative case when the meaning is "he does it" or "he describes it"; likewise, the *ṇic* suffix occurs after a base in the instrumental case when the meaning is "he surpasses by means of it. Examples: He makes sharp: *tīkṣṇayati*; he makes a rule: *sūtrayati* (Pāṇini III.1.26, 5). He describes a sentence: *vākyayati*, *vedayati*. He surpasses by means of an elephant: *hastayati*, *aśvayati*. And that [suffix] is the *ṇic*.

The operations of the *iṣṭhan* suffix occur extensively. What, then, are the purposes served by the treatment as if it were *iṣṭhan*? [They are: the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the nominal stem according to Pāṇini VI.4.155, the substitution of *r*, the elision of the *ṭi* portion, the elision of the semivowel and following vowel (*yaṇādilopa*), the preceding *guṇa* substitution, the substitution of *pra* and other elements, and the elision of the suffixes *-vin* and *-mat*. Examples: *harim ācaṣṭe* ("he describes him as a monkey") becomes *haritayati*; *pṛthum ācaṣṭe* ("he describes him as broad") becomes *prathayati*; *paṭum ācaṣṭe* ("he describes him as clever") becomes *paṭayati*; *dūram nayati* ("he leads him far") becomes *davayati*; *yuvānam īkṣate* ("he looks at the youth") becomes *yavayati*; *kṣipram bhuṅkte* ("he eats quickly")... [becomes *kṣepayati*].

He causes to throw (*kṣepayati*), he speaks meanly (*kṣudraṃ bhāṣate*: *kṣodayati*); he describes a youth as small (*yuvānam alpam ācaṣṭe*: *kanayati*); he describes one who wears a garland (*sragviṇam ācaṣṭe*: *srajayati*); he describes one who possesses wealth (*dhanavantam ācaṣṭe*: *dhanayati*); [the suffix] *ṇic* is applied after the word *bahula* when describing something as dear (*priyam ācaṣṭe*: *prāpayati*). By the rule *prakṛtyaikāj* (Pāṇini VI.4.163), there is no elision of the *ṭi* suffix because of the word *bahulam*; or rather, it is because the base (*prakṛti*) consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*): *sukhāpayati*, *duḥkhāpayati*. There is no application of the *neṣṭha*-suffix, nor does it occur.

In forms such as *prayati*, *sukhayati*, *duḥkhayati*, and likewise *prathayati*, there is no vṛddhi substitution for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). By stating that "the form of the verbal root (*dhātu*) becomes the nominal base (*prātipadika*)," he recalls the statement of Kātyāyana: "From a derivative action noun (*ākhyāna*), [one forms a verb] expressing that [action] by means of a kṛt-suffix; there is elision of the kṛt-suffix (*luk*), the restoration of the original form (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*), and the grammatical relations (*kāraka*) are as in the original. Thus, from *kaṃsavadha* ("the killing of Kaṃsa"), one says *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("he causes Kaṃsa to be killed"), but not *kaṃsavadhayati*; and *baliṃ bandhayati* ("he causes Bali to be bound").

It should not be said [that the rule applies] "only from verbal roots meaning 'to tell' (*ākhyāna*)," because it is observed here as well: *rājāgamanam ācaṣṭe* ("he tells of the king's arrival"), *rājānam āgamayati* ("he causes the king to arrive"). Nor should it be said that [the rule applies] only to the verb *ā-caṣṭe*, because it is observed even in the case of paintings and dolls (*citrapusta*). And the elision of the suffix *-lopa-* occurs when there is a connection with an extreme limit of time (*kālātyantasaṃyoga*) or a boundary (*maryādā*) (cf. Pāṇini III.3.167).

In the case of *śvetāśva*, *aśvatara*, *gāloḍita*, and *āhvaraka*, there is also the elision of the suffixes *-aśva*, *-tara*, *-eta*, and *-ka*. For these four beginning with *śvetāśva*, according to their respective order, when the suffix *ṇiṅ* is attached, there is the elision of *aśva*, *tara*, *eta*, and *ka*. *Śvetāśvam ācaṣṭe tenātikrāmati vā*: "He describes a white horse, or he surpasses it," [results in] *śvetayate*. *Aśvataram*: "A bay horse" [results in] *aśvayate*. *Gāloḍitam*: "Mixed with saliva" [results in] *galoḍayate*; [the form] *kaloḍita* is recorded by Guṇapāla, because the division between base and suffix cannot be established for *gāloḍita*. *Āhvarakam*: "One who brings back" [results in] *āhvarayate*.
The followers of the *Pārāyaṇa* carry over the causative suffix (*ṇic*) here as well, following the pattern of the *arthānuvṛtti*: *śvetayati*, *aśvayati*, *gāloḍayati*, *āhvarayati*. (394)

It is established that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) [is expressed] in the case of *puccha* and so forth. By the rule *pucchabhāṇḍacīvarāṇ ṇiṅ* (Pāṇini III.1.20), the suffix *ṇiṅ* is established after words such as *puccha* when the meaning of the root—such as "shaking off" (*udāsana*) and so forth—is to be expressed, because this was stated by Pāṇini himself. For example: *puccham udasyati* ("he shakes his tail") becomes *utpucchayate*, *paripucchayate*. *bhāṇḍāni samācinoti* ("he gathers up the goods") becomes *saṃbhāṇḍayate*. *cīvaram arjayati* or *paridadhāti* ("the monk acquires or puts on the robe") becomes *saṃcīvarayate bhikṣuḥ*. In the same way, the suffix *ṇic* is established after words such as *muṇḍa* and after those beginning with *satyāpa* and *pāśa* (Pāṇini III.1.21, 25). The use of the neuter gender in the citation is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgalārtha*). (395)
