201 Introduction:
Date of the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*

In his *Report on Kashmir* (1877), p. 73, Bühler states regarding Kṣīrasvāmin: "According to the perfectly credible tradition of Kashmir, he is the grammarian Kṣīra who instructed King Jayāpīḍa. This would place him at the end of the eighth century. In a footnote, Bühler refers to...

He refers to a lecture delivered by Shankar Pandit at the Oriental Congress in London (1874), in which the latter—though with rather unconvincing arguments—polemicized against Theodor Aufrecht, who had published in the same year’s *Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft* (p. ...).

Since Kṣīrasvāmin, who lived in the eleventh century, cites King Bhoja in his commentary on the *Amarakośa* while being cited himself by Vardhamāna in the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi*, it was still overlooked by Aufrecht that Kṣīrasvāmin also cites Rājaśekhara—who lived around 900—in that same work.

The first concluding verse of the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī* reads: "When the lord of the earth named Jayasiṃha, with his powerful long arms, governed the land of Kashmir, the son of the excellent minister, though possessing great wealth, wrote this *Dhātuvṛtti* with his own hand out of devotion (*bhaktyā*)."

The following second stanza provides the name of the author and the title of the work in the same manner as verse 2 of the introduction. In the colophons of several root-sections (*dhātupāṭha*), the father—who is here designated as a minister—is identified as the scholar (*bhaṭṭa*) Īśvarasvāmin.

To correctly understand the first stanza, it should be noted that the verb *likh* is not used in the higher sense of "to compose"—as we say one writes a book or a novel—but rather in a way where manual activity (*akṣaravinyāsa*) always remains in the foreground.

Thus the verse praises Kṣīrasvāmin for undertaking this task himself—contrary to the usual custom of noble persons who entrust the transcription to professional scribes, such as the Bāc-Bhaṭṭas (cf. Bühler, Report, p. 20)—apparently due to the particular difficulty of the text with its many, often abbreviated, introductory elements. (202)

Regarding the sūtra citations and other "thorns": one can see from manuscript P what such an ordinary copyist’s draft looked like, where the sūtra citations are almost invariably corrupted beyond recognition.
In contrast, the author—whose holy zeal for his task is evident from verse 7 of the praśasti—intended to leave behind an absolutely reliable *codex archetypus*.

I have enclosed these two rather clumsy concluding verses within brackets, as I harbor doubts regarding their attribution to Kṣīrasvāmin himself. Although *lilekha* could theoretically be a first-person singular form, such a tense would be strikingly anomalous for a stylist as meticulous as Kṣīrasvāmin. Furthermore, these verses are transmitted only in manuscript K.

P is incomplete at the end, breaking off in the middle of X, 392; however, C is complete, though lacking those same portions. Nevertheless, even if they were—as is probable—derived from a pupil of Kṣīrasvāmin or a copyist of the archetype, their contents need not be rejected on that account, as they are supported by other indications.

Jayasiṃha of Kashmir reigned from 1128 to 1154. If Kṣīrasvāmin wrote under him, he was thus a contemporary of his fellow countryman Kalhaṇa, who, according to Aurel Stein, began his *Rājatarangiṇī* (Chronicle of Kashmir) in 1148/49 and completed it the following year.

However, we can establish even narrower chronological limits for the date of the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī* by means of the information Bühler collected from primary sources regarding the composition of Hemacandra’s grammar in his *Life of the Jain Monk Hemacandra* (1889).

When Jayasiṃha, known as Siddharāja, having defeated his neighbor, King Yaśovarman of Mālava, from Gujarat, a number of manuscripts—including the grammatical treatise of King Bhoja of Dhārā—were included among the abundant spoils of war.

The praise bestowed by scholars at the court of Jayasiṃha regarding Bhoja’s patronage of the sciences aroused the king’s jealousy; he therefore exhorted Hemacandra to compose a new grammar that would bring glory to his own court and kingdom as well.

Hemacandra consented, but requested the king’s assistance in obtaining the necessary materials— specifically the entirety of the grammatical literature extant at that time, which was most complete in [the *Śākaṭāyana-vyākaraṇa*] (203 Introduction).

These works were located in the library of Kaśmīra. Jayasiṃha dispatched high-ranking officials to Pravarapura (present-day Śrīnagara) to obtain copies of these texts. This was successfully accomplished, and Hemacandra composed his grammar, which he named *Siddhahemacandra* in honor of the king, further embellishing it with a panegyric poem dedicated to the king and his ancestors.

The king provided scribes and caused the work to be disseminated throughout his own realm and across all of India; indeed, he sent copies even beyond the borders of India, to Ceylon, Nepal, and Persia.

Since the accompanying historical events are well known, the composition of Hemacandra’s grammar—which consisted of the five parts customary for a *mahāvyākaraṇa* at that time—can be dated to the years...

1139–41. It is now interesting to note that among the books brought from Kashmir to Aṇhilvāḍ there must have been a copy of the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*, for Hemacandra was acquainted with this work and utilized it extensively in his *Dhātupāṭha*. Even a comparison of the treatment of the first root, *bhū*, in both works bears witness to this.

The explanations of root meanings provided by Kṣīrasvāmin have been almost invariably adopted verbatim by Hemacandra. Occasionally, however, Hemacandra cites formations that appear to be unmotivated, which find their explanation and justification only as refutations of the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*.
This establishes the composition of the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī* at the beginning of the reign of the Kashmiri Jayasiṃha, between 1128 and 1138.

Furthermore, Kṣīrasvāmin’s second major work, his commentary on the *Amarakośa*, must have been composed prior to 1138; for it has long been known, and was proven by Eggeling in the preface to his edition, that Vardhamāna also utilized Kṣīrasvāmin in his *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi*, and it appears that he drew primarily from this second work.

Vardhamāna himself now provides the date of composition for the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi* in the concluding verse as the year Saṃvat 1197 (1140 CE). How did Vardhamāna come to know of this work so early, while the author of the *Durghaṭavṛtti*, written in 1172, has no knowledge of Kṣīrasvāmin? Did he live in Kashmir, or perhaps—as suggested by the curious chronological coincidence with Hemacandra’s grammar—did he reside elsewhere? Introduction to Hemacandra’s Grammar.

Could this have led to [the construction of] 204 *mātṛkas* even in Aṇhilvāḍ? To this, he himself provides the answer by citing twice from a poetic composition in his own work (verses 192 and 334), which he identifies as his own panegyric on King Siddharāja by introducing it both times with the words *mamaiva Siddharājavarṇane*.

Thus, it is highly probable that Vardhamāna likewise resided at the court of Gujarat and was therefore able to participate in the utilization of the works sent from Kashmir. All these indications and facts corroborate and support one another.

The grammar for which Vardhamāna composed his *Gaṇavṛtti* remains, as is well known, unidentified. It certainly cannot belong to Hemacandra, since that author’s work was not yet completed at that time.

If the *Śabdakalpadruma* of Bhoja Paramāra were to emerge one day, it might perhaps turn out that the very manuscript of Ujjayinī—which served as the indirect occasion for Hemacandra’s extensive activity in grammar and lexicography—also provided the basis for Vardhamāna’s excellent work.

It has been suggested that Kalhaṇa chose the name *Rājatarangiṇī* under the influence of Somadeva’s *Kathāsaritsāgara*, which is likewise divided into *taraṅgas*. It would not be too bold to postulate the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī* as an intermediary link here. The *Kathāsaritsāgara* was composed between 1063 and 1081.

It goes without saying that Kṣīrasvāmin, given his extensive erudition, was acquainted with this monumental work by his fellow countryman. It is no coincidence that he employs the same rare *pṛthvī* meter for his opening verse (*taraṅgasubhaṅgaṃ kvaṇan*) as Somadeva does for his own (*idaṃ gurugirīndrajā*), and that the title of his own *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*—composed approximately fifteen years earlier—serves as the model for the title of the latter.

Kṣīrasvāmin himself had already previously composed a work—likely a small treatise on transitive and intransitive verbs—to which he gave the somewhat grandiose title *Karmayogāmṛtataraṅgiṇī*. This was presumably his doctoral dissertation, as he mentions (above, p. 4) that Śaśāṅkadhara showed him his teacher’s fist for it. Thus, Kalhaṇa may have found [the source] in this work, the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*, a monograph concerning [the number] 205.

Introduction to Appendix I: The *Dhātupāṭha* prior to Kṣīrasvāmin.

We begin with a comparison of the two commentaries composed simultaneously and independently by Kṣīrasvāmin and Maitreyarakṣita. Although one was written in Kashmir and the other in Bengal, both authors encountered the text of the *Dhātupāṭha* in an identical form.
(Appendix 1)

This version of the *Dhātupāṭha* was received by Maitreya from Bhīma—that is, Bhīmasena—as mentioned in the opening verse (I.1); see my Introduction, section I.I.64. In terms of the forms of the verbal roots, as well as the appended meanings and intermediate remarks, the two versions agree with one another, barring a few minor exceptions.
The only significant difference is the absence of the roots numbered X, 243–260 in the *Maitreyavyākaraṇa* (see the synopsis), a deviation also noted by Sāyaṇa.

He first presents the list according to the *Maitreyavyākaraṇa* (with the remark: "This reading of the *daṇḍaka* is in accordance with Maitreya"), and then adds those missing there, noting: "These fifteen are written down according to Svāmī Kāśyapa."

There was a school of grammarians (the Pārāyaṇikas) who undertook the task of compiling, with as much completeness as possible, all the forms derivable from individual roots according to Pāṇini—both finite verbal forms and those produced by primary suffixes—under those respective roots.

Regarding nominal formations, they took into account both the regular stem formation of the *sūtra* and the irregular formation of the *uṇādi*. Secondary stems were only occasionally and exceptionally included. We still possess three works of this type. The oldest is the *Dhātupārāyaṇa* of Pūrṇacandra, which belongs to the Candra system (see regarding this, p. [number]).

This work is already cited by Kṣīrasvāmin in my edition of the *Candra-vyākaraṇa*. However, there must have been even more such works prior to Kṣīrasvāmin, as he refers to the *Pārāyaṇikas* in the plural.
This is followed by Hemacandra with his *Haima-dhātupārāyaṇam*, and thirdly Sāyaṇa, whose work—though titled merely *Dhātuvṛtti*—surpasses all others in its extent and often tedious prolixity.

In contrast, both Kṣīra and Maitreya, eschewing completeness and constant repetitions, were content to provide only the more important verbal forms and derivatives. In their detailed execution, both [follow] as [stated]:

"By the grace of Mañjughoṣa, I shall begin the exposition of these roots; just as Bhīma has spoken of them many times, so [I shall do] according to tradition (or: according to that which has come down).
(v. 1. *tadupāgamāt*)
Appendix 1, p.

212, expects these two works to be entirely independent of one another. It is probable that both are extracts from older *Dhātuparāyaṇas*, wherein one chose one form and the other another, even though the most important formations naturally recur in both.

Kṣīrasvāmin almost always cites the rule from which a given formation is derived, whereas Maitreya does this much less frequently, usually contenting himself with merely placing the verbal forms and derivatives side by side.

Kṣīrasvāmin is also much richer in other citations; in the long list in Appendix I, Maitreya has only sixteen names of cited authors and works compared to him. Furthermore, the *dhātupāṭhas* of Candra and Durga, which are most frequently cited by Kṣīrasvāmin, are not mentioned as such by Maitreya, even though he was familiar with both works.

A valuable peculiarity of Kṣīrasvāmin is that he regularly paraphrases the meanings provided by Bhīmasena—excluding those that are extremely common—a practice which, as far as I recall, Maitreya never does. That Hemacandra has adopted these explanations with great audacity has already been mentioned above (p. 203).
If we proceed chronologically upward from Kṣīrasvāmin, we encounter within the five hundred years between him and the *Kāśikā* the *Dhātupāṭha* of Śākaṭāyana (c. 870; cf.

Appendix III), as well as two brief citations of verbal roots by the rhetoricians Bhāmaha and Vāmana; the latter is placed in the last quarter of the eighth century, while the former is assigned to the third quarter of the seventh.

Both provide a series of stylistic observations in their final chapters, wherein certain formations of the *bhāṣā*—the cultivated colloquial language taught or permitted by grammar—are nonetheless deemed unsuitable for the language of poetry, while others are recommended. Regarding the *dhātupāṭha*, however, not much follows from this.

The root *mil* occurs in the ancient *Kātantra-Dhātupāṭha*, but not in *Candra*, who—apparently on the basis of the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*)—has incorporated it into his own system as VI.7, *mila saṃgame*, and has classified it as *vibhāṣita* (optionally active), thus yielding both *milati* and *milate*. *Śākaṭāyana* (VI.76): *mila saṃghāte*, as an active verb. Following *hil* (VI.69), Kṣīrasvāmin states: "Regarding *mila śleṣaṇe*, [Durga says] 'it mils' (*milati*), [and] 'mela'. Maitreya (VI.83): "Regarding *mila śleṣaṇe*, some say this belongs among the parasmaipada roots."

They read [the root] *mila* in the sense of "meeting" (*saṃgama*) as an *ubhayapadī* (taking both voices), thus juxtaposing the statements of Durga and Candra. Both Bhāmaha and Vāmana reveal themselves in these sections as profound masters of the *śabdasmṛti*, which Bhāmaha refers to as the *Vyākaraṇaśāstra*; this is not surprising, given that according to I-tsing, Indian students spent nine years studying grammar before they began learning the composition of verse and prose.

From his presentation it follows that with the *Kāśikā* concluded the common preliminary study for all disciplines, such as poetics, philosophy, and so forth, whereas the *Bhāṣya* and the works of Bhartṛhari fell to the specialists of grammar.

This also explains how, during occasional declines in the general level of cultural attainment, the *Bhāṣya* was more prone than the *Sūtra* and *Vṛtti* to vanish from living study until it was revived to new life by a spiritual hero. The text itself need not necessarily suffer as a result.
The *Vākyapadīya* has not been studied in India for centuries, yet it remains fully preserved.
The *Kāśikā* cites dozens, perhaps hundreds, of roots from the *Dhātupāṭha*, always in the forms provided by Bhīmasena and as recorded by Kṣīra and Maitreya.

Between the *Kāśikā* and *Candra* lies the *Jainendra-vyākaraṇa* of Devanandin, whose *dhātupāṭha* appears not to have been preserved; for this grammar, see the introduction to Appendix III. Its *dhātupāṭha* is cited in Abhayanandin’s *Vṛtti*, by Kṣīrasvāmin (twenty-nine citations under the name Nandin), and by Sāyaṇa.

In Jainendra I.2.3, Abhayanandin cites *ṇimidā* in the sense of "moistening" (*snehane*), *ṭunadi* in the sense of "prosperity" (*samṛddhau*), and *ḍukṛñ* in the sense of "making" (*karaṇe*), all exactly as in Pāṇini.

Introduction to Appendix II: The *Dhātupāṭha* prior to Kṣīrasvāmin (Continued)

By a fortunate coincidence, the *Kātantra-Dhātupāṭha* has been preserved for us in the Tanjur in a form that, following its revision by Durgasiṃha, was certainly no longer studied or copied in India itself, and therefore likely no longer exists there. Appendix II, p. 233.

At the time of Hemacandra, the grammatical system consisted of five main components: the *Sūtrapāṭha*, the *Dhātupāṭha*, the *Vṛtti* (along with the *Gaṇapāṭha*), the *Uṇādi*, and the *Liṅgānuśāsana*. Of these, the last—the teaching on the genders of nouns—was not yet included in the grammatical canon during the time of Candra, for he... [as noted in the source].

At the end of the concordance for Pāṇini-Candra (Candra-Paribhāṣā 74), [the author] maintains Pāṇini’s principle that gender is not to be taught theoretically because it is sufficiently well-known from worldly usage (*liṅgam aśiṣyam lokāśrayatvāl liṅgasya*).

Furthermore, since Śarvavarman, the author of the *Kātantra*, excludes even the regular derivation of nominal stems as superfluous for his elementary grammar, it follows *a fortiori* that this applies to irregular derivations as well; this is in agreement with the fact that Durgasiṃha is named as the author of the *Kalāpa-Uṇādi-Sūtra* in the Tanjur (No. 3725).

Finally, although the *vṛtti* was always composed together with the *sūtra*, in earlier times it was transmitted to students only orally. Thus we know that the *Kātantravṛtti* was first committed to writing by Durgasiṃha, and the *Pāṇinivṛtti* by Kuṇi and others.

Thus, we must regard only the *Sūtra* and the *Dhātupāṭha* as originating from Śarvavarman’s own hand. Even older than these would be the *Dhātupāṭha* of Bhīmasena, provided that the manuscripts attributed to his name could be considered authentic.
Since this is not the case (see below), this *Kātantra-Dhātupāṭha* should be regarded as the oldest extant *dhātupāṭha* overall; this historical interest justifies its publication.

The *bhū*-class contains here 214 roots, which is only about one-fifth compared to the other *dhātupāṭhas*. No single underlying principle of arrangement can be discerned here; according to Kaiyaṭa on *Mahābhāṣya* I.1.75, this *kuṇi* was older than Patañjali.

It appears to me that the author worked in great haste, having found no time for some reason to allow his work to reach full maturity; nothing of this sort is found in the Sūtrapāṭha (see Appendix II, p.

One should take note: where entire large chapters are completely missing, this is due to the author’s specific intention; however, what he does present is internally coherent and consistent. As for the supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*), it appears that his time was no longer sufficient for it.

In the first class, he attempted once more an independent revision in the manner of a *sūtrapāṭha*, but without achieving his goal; as for the remaining classes, he accepted them as they were found and contented himself with deleting here and there a root that seemed superfluous to him (cf. above II, 12 and 71).

However, the Tibetan translator certainly would not have chosen such a distorted representation of a scientific treatise for his purpose if the *Kātantra-Dhātupāṭha* had been known to him or accessible in a better form. I have pointed this out [in the Introduction I, p. 6].

The fact that the rule whose ignorance caused such great distress to King Śātavāhana stands as one of the very first rules at the beginning of the *Kātantra* suggests that there may indeed be a kernel of truth in the account of Śarvavarman’s wager regarding the state of the *dhātupāṭha*.
To dismiss the entire narrative—which is attested in four or five independent versions—as a mere fairy tale, as has recently been done once again, seems to me to be hypercritical.

There is also a modern scientific myth-making, which sometimes stands on even weaker feet. The discovery by the young Bühler (1863) that "Pāṇini’s work was an improved, completed, and partially revised edition of Śākaṭāyana" already belongs to the past; however, Burnell’s Aindra school...

(1875) is still encountered here and there. Burnell’s thesis—that the scheme of the *Kātantra* grammar dates back to a period long before Pāṇini and reappears after him, such that Pāṇini stands outside the normal line of development which, as it were, revolves around him—fails already on simple grounds.

The fact that Śarvavarman utilized no source other than Pāṇini himself (cf. Böhtlingk, ZDMG 41, 659; my Introduction, Part I, p. 5). Nevertheless, despite this lack of originality and other defects, Śarvavarman nonetheless established a truly significant [tradition] through his grammar. [End of Part II, p. 37]

Having taken account of this deficiency, he established for India the model of a practical elementary grammar; consequently, his work has not fallen into oblivion, but has been gradually rendered more effective through additions and supplements, and has subsequently been widely imitated in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Dravidian, and Indo-Aryan languages.

Thus, he employs *tc*, *tch*, *ds*, and *sh* to represent Csoma’s *ts*, *tsh*, *ds* (which correspond to Jaeschke’s *ts*, *tʂ*, *dz*), and *zh* (Jaeschke’s *z*), all of which are more or less incorrect.

Here a point is touched upon that indeed urgently requires regulation, all the more so since the correct solution—in the case of Tibetan—presents itself almost of its own accord through as close an adherence as possible to the Indian alphabet.

Jäschke’s method of transliteration was certainly an improvement over that of Csoma; however, even his own system no longer suffices, as it relies upon the outdated Lepsius standard alphabet and stands in contradiction to several principles of the Geneva resolutions—specifically points 1 and 7.

For this reason, shortly before his death—which was far too premature for science—H. Wenzel and I established a transcription together through our consultations, primarily designed to meet the needs of Indologists and facilitate their entry into the Tibetan language.

Since the Tibetan alphabet is based on the Indian, and since there is almost complete consensus regarding the transcription of Indian terms—provided they pertain to scientific works—we proceeded from the following principle: every phonetic symbol that was adopted unchanged from Indian into Tibetan is to be represented by the same Latin letter as its Indian prototype.

Those Tibetan letters which are derived from Indian letters by means of a diacritic mark must likewise be derived and represented in transliteration by applying a corresponding diacritic mark to the respective Latin letter.

Subsequently, in Tibetan, we first have the same thirty-three consonants as in Sanskrit, all transcribed in the identical manner. Regarding the signs for initial vowels, only that for short *a* has been transferred into Tibetan; all other initial vowels are represented by this *a* combined with an internal vowel marker.

There remain six characters unique to Tibetan: the three so-called palatal sibilants by Jäschke—differentiated from the palatals by an added hook (*c*, *ch*, *j*) and used to represent the Indian palatals; furthermore, two characters for soft spirants, one of which (*z*) is formed by the inversion of *j*.

Other [soft consonants] are derived from ś (i.e., zh), and finally there is the sign of which Jäschke (Grammar, p. 2) claims was (as the sole instance) newly invented. However, this is not the case; it has originated from the avagraha, and is therefore most naturally represented by an apostrophe.
It serves primarily as a vowel-support within the interior of a word and can often be omitted entirely in transliteration where confusion with the other vowel-support is impossible.
Thus, the alphabet of the *Thon mi Sambhota* appears in our transliteration as follows: k kh g ṅ; c ch j ñ; t th d n; p ph b m; ts tsh dz w zh z; y r l ś sh s h.

There are natural transcriptions that are easily impressed upon the mind, and artificial ones that are received only with a certain degree of resistance.

Among the former belongs the sign for the velar nasal *ṅ*, which—by bearing a dot in its upper half—effectively pre-empted the corresponding Devanāgarī character; it thus triumphantly defeated its rivals, such as *n* with a stroke above it, or the monstrosity invented by Rhys Davids.

Furthermore, this ṅ naturally associates with the similarly sounding *m* and *ṃ*. The dot beneath the letter used to mark the retroflexes may also be regarded as a natural transcription, since it is occasionally found in North Indian manuscripts to distinguish *ḍ* from similar characters, from which it likely originated.

The use of ṃ for the *anusvāra* is unnatural, especially as it stands in open contradiction to Kuhn’s own guiding principle No. 10: "Cerebrals are indicated by a subjoined dot," and furthermore misleads and confuses learners through a false association with the letter ṇ.

The fact that this sign nevertheless found favor—particularly among German specialists—is likely explained by the circumstance that when using the German Fraktur script, and indeed only in that script, *ṃ* can easily be mistaken for *m*.

Kuhn would have done better, rather than burdening science with this poor symbol, to advise his German-writing colleagues to habituate themselves to using the Antiqua type for this symbol, just as an Orientalist must memorize so many specific signs.

Now, in the age of the typewriter, even this transcription has lost its last vestige of apparent justification; it would be desirable if this question were once again addressed and properly resolved at the next German Orientalist Congress, whereby unity could finally be achieved in reality.

It is curious that the goal which has been placed at the very forefront by everyone from William Jones to James Burgess—namely, the uniform spelling of Oriental proper names far beyond the *consensus of specialists*—remains today, in essence, as distant from realization as it was a hundred years ago. Let us consider, for instance: [Insert relevant examples here] ...we see that [the situation remains unchanged].

It is noteworthy that Johannes Hertel, who employs the Geneva transcription system in his scientific works, prefers a completely different transliteration—reminiscent of Böhtlingk’s—in more popular works such as the *Indische Erzähler*, evidently in order to present the Indian sound-image to the German reader without the "English spectacles."
One should draw from this the lesson that this goal is likely as utopian as the aim of employing a single script for all the languages and peoples of the earth in their daily usage.

Therefore, linguistic science should strive all the more diligently within its own domain to agree upon a transliteration for every language that guarantees the possibility of an unambiguous back-translation into the original script.

Indeed, the languages of indigenous peoples who do not yet possess their own writing systems are all recorded using the Latin alphabet; however, that alone is insufficient: we must also bring every cultural language, whether living or dead, onto the common denominator of the Latin script in terms of its phonetic status.

Texts, abundant texts from Antigua, accompanied by a translation and a complete glossary—this is the necessary toolkit of the linguist; he will prefer to determine the structure of each language from the texts themselves, unencumbered by the blinkers of Latin grammar.

Only then, when one can trace any single question through any number of languages—ancient and modern, past and present—unimpeded by the barriers of individual linguistic scripts, will we gradually obtain monographs that prove truly beneficial even for psychology.
For just as language is not the sole means for the cognition of the soul, it is certainly one of the most important tools for the investigation of the mind.

I-tsing lists (translated by Takakusu, Oxford 1896, pp. 178–180) the linguistic works of Bhartṛhari: the commentary on the *Mahābhāṣya*, the *Vākyapadīya*, and the *Prakīrṇa* (which he designates as *Peina*). Regarding the extent of the second [work], 267 Appendix III.

Since he assigns 700 *ślokas* to the first book and 3,000 *ślokas* to the third, it is clear that even at that time—as occasionally also later—the third book of the *Vākyapadīya*, namely the *Padakāṇḍa* or *Prakīrṇa*, was regarded as a separate work because of its extent and its fundamentally different treatment of the subject matter.

For, according to the Benares edition, the first two books together comprise 650 *ślokas*, whereas according to Kielhorn’s manuscript (now in the University Library at Göttingen), they comprise 681 *ślokas*; meanwhile, the third book, whose edition is not yet complete, contains 1,315 *ślokas* in 14 chapters (*samuddeśa*) in this manuscript.

Thus, the extent of the first two books was specified very precisely by I-tsing. As for the third book—which its commentator Helārāja likewise designates as *prakīrṇa* (miscellaneous) in his colophons—it was either more extensive during I-tsing’s time, or its extent was inaccurately stated by him.
*Prakīrṇa* means "miscellanea," and since I-tsing heard it designated by the term *peīṇṇa* (the colloquial form), his rendering of the name is as precise as one could expect.

However, I-tsing tells us even more: the narrower sense of the *Vākyapadīya*—namely, the *Brahma* and *Vākya* sections—already possessed a commentary, the extent of which he estimates at 7,000 *ślokas*.

We know of only one commentary on the first two books, that of Puṇyarāja, who identifies himself as a direct disciple of Bhartṛhari; since its extent also roughly corresponds (I estimate it at approximately 5,000 ślokas based on the printed edition), it is likely that I-tsing had this very commentary in mind.

Furthermore, in the summary of contents at the end, the teacher Vasurāta is mentioned once more in verse 54.

Vasurāta is a rare name; Indian literary history knows of only one other Vasurāta, who is mentioned in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* as belonging to mythological antiquity. Thus, we cannot help but identify the person mentioned here with the grammarian Vasurāta mentioned in Paramārtha’s biography of Vasubandhu.

There we learn (*T’oung-pao* 1904) that this Vasurāta was a brahmin and the brother-in-law of Crown Prince Bālāditya. He engaged in a literary dispute with Vasubandhu, the great Mahāyāna teacher and preceptor of the crown prince, accusing him of grammatical errors in his *Abhidharmakośa*.

The *Abhidharmakośa* must have been composed prior to 470 CE, as it falls within the period when Vasubandhu still adhered to the Hīnayāna. It was only later in life that he was converted to the Mahāyāna by his elder brother Asaṅga shortly before the latter’s death; subsequently, he composed his famous commentaries on the Mahāyāna sūtras as well as his own original Mahāyāna treatises.

Takakusu dates the lifespan of Vasubandhu, who lived to the age of eighty, to approximately 420–500 CE, and that of Asaṅga, who died at seventy-five, to 410–485 (or perhaps better 400–475, since according to Tāranātha Vasubandhu was born the year after Asaṅga’s ordination and outlived him by twenty-five years; Tār.).

According to Paramārtha, Vasubandhu was born in Puruṣapura (Peshāwar). After he had already migrated to Ayodhyā, his brother Asaṅga—who still resided in Puruṣapura—sent him a messenger with the message that he was gravely ill and wished to see him, intending thereby to convert him to the Mahāyāna.

Faxian (399–414 CE) found Gandhāra in a state of magnificent prosperity. The country was densely populated, and its inhabitants were for the most part followers of the Hīnayāna. In the capital, Puruṣapura, he marveled at the stūpa of Kaniṣka, remarking: "Of all the stūpas and temples seen by the traveler, none can compare with this in terms of the beauty of its form and its structural strength."

When Xuanzang arrived in Gandhāra, the country was a wasteland. "The cities and villages were deserted, and only a few inhabitants were to be seen. At one corner of the royal residence, there were a thousand households. In the ruins of the city, he still saw the house where Vasubandhu had composed the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Hsüan-tsang provides further details regarding this devastation of a vast and fertile land elsewhere (Julien II, 190 ff.). Tradition attributes it to Mihiragula, the son and successor of the Hūṇa Toramāṇa, who must have ascended the throne around 500 CE.

He had conceived an interest in the teaching of the Buddha and desired to meet a distinguished theologian who might instruct him therein. Perhaps under other circumstances he would have been a second Kaniṣka; on this point, those who wish to identify Vikramāditya in Hiuen-tsang’s (and Kālidāsa’s) [account] with Candragupta II or Samudragupta may be referred to Appendix III, p. 274.

However, it turned out otherwise. At that moment, none of the monks dared to answer the king’s call. Having few desires and no taste for worldly activity, they were not concerned with acquiring fame; on the other hand, those who possessed profound knowledge and great brilliance feared his imposing authority.

He divided his task by entrusting the mission to an old royal servant who had long been a monk and was eloquent in speech. This negligence proved disastrous. The king, deeply wounded in his sensitive barbarian pride, issued an edict commanding the total eradication of Buddhism throughout all the lands under his dominion.

He himself cooled his vengeance upon Buddhist Gandhāra; he defeated and killed the king, exterminated the royal family, overthrew the *stūpas*, and destroyed the monasteries, numbering one thousand six hundred. Aside from those who perished by the sword, ninety thousand people remained, for whom his ministers vainly entreated mercy.
The king released the prisoners.

He led them to the banks of the Indus and divided them into three groups according to rank and status. He ordered the first group to be massacred, the second to be drowned, and the third to be distributed as slaves among his warriors. While the number may be exaggerated, this slaughter is attested by other sources (as will be seen later), and Hiuen-tsang himself, as an eyewitness, reported the consequences of the devastation.
In Ayodhyā, the pilgrim visited the house where Vasubandhu had composed his Mahāyāna works.

It is particularly striking that both Paramārtha and Xuanzang (Hiuen-tsang) mention the reappearance of the ancient city name Ayodhyā—the old capital of the kingdom of Kośala—whose name survives today in the designation of eastern Hindustan as Oudh.

The name means "the Unconquerable," and she appears to bear it with justification, for as far as we know, she was never conquered by an enemy hand. The city of Rāma fell into ruin because his successors transferred their residence to Śrāvastī. In the vicinity of the ancient capital, Sāketa flourished, which—as already noted by Jacobi (*Das Rāmāyaṇa*, p. [page number])—...

As has been pointed out, this place is referred to by Buddhists and Jainas, as well as by the Greeks and Patañjali, as Ayodhyā. Kālidāsa uses both names interchangeably. It is natural to assume—Appendix III, 275—[that this was the case].

That Bālāditya transferred his capital here after the destruction of Pāṭaliputra by the Huns (cf. S 269), and perhaps the ancient prophecy found at the end of the *Rāmāyaṇa*—that a king like a bull (*ṛṣabha*) would repopulate Ayodhyā after a long period of desolation—played a role in the choice of this location. (I 16)

In the *Raghuvamśa*, the tutelary goddess of Ayodhyā appears at night to Kuśa, the successor of Rāma who has relocated his capital away from that city; appearing in the garb of an abandoned woman in mourning, she describes with such poignant emotion the decline brought about by his departure that Kuśa promises to return to her.

The poet describes the image of the deserted city, its migration, and its subsequent flourishing in sixty-three stanzas with such vividness that one feels he has not merely captured scenes from his imagination, but has recorded and rendered them as vividly as if they were witnessed in reality.

274) He issued an edict against the Buddhists; however, when the [King of Magadha] advanced with an army to punish that disobedient vassal, his courage failed him, and he said to his ministers: "I have just learned that the enemies are approaching. I cannot resolve to fight their forces."
I venture to hope that all the magistrates will forgive me for this and not hold it against me as a crime, and will permit my wretched person to seek secret refuge amidst the marshes.

Thus, Bālāditya surrendered his capital to the enemy without a fight and withdrew into inaccessible terrain; Mihiragula pursued him, fell into an ambush, and was captured. However, Bālāditya was not the man to utilize this stroke of fortune with wisdom.

At the instigation of his mother, who was enamored of that stately man, he not only spared this dangerous predator his life, but even granted him his freedom. Since his own throne at Sākala had meanwhile been seized by his brother, Mihiragula departed for Kaśmīra, where he was received with hospitality by the king.

He treacherously murdered his benefactor and seized the sovereignty of the land. This was followed by the terrible campaign against Gandhāra (see above, p. 274). Not long thereafter, according to Buddhist tradition, he died.

According to Xuanzang—though some reservations have been raised against his report—there was first a Yaśodharman of Mālava, whose origins and descendants are otherwise unknown; perhaps a *homo novus*, as the confusion [suggests].

1. Cosmas Indicopleustes (see below) tells of Gollas, king of the White Huns and overlord of India, from whose lands he extorted tribute by virtue of his two thousand war elephants and his immense cavalry force.
Appendix III, 278.

After the fall of the Gupta Empire, [Yaśodharman] wished to bring to the surface his own achievements, which he boasts of on a pillar inscription: having united a confederacy of Indian princes and, with them, having defeated the Hūṇa Mihirakula. There appears to be no doubt regarding the authenticity of this inscription; however, Bālāditya is not mentioned therein.

Furthermore, Xuanzang knows nothing of allies for the latter, and thus these two accounts might perhaps be reconciled with one another. When Mihiragula attacked Bālāditya, he was at the height of his power, and no one dared to oppose him.

When, by that unfortunate turn of events, he lost his throne and consequently his sovereignty over Northern India, he first arrived in Kashmir as a powerless adventurer; and even when he had raised himself to the status of lord of this small land, his power must have remained limited.
This circumstance, along with rumors of his demonic cruelty in Gandhāra, likely provided the occasion for that confederacy under Yaśodharman.

One now tends to dismiss the entire report of the Chinese pilgrim as legendary, but this seems to go too far. That Mihiragula was king of Kaśmīra we also learn from Kalhaṇa; the cities of Mihireśvara and Mihirapura, founded by him in Kaśmīra, bore witness to his name (Rājat. I, 306).

At the time of Kalhaṇa, those three hundred thousand noble men whom the king had caused to be massacred by him on the Indus according to the account of the pilgrim, had increased to thirty million; Kalhaṇa calls him *trikoṭihan* and states in I.322: "Then, in his fury, the king slaughtered three crores of women of respectable birth, together with their husbands, brothers, and sons."
According to I, 315, after slaying the inhabitants of Āryadeśa, he granted one thousand agrahāras at Vijayeśvara in Kashmir to Brāhmaṇas from Gandhāra.

Since his conflict had been directed against the Buddhists, while the Brāhmaṇas were deprived of their revenues due to the devastation of their country, it is understandable that he sought to compensate them in his own land.
Pathak (IA 47, p. 19), following a Jaina source that refers to the tyrant as Kalkirāja, places the lifetime of Mihiragula in the year 279; the word *nāṇe* is Persian and means "sunflower."

472–542 is calculated; he must have come to power in 502. In *Rājatarangiṇī* I, 309 it says: "after ruling the land for seventy years"; here, there appears to be a confusion between the duration of his reign and his total lifespan.

The pilgrim had heard the brief account of Bālāditya and Mihiragula mentioned above while in Sākala, the former capital of the latter. Furthermore, at the great Buddhist university of Nālandā Vihāra, which was in its peak of prosperity during the seventh century, he learned another story concerning Bālāditya.

However, what he relates here casts doubt upon whether these refer to the same individual. This Bālāditya built a magnificent monastery at Nālandā and subsequently entered it himself as a novice; yet, he could not endure having to accept the lowest seat as the youngest member.

He complained about this to his superiors, who were wise enough to take his sensitivities into account. They ordered that in their monastery, the novices should sit according to their actual age rather than the date of their entry into the order. This custom persisted until the time of Xuanzang:
"It is for this reason that this monastery is the only one where such a regulation exists."
The pilgrim names the three successive ancestors of this Bālāditya, who had likewise each founded a monastery at Nālandā. They were, in ascending order: Tathāgatagupta, Buddhagupta, and Śakrāditya.

In this regard, a grave error has been committed by him or his authorities, which—if correctly transmitted—would cast the Indians' lack of historical sense into sharp relief: Sakrāditya lived shortly after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*. However, it is certain that the foundation of the Nālandā Vihāra at the time of Xuanzang was a relatively recent event.

It is not mentioned anywhere in the Jātakas, nor indeed in the Pāli Tripiṭaka; at this point, one finds there only the village of Nālandagrāma, where Sāriputta was born and died. Likewise, even according to Faxian, who traveled through this region around 400 CE (p. 81), it says: "One yojana to the southwest..."

He brought them to the village of Nāla, where Śāriputra was born, and to which he also returned, and where he attained his *parinirvāṇa*. Over that spot [where his body was cremated], there was... [Anhang III 280]

A stūpa, which still exists today. Regarding Nāla, Legge provides the following note: "Or Nālandā; identified with the present Baragong. A grand monastery was subsequently built there, famous for being the place where Xuanzang resided for five years."

The name Tathāgatagupta appears to have been chosen in opposition to the Śaivite kings Skandagupta and Kumāragupta of the Gupta dynasty’s past; likewise, Buddhagupta—if this name is not a misreading of Budhagupta ("protected by Mercury"), who is attested in inscriptions from the last quarter of the fifth century.

If the aforementioned names possess historical value, they must refer to a collateral branch of the later Guptas who held some insignificant dominion somewhere in India and presented themselves as patrons of Buddhism— much like that king of Central India of whom Hsüan-tsang relates that he enclosed all the monasteries within a high wall and consolidated them together.

More serious is another chronological inconsistency. V. Smith⁴ assigns the reign of Bālāditya-Narasiṃhagupta to approximately 467–473 CE. However, we have two pieces of evidence that Mihiragula was still in possession of Gandhāra around 520 CE.

Cosmas Indicopleustes, whose *Topographia Christiana* was written in 547, encountered him during his travels—which must have taken place around that time—as still a powerful sovereign of North India; he calls him Gollas.

The Chinese monk Seng-yun, who arrived in India in 520 CE, speaks of the king of Gandhāra—though unfortunately without naming him—but from his report we can see that the devastation of the country described by Xuanzang had not yet occurred at that time.

However, upon closer examination, it becomes evident that the aforementioned figures for Narasiṃhagupta rest on very weak foundations; nevertheless, the gap between the two sets of data is too great to be bridged by our current knowledge.
We must await new discoveries of inscriptions or literary texts to achieve clarity in this matter.

S. Lévi will likely no longer maintain his identification of Candragomin with I-tsing’s Candradāsa, despite the defense offered by Finot in the same volume (pp. 681 ff.). This was already noted by Kern (*Manual of Indian Buddhism*, p. 130, note 2¹, Appendix III).

I have pointed out that Dharmakīrti flourished between the period of Hiuen-tsang’s stay in India and that of I-tsing, who indeed mentions him by name. Dharmakīrti was the last great theologian produced by Indian Buddhism, whereas the generation surrounding Candragomin, Candrakīrti, and Dignāga represents the highest flowering of Buddhist scholasticism.
In that case, the two would coincide in time, which is impossible.
I conclude this somewhat lengthy discussion with a verse attributed by tradition to Dharmakīrti (*Tāranātha*, p. 181):
"In wisdom, he was a Dignāga; in purity of speech, a Candragomin; and in the metrics of the poet Śūra, who [could]..."

Am I different from the Conqueror of All Quarters (*digjaitra*)? By *Śūra*, no one other than Āryaśūra, the author of the *Jātakamālā*, can be intended—he who lived at least three hundred years prior to Dharmakīrti. Clearly, the verse intends to state that he was not inferior to these renowned giants of the past.

I believe we can express ourselves somewhat more definitively regarding certain points in I-tsing’s exceedingly valuable report than Takakusu does. We must bear in mind that I-tsing studied at Nālandā for ten years and personally knew, for the most part with great precision, the works he describes and recommends to his compatriots; furthermore, almost all of these works still exist today.

I. The *Si-t'an-chang* (*Siddha-paddhati*) for Beginners. The first section was titled *siddhir astu*. It taught the forty-nine letters of the alphabet and their combinations. It was intended for boys of six years of age; the duration of instruction was six months.

This appears to be a primer for reading and writing, also mentioned by Hiuen-tsang (I, 166). Takakusu states in his scholarly notes: "I-tsing may be referring to the *śivasūtra*. However, what would beginners have to do with the *śivasūtra*s? This was merely a desperate suggestion by Max Müller, prompted by I-tsing’s remark: [text fragment].

This is said to have been originally taught by the deity Maheśvara; however, he evidently confuses the *Brahmarāśi* with the *Śivasūtra* due to their shared content, perhaps under the influence of the well-known verse beginning: *yenākṣarasamāmnāyam adhigamya Maheśvarāt*, etc. (III.282).

By a fortunate coincidence, we have preserved something very similar—if not identical—to the elementary primer used at that time. Halhed, the first Englishman who attempted to learn Sanskrit, describes the book used for his instruction (see *A Grammar of the Bengal Language*, Hugly, 1778, p. 24). It began: *Siddhir astu!*;
*a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au am aḥ*, etc.

II. The *Pāṇinīya-sūtra* and III. the *Dhātupāṭha*, each consisting of approximately 1,000 *ślokas*. Since the extent of the former is very accurately stated [by Pāṇini]—being 956 *ślokas* according to Takakusu’s own count—whereas the latter, in the version of Bhīmasena, is only about 300 *ślokas* long, it appears that in the instruction of that time, the latter was accompanied by a brief commentary, a precursor to those of Kṣīrasvāmin and Maitreya.

IV. The Book on the Three *Khilas*. The term *khilapāṭha* is also used in the same or a similar sense in *Kāśikā* I, 3, 2. From I-tsing’s description, the character of these grammatical auxiliary texts can be recognized with sufficient clarity.
The first, *Aṣṭadhātu*, was a collection of declensional and conjugational paradigms as they appear in each of the Indian grammatical systems and also in the Tanjur.

The second, whose name (*Wench’a*, after Xuanzang’s transcription *Mentsékia*) has not yet been interpreted, was—according to I-tsing’s description—clearly a compilation of regular stem formation, a systematic extract from the *Sūtrapāṭha* and the *Vṛtti*. The name...

The third [the *uṇādi*] speaks for itself. V. The *Vṛtti-sūtra* (*Kāśikāvṛtti*): This work was particularly warmly recommended by I-tsing to his compatriots—and rightly so—stating that if those from China go to India for study, they must first master this work before proceeding to other subjects; otherwise, their labor will be wasted. Therefore, it is certain that he himself also studied it thoroughly.
Since he says nothing regarding the incompleteness of the *Kāśikā* (otherwise it likely would not have been used in formal instruction), its length is [as follows]—Appendix III, p. 283.

Since he correctly identifies [the author], it can already be inferred from this that the entire work was at his disposal; in other words, Vāmana, the author of the *Kāśikā*, is not identical with the minister and poet of the same name who lived in Kashmir one hundred years after I-tsing. Takakusu takes some offense at I-tsing’s expression:

It reveals the laws of the universe and the regulations of gods and men. Since he has already previously discussed the subsequent grammatical purpose of the work (citing the text of the *sūtra* and explaining its manifold meaning in detail), that remark can likely refer only to the content of the examples, which are indeed so abundant.
It is well-chosen that, as is well known, even Albrecht Weber attempted to draw a "cultural portrait according to Pāṇini" in the first volume of the *Indische Studien*.

Belvalkar (*Systems*, p. 35) takes issue with I-tsing’s use of *vṛttisūtra* instead of *sūtravṛtti* and criticizes him for not mentioning Vāmana as a collaborator. As far as I-tsing’s purpose was concerned, the latter was certainly superfluous; regarding the inversion of the compound, I would say:

I am not surprised by such minor lapses; rather, I marvel at the manner in which Chinese students in India have solved the difficult task of bringing home to their compatriots—who know nothing of morphology from their own mother tongue—the essence of an inflected language, that is, one whose structure is so entirely different.

The aforementioned shift appears to indicate that I-tsing lacked certainty regarding the mutual relationship between the governing and governed members of a Sanskrit compound. Indeed, Tibetan—whose grammar was fashioned after Indian models—presents us with cases of precisely this nature. The title of No. [ ]...

In the Tanjur, the title of No. 3723 reads: *Ka·la·pa·dha·tu·sū·tra* (in Tibetan: *ka·lā 'pai byiṅs kyi mdo*), while the title of No. 3724 reads: *sū·tra·dha·tu* (in Tibetan: *byiṅs kyi mdo*). Here too, we see that the components of the compound have been transposed within the second Indian name;
the translator takes no notice of this, and rightly so.

VI. The *Cūrṇi*. That this is merely another name for the *Mahābhāṣya*, which is otherwise well known, was already pointed out by Max Müller in the third appendix (*p. 284*) of his *Record of the Buddhist Religion as Practised in India and the Malay Archipelago* (1896). His description of this work is brief yet accurate: "Next, there is a commentary on the *Vṛttisūtra* entitled *Cūrṇi*, containing 24,000 *ślokas*. It is a work of the learned Patañjali."

Furthermore, this work cites the former *sūtra* (of Pāṇini), explaining its obscure points and analyzing the principles contained therein, while illustrating the latter commentary (*vṛtti*), clearing away many difficulties.

Belvalkar criticizes I-tsing for referring to the *Cūrṇi* as a commentary on the *Vṛtti-sūtra* (read *Sūtra-vṛtti*), and based on this and the reasons mentioned under V, he goes so far as to make the startling statement: "I-tsing’s account of the *vṛttisūtra* by Jayāditya may, after all, not refer to the *Kāśikā*."

One might be content to point out that if one first studies the *Kāśikā* and then the *Bhāṣya*, this interpretation appears very plausible; indeed, difficult passages in the *Vṛtti* are clarified by the discursive treatment found in the *Bhāṣya*.
But has not I-tsing essentially grasped the matter as well? It must be emphasized again and again that the actual core of grammar is not the *sūtra*, but rather the *vṛtti*.

This is a work in which the meaning of the *sūtras* is primary (*sūtrārthapradhānaḥ granthaḥ*, according to Haradatta); that is, each individual *sūtra* is more like a mnemonic heading or keyword belonging to the corresponding section of the *vṛtti*, in which the *sūtra* is indeed contained in full. How often does the discussion in the *Mahābhāṣya* begin with the question: "What is the example? (*kim udāharaṇam*)?

However, according to the Bhāṣya on page 11 of the first [chapter], the example (*udāharaṇa*), the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), and the supplementation of the sentence (*vākyādhyāhāra*) constitute the essential components of the *vṛtti*.
This *vṛtti*, or running commentary, must in its original form always have been conceived by the author of the *sūtras* (*sūtrakāra*) himself, either prior to or simultaneously with the *sūtra*.

The *Bhāṣya*, however—the critical commentary—is always the work of another who seeks to critically establish and, where necessary, further develop the system created by the *Sūtrakāra*, just as the *Vārttikakāra* or *Vākyakāra* does; it follows implicitly from this that the *Bhāṣya* addresses only those *sūtras* where its author or the *Vākyakāra* finds occasion for critical remarks or supplementary additions. (285 Appendix III)

From several quarters, the question has been raised as to why I-tsing does not mention Candragomin in his report, and various unfounded conjectures have been attached to it. The reason is not difficult to discern.
I-tsing did not go to India to pursue literary historical-linguistic studies, but solely with the motive of thoroughly mastering the Sanskrit language for the purpose of translation;
these circumstances have recently been insufficiently noted by a younger scholar who has already established a reputation in the academic world through other works.
(Appendix III, p. 286)

Regarding the translation of Buddhist scriptures into Chinese (cf. his remarks on pp. 168 and 169), his studies—apart from brief preparatory stays in Bhoja (Sumatra) and Tāmralipti, which were primarily intended for the practical mastery of the Indian language—were conducted exclusively at Nālandā.

The university there was not merely a Buddhist college, but more resembled a true *universitas litterarum* where all branches of scientific learning were taught. Consequently, the grammatical system prevailing there was naturally that of Pāṇini; and as for what I-tsing reports regarding the scholarly acquisition of the Indian high language (*saṃskṛta*)...

Therefore, the report refers exclusively to the textual manuals used within that school. Whatever was new in Candragomin’s own grammar in terms of its content had been incorporated into the *Kāśikā*; consequently, following the appearance of this work, there was no further need for the study of the *Cāndravyākaraṇa* alongside Pāṇini, except among specialized grammarians.

In his *Dhātupāṭha*, Śākaṭāyana reorders Pāṇini’s seventh and eighth classes, while inserting the ninth class between the fifth and sixth; consequently, the tenth class follows immediately after the seventh.

A glance at the synopsis provides the best orientation regarding the general arrangement. Within the classes, the primary principle of division here, as with Candragomin, is the genus of the verb. However, while the standard sequence in Candra (and Hemacandra) is as follows:

Active, middle, and common-voice; Śākaṭāyana (following the ancient method) places the middle voices first, which is particularly evident in the first class. Since he marks middle verbs ending in a consonant with the *anubandha* *i*, and those ending in a vowel with *ṅ*—just as Pāṇini does—he refers to the middle [voices]...
[Anhang III 288]

To summarize the roots: those with the marker *ṅ* or *it* are designated as *ṅiditaḥ*; those that are both [active and middle] accordingly as *ñīditaḥ* (*ñ* denotes those ending in a vowel, like Pāṇini’s *ubhayapadins*, while *ī* denotes those ending in a consonant); and by elimination, those that are active are *aṅiññīditaḥ*. If another marker-vowel (*anubandha*) follows a consonantal root, that root is also treated as if it were vocalic;
for example, *edhi* [is treated as vocalic], but *gādhṛṅ* [is treated as consonantal]; likewise, *hikkī* [is treated as vocalic], but *dhāvūñ* [is treated as consonantal], just like *veñ*.
The meanings added by Bhīmasena are not reduced to a single sense each as in the case of Candra, but are generally fully represented.

Introduction to Appendix IV: The Date of Maitreyarakṣita It must first be established that neither Kṣīrasvāmin mentions Maitreya’s work, nor does Maitreya mention the *Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī*; thus, it is probable that he was not even aware of it. This suggests *a priori* that both works were composed approximately at the same time, though not in close geographical proximity.

The lower limit for the *Dhātupradīpa* is the *Durghaṭavṛtti* composed by Śaraṇadeva in 1172, who cites it approximately eighty times and even three times refers to a *Dhātupradīpaṭīkā*, a super-commentary on Maitreya’s work.

We determine the upper limit through Maitreya’s mention by Kaiyaṭa, provided that Kaiyaṭa was indeed the brother of Mammaṭa, as the Kaśmīrian paṇḍits relate. De (Sanskrit Poetics I, p. 160) places the latter in the last quarter of the eleventh century.
Consequently, Chakravarti, the editor of the *Dhātupradīpa*, dates the author’s time to approximately 1100 A.D.

If I believe that the *Dhātupradīpa* must be dated somewhat later, it is for the following reasons: the aforementioned Śaraṇadeva frequently cites (more than forty times) the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* of Puruṣottamadeva, who in turn does not mention Maitreya.

He composed this work at the request of King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal, who ascended the throne in 1119 according to Kielhorn and lost it to the Arabs in 1194; his exceptionally long reign is emphasized by both Indian and Muslim sources.

If the *Dhātupradīpa* had been composed prior to 1120, it would likely not have remained unknown to Puruṣottama, as both lived in Bengal. Kaiyaṭa was a Kashmiri and is said to have composed the *Bhāṣyapradīpa* in Vārāṇasī.

The timeframe for the dissemination of the work from Vārāṇasī or Kaśmīr to Bengal seems somewhat too short according to Chakravarti’s proposal, given that Śaraṇadeva—in 1172—shows no knowledge of Kṣīrasvāmin’s literary activity, even though that work had already been in existence for approximately forty years by then.

The author of the *Puruṣakāra* (Trivandrum Sanskrit Series 1), who lived in the thirteenth century, then cites both Kṣīrasvāmin and Maitreyarakṣita equally, just as Sāyaṇa does in the fourteenth century. Appendix IV, 361.

Saraṇadeva is, according to the plausible conjecture of Chakravarti (*Bhāṣāvṛtti* Introduction, p. 7), identical with the *śaraṇa* at the court of Lakṣmaṇasena, concerning whom Pischel treated in his well-known monograph: *Die Hofdichter des Lakṣmaṇasena* (1894). This refers to the obscure passage in Jayadeva’s *Gītagovinda* I.4: [The text continues with the verse: *śrījayadevakaveridam matam madhuripor madhurādharapānavidhau śaraṇam...* (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the context established by the introduction.)

The fact that Śaraṇa reveals himself as a Buddhist in his grammatical work—just as Maitreya and Puruṣottamadeva do—while simultaneously composing verses on Kṛṣṇa as court poet to a Vaiṣṇava king, does not contradict this identification. Just as Buddhism coexisted with Śaivism in Kashmir, it did so with Vaiṣṇavism in Bengal.

Nevertheless, there remained a distinction: in Kashmir, it was always merely tolerated with friendliness alongside the state-recognized Śiva cult, whereas in the East, it was sometimes equal in status and at other times even dominant. The link between the worship of Viṣṇu and the Buddha was the recognition of the Buddha as an *avatāra* of Viṣṇu (cf. also Bühler Report, p. 41).

The Bengali school of poets met with a shameful and barbaric end—a fact which Pischel has omitted to mention—through the audacious coup of Muhammad ibn Bakhtiyār, who in 1194 entered Nadīyā (Nuddea) with a small retinue and gained unhindered access to the palace courtyard; for the small band, which likely brought replacement horses with them, was not suspected.

They stayed there, posing as horse-dealers. Upon arriving, they drew their concealed weapons and struck down whoever stood in their way. The elderly king, caught by surprise while sitting peacefully at his meal, fled in distress through a side gate, and the capital was utterly destroyed by the pursuing army.

A year earlier, that same adventurer had overthrown the Buddhist Pāla kingdom in Bihar; according to the *Tabaqāt-i-Nāṣirī*, the "shaven-headed Brahmins"—that is, the Buddhist monks—were so utterly exterminated that no one remained capable of explaining the contents of the books in the monastic library of Bihar (cf.).
(Elliot, *History of India as Told by Its Own Historians*, Vol.

II, p. 306). The news of the fall of Bihār caused great consternation in the neighboring lands, and most of Lakṣmaṇasena’s brahmins and courtiers abandoned the court and departed for other countries; however, the king could not bring himself to follow their example. Regarding him, the author of the *Tabaqāt* reports:

He was a great king who sat upon the throne for eighty years. When his father departed from this world, he was still within his mother’s womb; therefore, the crown was placed upon her belly, and all the great men of the realm swore their fealty before her.

His family was honored by all the Rajas of Hindustan and held the highest rank (being regarded as holding the status of a Caliph, or sovereign). When the time of his birth drew near and the labor had already begun, his mother assembled the astrologers and Brahmins so that they might investigate whether the aspect of the hour was auspicious.

They declared that a child born at this hour would become very unhappy and would not attain the throne; however, if the birth were to take place two hours later, the child would rule for eighty years.
When his mother heard this assessment, she had her legs bound together and caused herself to be suspended with her head downward. She then commanded the astrologers to observe the auspicious moment.

When they announced that the time for delivery had arrived, she was helped down from the throne, and Lakhmaṇīya was born immediately; however, as soon as he was born, his mother died from the agony she had endured. Lakhmaṇīya was then placed upon the throne. (Appendix IV, 363)

He reigned for eighty years. Reliable persons say that no one, whether high or low, ever suffered injustice at his hands. The author further adds that Lakṣmaṇasena fled to Oḍḍiyāna (Orissa) and died there shortly thereafter. What a poignant picture of a great culture, yet one tainted by Buddhist pacifism!
In addition to the *Dhātupradīpa*, Maitreyarakṣita also composed a *Tantrapradīpa* (the title of his works likely modeled after Kaiyaṭa’s *Bhāṣyapradīpa*).
The *Tantrapradīpa* is a commentary on Jinendrabuddhi’s *Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā*; since that work is commonly cited simply as the *Nyāsa*, the super-commentary is also known as the *Anunyāsa*.
What De (History of Sanskrit Poetics I, p. 47) says regarding Jinendrabuddhi, citing Trivedī and Jacobi, is entirely mistaken.

In Gewiṣ 6, some later systems also appended a *nyāsa* to their respective works following the model of the Pāṇinīyas—such as the *Śiṣyahitānyāsa* for the *Kātantra*, the *Śākaṭāyananyāsa*, the *Kṣapaṇakamahānyāsa*, and the *Bodhinyāsa*—yet none of these is ever simply referred to as "the *Nyāsa*" except perhaps where the context precludes any possible misunderstanding.

The *Nyāsa* par excellence is always the famous work of Jinendrabuddhi, who is cited repeatedly throughout the period prior to 1100 CE, whereas I am not aware of any citation of the *Padamañjarī* before 1200 CE. Jinendra’s date has been established by his editor as 725–750 CE.

He does not cite predecessors, merely occasionally lamenting textual corruption in the *Kāśikā* caused by poor scribes (*kulekhaka*), and he is likely the very first commentator on the *Kāśikā*. 13) It is pointed out that, according to the tradition of the Kaśmīrian paṇḍitas, there existed in ancient times a Buddhist settlement at Huṣkapura—present-day Uṣkar near Bāramūla in Kaśmīr—to which Jinendrabuddhi, the commentator on the *Kāśikāvṛtti*, also belonged.
That Jinendra was a Buddhist is confirmed by his designation as *Bodhisattvadeśīyācārya* in the colophons of his work.

The two extant European manuscripts of the *Dhātupradīpa*, housed in the India Office Library, originate from the legacy of T. H. Colebrooke and represent two distinct recensions that differ continuously, though more in terms of wording than of meaning.
The text of the edition by Chakravarti agrees with the recension of manuscript 649, and it appears to agree also with that used by Sāyaṇa.

Precisely because of these textual discrepancies, it was not possible to produce a satisfactory edition from these two manuscripts; thus, the appearance of the *Dhātupradīpa* in the Varendra Research Society was most welcome to me at the very moment when I required it.

Between Kṣīrasvāmin and Maitreya on the one hand, and Sāyaṇa on the other, there appears to have been no significant commentator on the *Pāṇinīya-Dhātupāṭha* thereafter, as Sāyaṇa consistently addresses these two authorities first and foremost.
That Sāyaṇa is not identical with Mādhava, as Burnell suggested, is evident from verse 13 of the introductory *Praśasti*: "by that wise Sāyaṇa, the son of Māyaṇa..."
This commentary on the roots (*dhātuvṛtti*) is composed under the title *Mādhavīyā*.
We learn from verse 6 of the introduction to his commentary on the *Parāśarasmṛti* that Mādhava was the elder brother of Sāyaṇa. (Appendix 1Y, p. 365)
"His mother was Śrīmatī, his father was the renowned Māyaṇa,
and his two uterine brothers were Sāyaṇa and Bhoganātha, who were his mind and intellect.
And from verse 9 of the introduction to the *Taittirīyasaṃhitābhāṣya*:
He said to the king: "O King, my younger brother, the noble Sāyaṇa, knows everything; let him be appointed to the task of commenting upon the Vedas.

Thus, Sāyaṇa gave the name *Mādhavīya-Dhātuvṛtti* to his own commentary on verbal roots in honor of his elder brother, likely with reference to the latter’s *Jaiminīya-Nyāyamālāvistara*, because of the high status accorded to the verb (*dhātu*) by the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* over other parts of speech.

The authors of the *Kaumudīs* have incorporated the text of the *Dhātupāṭha*—in the version revised by Bhīmasena, which also serves as the basis for the *Mādhavīya-Dhātuvṛtti*—into their *Uttarārdha*.

The two editions of the *Siddhāntakaumudī* published by the Nirṇaya-Sāgar Press—the highly accurate text edition of 1885 and the commented version of 1899—furthermore provide the text of the *Dhātupāṭha* separately within the *Pariśiṣṭas*. I have pointed out their clear dependence on Sāyaṇa in the introduction, section III § 3, and in the notes to my printed edition (ibid.).
